title: Act 8: SOLA as an Inversion in Disguise | My Take on SOLA | Adrian Mag
desc: Act 8 of My Take on SOLA: Examining the resolution control pillar. SOLA's resolving kernels are target kernels passed through the adjoint of a resolution operator, not a new kind of resolution, but the same operator viewed from the other side.
text: Act 8: SOLA as an Inversion in Disguise The second pillar under examination: resolving kernels are target kernels through an adjoint resolution operator. Part of My Take on SOLA . « Overview 1 The Kernel Game 2 Building SOLA 3 Averages Need Mass 4 Beyond Averages 5 Noise Enters 6 What Did SOLA Estimate? 7 Cautionary Tale 8 Inversion in Disguise 9 Uncertainty 10 What SOLA Is Good For The Second Pillar: Resolution Control The previous act tested the first pillar of SOLA, the claim that no prior information is needed. We showed that the absence of a prior is not a free lunch: it leaves the interpretation gap between resolved properties and true target properties unbounded. The method was not broken, but a boundary was found. Now we turn to the second pillar: resolution control . SOLA is often presented as offering something that classical linear inversion does not, direct, user-designed control over resolution through the choice of target kernels. Instead of accepting whatever resolution operator a standard inversion happens to produce, the practitioner specifies what kind of localized average or property they want, and SOLA builds the closest resolving kernel the data can support. This is an attractive feature, and it is real. But how different is it, fundamentally, from what classical inversion has been doing all along? What follows is not an attack on resolution control. It is an examination of what that control actually amounts to, and a reminder that the resolving kernels SOLA produces are not a new kind of object. They are target kernels passed through a resolution operator, viewed from a different angle. The Proxy Model From data map to proxy model One of the standard ways to describe SOLA is to say that it avoids reconstructing the whole model. This is a good description of the practical workflow. SOLA does not ask us to first build a model estimate \(\hat m\) and then evaluate its properties. It goes directly from data to properties: \(\widetilde{\mathbf p} = \widetilde{\mathbf X}_c\widetilde{\mathbf d}.\) But algebra has a habit of opening side doors. For the constrained SOLA operator, the estimate can also be written in the form \[\widetilde{\mathbf p} = \widetilde{\mathbf X}_c\widetilde{\mathbf d} = \Tau(\hat m),\] for a particular model \(\hat m\in\M\), provided that the calibration pairs \((\mathbf v_\ell,\mathbf w_\ell)\) are jointly realizable by some \(f_\ell\in\M\) satisfying \(G(f_\ell)=\mathbf v_\ell\) and \(\Tau(f_\ell)=\mathbf w_\ell\). This is automatic when the constraints are built from test models \(q_\ell\) (take \(f_\ell=q_\ell\)), but for arbitrarily prescribed \((\mathbf V,\mathbf W)\) such \(f_\ell\) need not exist. The proxy model \(\hat m\) is not the true model. It is constructed from the data and from the same ingredients that define the SOLA operator. So there are two equivalent ways to read the same number: \(\widetilde{\mathbf p} = \widetilde{\mathbf X}_c\widetilde{\mathbf d}\) as a direct data-to-property estimate, or \(\widetilde{\mathbf p} = \Tau(\hat m)\) as the exact target property of a particular proxy model. Intuition SOLA walks past the front door of model reconstruction, but the algebra leaves a side entrance open. This does not make SOLA bad. It makes SOLA more interpretable, and more familiar. The proxy model shows what kind of model-side representative is hiding behind the data-to-property map. As we shall see, that representative is not so different from the one hiding behind classical inversion. Let \(\mathbf M:=GG^*+\mathbf C_D,\; \mathbf U:=\mathbf M^{-1}\mathbf V,\; \boldsymbol\Gamma:=\mathbf V^*\mathbf U.\) Recall that the constrained noise-aware SOLA operator is \[\widetilde{\mathbf X}_c = \Tau G^*\mathbf M^{-1} - (\Tau G^*\mathbf U-\mathbf W)\boldsymbol\Gamma^{-1}\mathbf U^*.\] Apply this operator to the observed data: \[\widetilde{\mathbf X}_c\widetilde{\mathbf d} = \Tau G^*\mathbf M^{-1}\widetilde{\mathbf d} - (\Tau G^*\mathbf U-\mathbf W)\boldsymbol\Gamma^{-1}\mathbf U^*\widetilde{\mathbf d}.\] Define the coefficient vector \(\mathbf c := \boldsymbol\Gamma^{-1}\mathbf U^*\widetilde{\mathbf d}\in\mathbb R^L.\) Then \[\widetilde{\mathbf X}_c\widetilde{\mathbf d} = \Tau G^*\mathbf M^{-1}\widetilde{\mathbf d} - (\Tau G^*\mathbf U-\mathbf W)\mathbf c.\] If we can find models \(f_1,\dots,f_L\in\M\) satisfying \(G(f_\ell)=\mathbf v_\ell,\; \Tau(f_\ell)=\mathbf w_\ell,\; \ell=1,\dots,L,\) then \(\mathbf W\mathbf c = \sum_{\ell=1}^L c_\ell\,\mathbf w_\ell = \sum_{\ell=1}^L c_\ell\,\Tau(f_\ell) = \Tau\!\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^L c_\ell f_\ell\right),\) and similarly \(\Tau G^*\mathbf U\,\mathbf c = \Tau\!\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^L c_\ell\, G^*\mathbf u_\ell\right),\) where \(\mathbf u_\ell\) are the columns of \(\mathbf U\). Therefore \[\widetilde{\mathbf X}_c\widetilde{\mathbf d} = \Tau\!\left( G^*\mathbf M^{-1}\widetilde{\mathbf d} + \sum_{\ell=1}^L c_\ell\bigl(f_\ell - G^*\mathbf u_\ell\bigr) \right).\] This motivates the definition \[\hat m := G^*\mathbf M^{-1}\widetilde{\mathbf d} + \sum_{\ell=1}^L c_\ell\bigl(f_\ell - G^*\mathbf u_\ell\bigr), \qquad \mathbf c=\boldsymbol\Gamma^{-1}\mathbf U^*\widetilde{\mathbf d}.\] Then \(\widetilde{\mathbf p} = \widetilde{\mathbf X}_c\widetilde{\mathbf d} = \Tau(\hat m).\) Checkpoint The constrained SOLA estimate can be interpreted as the exact target property of a proxy model \(\hat m\), provided the calibration pairs are jointly realizable in \(\M\). This statement should be handled carefully. It does not say \(\hat m=\bar m.\) It only says that the SOLA property estimate can be factored through one particular model-space representative. The proxy formula Let us inspect the proxy model: \[\hat m = G^*\mathbf M^{-1}\widetilde{\mathbf d} + \sum_{\ell=1}^L c_\ell\bigl(f_\ell - G^*\mathbf u_\ell\bigr).\] It has two pieces. The first piece is \(G^*\mathbf M^{-1}\widetilde{\mathbf d}.\) This resembles a regularized or noise-weighted back-projection of the data into the model space. It is the model-space object produced by taking the data, weighting them by \(\mathbf M^{-1}\), and applying the adjoint \(G^*\). The second piece is \(\sum_{\ell=1}^L c_\ell\bigl(f_\ell - G^*\mathbf u_\ell\bigr).\) This is the correction associated with the resolving constraints \(\widetilde{\mathbf X}_c\mathbf V=\mathbf W.\) The coefficient vector \(\mathbf c=\boldsymbol\Gamma^{-1}\mathbf U^*\widetilde{\mathbf d}\) depends on the data, while the model-space directions \(f_\ell - G^*\mathbf u_\ell\) depend on the constraints. The functions \(f_\ell\in\M\) are chosen so that \(G(f_\ell)=\mathbf v_\ell,\; \Tau(f_\ell)=\mathbf w_\ell.\) For averaging constraints, this says that each \(f_\ell\) has the desired data response to the corresponding test model and the desired property response. In the simplest average-preserving case, the \(f_\ell\) play the role of model-space representatives that make the constraints visible inside \(\Tau\). Remark: Non-uniqueness of \(f_\ell\) The functions \(f_\ell\) need not be unique. If \(f_\ell\) and \(f_\ell'\) both satisfy the conditions for a given \(\ell\), their difference lies in the joint nullspace \(f_\ell-f_\ell'\in\kernel(G)\cap\kernel(\Tau).\) Changing \(f_\ell\) by such a direction changes the proxy model, but not its data response or target property. This is another reminder that the proxy model is not a unique physical truth. In the noise-free case, where \(\mathbf C_D=\mathbf 0,\;\text{and hence}\; \mathbf M=GG^*,\) we have \(G(G^*\mathbf u_\ell) = GG^*(GG^*)^{-1}\mathbf v_\ell = \mathbf v_\ell.\) Since \(G(f_\ell)=\mathbf v_\ell\), each correction direction satisfies \(G\bigl(G^*\mathbf u_\ell-f_\ell\bigr)=\mathbf 0.\) Thus, in the noise-free constrained case, each correction lives in the nullspace of \(G\). In the noise-aware case, the situation is slightly different. Since \(\mathbf M=GG^*+\mathbf C_D,\) we have \(GG^*\mathbf u_\ell = \mathbf v_\ell-\mathbf C_D\mathbf u_\ell.\) Therefore \(G\bigl(G^*\mathbf u_\ell-f_\ell\bigr) = -\mathbf C_D\mathbf u_\ell.\) So the corrections are not generally exact nullspace corrections when data noise is included. Rather, they are noise-weighted corrections tied to the SOLA objective. Warning In the noise-free constrained case, the proxy correction is a true nullspace correction. In the noise-aware case, it is better interpreted as a correction relative to the noise-weighted SOLA geometry. This distinction matters because it prevents us from saying something too strong. The proxy model is a useful algebraic representative, not a magical recovery of the true model. The meaning of the proxy The proxy model \(\hat m\) is not claimed to be the true model. It is one model-space object whose target property equals the SOLA estimate: \(\Tau(\hat m)=\widetilde{\mathbf p}.\) This gives a second interpretation of SOLA: \[\text{direct view:} \qquad \widetilde{\mathbf p} = \widetilde{\mathbf X}_c\widetilde{\mathbf d},\] and \[\text{proxy-model view:} \qquad \widetilde{\mathbf p} = \Tau(\hat m).\] The direct view is the standard SOLA story. It emphasizes that the method avoids a full model reconstruction. The proxy-model view emphasizes that the same data-to-property map can be factored through a particular model-space representative. Both views are useful. The first explains why SOLA is computationally attractive. The second explains why SOLA is not entirely separate from classical inversion. If the true model \(\bar m\) is close to the proxy model \(\hat m\), in the geometry relevant to \(\Tau\), then \(\Tau(\bar m)\approx \Tau(\hat m)=\widetilde{\mathbf p}.\) But if \(\bar m\) differs from \(\hat m\) by a direction that is hard for the data to see and easy for \(\Tau\) to see, then \(\Tau(\bar m)\) can be very different from \(\Tau(\hat m).\) Thus the proxy interpretation does not remove the caution from the previous act. It sharpens it. Lesson SOLA may avoid explicitly reconstructing the model, but its algebra often carries an undercover proxy reconstruction. The proxy model is not the villain. It is a useful witness. It tells us what kind of model the SOLA estimate is silently willing to be the property of. Resolving Kernels and Resolution Operators Classical resolution operators In a classical linear inversion, one builds a reconstruction operator \(G^\dagger:\D\to\M.\) Given data \(\mathbf d\in\D\), the reconstructed model is \(\hat m=G^\dagger\mathbf d.\) If the data are noise-free and generated by a true model \(m\), then \(\mathbf d=G(m),\) so the reconstruction is \(\hat m=G^\dagger G(m).\) The composite map \(\mathcal R:=G^\dagger G:\M\to\M\) is called the resolution operator. The resolution operator tells us what the inversion does to the true model: \(m \longmapsto \mathcal R m.\) If \(\mathcal R=I\), then the inversion recovers every model exactly. In finite-data inverse problems, this almost never happens. More commonly, \(\mathcal R\) is a smoothing, filtering, or projection-like operator. Intuition A resolution operator is the fingerprint left by the inverse method on the model. It tells us not what model we wished to recover, but what version of the model the data and method can return. This is the classical resolution story: \[\text{true model} \quad \xrightarrow{\;\mathcal R\;} \quad \text{resolved model}.\] The reconstructed model \(\hat m\) should therefore be interpreted as \(\hat m=\mathcal R m\) in the ideal noise-free case, not automatically as \(m\). This is old knowledge. Classical inversion has carried this scar for decades: the method does not return the true model, it returns a resolved version of it. Everyone who uses least squares or regularized inversion knows this. It is part of the working knowledge of the field. The resolution matrix is a fixture of every inverse-theory course, see Menke [Men18] for the discrete story and Nolet [Nol08] for its life in seismic tomography. SOLA resolving kernels SOLA defines the approximate property map \(\mathcal{A}:=\mathbf XG:\M\to\Pspace.\) For each component, \([\mathcal{A}(m)]_k = (R_k,m)_{\M},\) where \(R_k = \sum_{i=1}^{N_d}[\mathbf X]_{ki}K_i.\) The functions \(R_k\) are the resolving kernels. Thus SOLA has the property-space resolution story \[\text{true model} \quad \xrightarrow{\;\mathcal{A}=\mathbf XG\;} \quad \text{resolved properties}.\] The target map is \(\Tau:\M\to\Pspace.\) If SOLA achieved perfect resolution, then \(\mathcal{A}=\Tau.\) But in general, \(\mathcal{A}\neq\Tau.\) The resolving kernels describe the actual linear questions asked of the model. Here is where the second pillar's claim gets interesting. SOLA is said to offer resolution control : the practitioner chooses target kernels, and the method builds the closest resolving kernels the data can support. This is contrasted with classical inversion, where the resolution operator is whatever the inversion produces, take it or leave it. But is the contrast as sharp as it sounds? Now connect this with the proxy-model view. Suppose there exists a linear reconstruction-like operator \(G^\dagger:\D\to\M\) such that \(\mathbf X=\Tau G^\dagger.\) Then \(\mathcal{A}=\mathbf XG=\Tau G^\dagger G.\) Using the classical resolution operator \(\mathcal R:=G^\dagger G,\) we obtain \(\mathcal{A}=\Tau\mathcal R.\) This identity is the bridge: \[\boxed{\text{SOLA resolving map} = \text{target map after a model-space resolution operator}.}\] Making this bridge precise, and then exploiting it to combine the strengths of both traditions, is the subject of our paper on SOLA and deterministic linear inference [MKZ25] ; this act is its narrative version. At the kernel level, if \([\Tau(m)]_k = (T_k,m)_{\M},\) then \([\mathcal{A}(m)]_k = [\Tau(\mathcal R m)]_k = (T_k,\mathcal R m)_{\M}.\) Using the adjoint \(\mathcal R^*\), \([\mathcal{A}(m)]_k = (\mathcal R^*T_k,m)_{\M}.\) Therefore the resolving kernel is \(R_k = \mathcal R^*T_k.\) This is a revealing formula, when it applies. The SOLA resolving kernel is the target kernel passed through the adjoint of a resolution operator. Not a different kind of resolution. Not a new species of object. The same resolution operator that classical inversion has always carried, just viewed from the other side. The caveat is that this factorization \(\mathbf X=\Tau G^\dagger\) need not hold for every SOLA map; when it does, the bridge formula \(R_k=\mathcal R^*T_k\) is available, and when it does not, the resolving kernels are still well-defined but cannot be written in this compact form. Checkpoint Classical inversion modifies models through \(\mathcal R\). SOLA modifies target kernels through \(\mathcal R^*\). Same operator, different adjoint direction. The shared resolution story So what does the second pillar actually claim, and what does the algebra say? The claim is that SOLA offers better resolution control than classical inversion. Instead of accepting whatever resolution operator the inversion produces, the practitioner designs target kernels and SOLA finds the closest resolving kernels. The resolving kernels are put on the table, inspected, and compared to the targets. This is a genuine practical advantage. But the algebra says: whenever the SOLA map factors as \(\mathbf X=\Tau G^\dagger\), the resolving kernels are not a new kind of object. They are target kernels mapped through the adjoint of a resolution operator. Classical inversion modifies the model through \(\mathcal R\); SOLA modifies the target kernel through \(\mathcal R^*\). The underlying operator is the same. The data geometry, the sensitivity kernels, the noise covariance, these still decide what is reachable. SOLA does not escape the resolution operator. It views it from the adjoint side. We can now compare the two pictures directly. Classical inversion says: \(\mathbf d=G(m),\; \hat m=G^\dagger\mathbf d,\; \hat m=G^\dagger G(m)=\mathcal R m.\) The method does not return \(m\). It returns \(\mathcal R m\). SOLA says: \(\mathbf d=G(m),\; \widetilde{\mathbf p}=\mathbf X\mathbf d,\; \widetilde{\mathbf p}=\mathbf XG(m)=\mathcal{A}(m).\) The method does not necessarily return \(\Tau(m)\). It returns \(\mathcal{A}(m)\). If the SOLA map factors as \(\mathbf X=\Tau G^\dagger,\) then \(\mathcal{A}=\Tau\mathcal R.\) In that case, the SOLA estimate is the target property of the resolved model: \(\widetilde{\mathbf p} = \Tau(\mathcal R m).\) Equivalently, it is the true model tested against resolved target kernels: \([\widetilde{\mathbf p}]_k = (\mathcal R^*T_k,m)_{\M}.\) These are two sides of the same coin: \(\Tau(\mathcal R m) \quad\text{and}\quad (\Tau\mathcal R)(m).\) Intuition Classical inversion blurs the model and then asks the target question. SOLA can be read as blurring the target question and then asking it of the true model. Same blur, different order of operations. What is genuinely different There is a real advantage here, and it should not be understated. SOLA lets us design the target question and inspect the blurred version that the data can actually support. Instead of hiding resolution inside a reconstructed model, SOLA puts the resolving kernels on the table. That is useful. It is a genuine ergonomic and interpretational improvement over classical inversion, where the resolution operator may be implicit or harder to inspect. But the limitation is that this is still resolution-limited information. The data do not grant perfect access to \(\Tau(m)\) just because we avoided reconstructing \(m\). They grant access to \(\mathcal{A}(m)=\mathbf XG(m),\) which is a resolved version of the desired property. The resolving kernel is the target kernel after \(\mathcal R^*\). The resolution operator has not been bypassed, it has been moved to a different place in the formula. Warning Avoiding an explicit model reconstruction does not avoid resolution. It only changes where the resolution appears. This is why the slogan that SOLA gives “resolution control” should be read carefully. SOLA does give meaningful control over the resolving kernels, the practitioner chooses targets and inspects what the data can deliver. That is a real advantage over methods that bury resolution inside an opaque reconstructed model. But it is not a new kind of resolution. The resolving kernels are target kernels passed through \(\mathcal R^*\). The sensitivity kernels, noise covariance, constraints, and data geometry still decide what is reachable. SOLA does not give sovereignty over resolution. It gives visibility. Lesson SOLA does not bypass the resolution operator. It views it from the adjoint side. The resolving kernel is the target kernel after \(\mathcal R^*\). That is useful, but it is not a different species of resolution. The next act turns from resolution to uncertainty, the third pillar. Once again, the theme will be the same: the formula is mathematically correct, but its interpretation needs careful labels. References William Menke (2018). title: Act 9: Uncertainty | My Take on SOLA | Adrian Mag
desc: Act 9 of My Take on SOLA: The shifted-noise pushforward, why SOLA cannot produce posteriors without a prior, and the frequentist interpretation of SOLA as a transformed observation problem with calibrated confidence sets.
text:
Act 9: Uncertainty No prior, no posterior, but a frequentist confidence story that works. Part of My Take on SOLA . « Overview 1 The Kernel Game 2 Building SOLA 3 Averages Need Mass 4 Beyond Averages 5 Noise Enters 6 What Did SOLA Estimate? 7 Cautionary Tale 8 Inversion in Disguise 9 Uncertainty 10 What SOLA Is Good For The Third Pillar: Uncertainty Quantification The first act of this series tested the “no prior” pillar and found a boundary: without model-side information, the interpretation gap is unbounded. The second act tested the “resolution control” pillar and found that SOLA's resolving kernels are target kernels passed through the adjoint of a resolution operator, useful, but not a new species of resolution. Now we turn to the third pillar: uncertainty quantification . SOLA is said to come with built-in uncertainty estimates. The propagated covariance \(\mathbf C_P=\mathbf X\mathbf C_D\mathbf X^*\) is presented as a quantification of uncertainty in the SOLA output, often displayed as error bars on the estimated properties. This is an attractive feature, and the calculation itself is correct. But what question does it actually answer? And is that the question we want to ask? What SOLA Does in Practice for Uncertainty The shifted-noise pushforward Let us start with a simple observation that is easy to miss. In the noisy setting, the observed data are \(\widetilde{\mathbf d} = G( ar m)+ oldsymbol\eta,\;  oldsymbol\eta\sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf 0,\mathbf C_D),\) where \( ar m\in\M\) is the unknown true model and \(\mathbf C_D\) is the data-noise covariance. The SOLA estimate is \(\widetilde{\mathbf p} = \mathbf X\widetilde{\mathbf d}.\) The standard uncertainty display is the covariance \[\mathbf C_P = \mathbf X\mathbf C_D\mathbf X^*,\] shown as error bars \([\widetilde{\mathbf p}]_k \pm 2\sqrt{[\mathbf C_P]_{kk}}.\) This is the advertised uncertainty quantification, the third pillar. (The display itself is standard across the SOLA literature, from the original error propagation [PT92] to tomographic practice [Zar16] .) Now here is the observation. Once the data \(\widetilde{\mathbf d}\) have been observed, one can construct a probability measure on data space by centring the noise law at the observation: \[\mathbf z_{\mathrm{shift}} = \widetilde{\mathbf d}+ oldsymbol\xi,\;  oldsymbol\xi\sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf 0,\mathbf C_D).\] This is the shifted-noise measure \(\mathcal{N}(\widetilde{\mathbf d},\mathbf C_D)\) , the noise distribution shifted so that its mean is the observed data. Pushing it through \(\mathbf X\) gives \[\mathcal{N}(\widetilde{\mathbf d},\mathbf C_D) \xrightarrow{\;\mathbf X\;} \mathcal{N}(\mathbf X\widetilde{\mathbf d},\mathbf X\mathbf C_D\mathbf X^*).\] That is exactly the SOLA uncertainty display. The measure \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf X\widetilde{\mathbf d},\mathbf C_P)\) is the pushforward of the shifted-noise measure. The covariance \(\mathbf C_P\) is a summary statistic of this pushforward measure. Checkpoint By default, SOLA's uncertainty quantification is the pushforward of the shifted-noise measure \(\mathcal{N}(\widetilde{\mathbf d},\mathbf C_D)\) through the SOLA matrix \(\mathbf X\). The covariance \(\mathbf C_P\) is a summary statistic of that pushforward. This is mathematically valid. The pushforward exists, the covariance is correctly computed, and the error bars are a faithful summary of this particular measure. Nothing is wrong with the calculation. But now the real question arrives. What is the point of this measure? What question does it answer? And is that a question worth asking in the context of an inverse problem? What does the pushforward measure mean? We know by now that SOLA targets the approximate property \(\mathcal{A}(m)\), not the desired property \(\Tau(m)\). That distinction was established in earlier acts. The question now is narrower: what does the pushforward measure \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf X\widetilde{\mathbf d}, \mathbf C_P)\) say probabilistically about the approximate property \(\mathcal{A}(m_{\mathrm{true}})\)? Should we interpret it as “the approximate property of the true model is distributed according to this measure”? It is not a posterior measure on the model or its properties, that much is clear, and we will see why shortly. But the plotted interval \([\widetilde{\mathbf p}]_k \pm 2\sqrt{[\mathbf C_P]_{kk}}\) does have a perfectly legitimate frequentist interpretation as a confidence interval for the resolved quantity \(\mathcal{A}(m_{\mathrm{true}})\). We will derive that interpretation later in this act. The point of the present discussion is not to say the interval is meaningless, but to clarify what it is and is not: it is not a Bayesian posterior, but it can be a calibrated frequentist confidence statement. No Prior, No Posterior The shifted-noise measure \(\mathcal{N}(\widetilde{\mathbf d},\mathbf C_D)\) is a probability measure on data space. Pushing it through \(\mathbf X\) gives a probability measure on property space. But what does that measure mean ? If we had a prior on the model space \(\M\), we could combine it with the likelihood to form a posterior. The observed data \(\widetilde{\mathbf d}\) would update the prior into a posterior measure on \(m\), and pushing that posterior through \(\mathcal{A}\) would give a posterior on the approximate property \(\mathcal{A}(m_{\mathrm{true}})\). That is the Bayesian route, and it is the only route that produces a genuine posterior probability measure on the model or its properties. (For the Bayesian formulation of inverse problems, and the central, non-negotiable role of the prior in it, the standard reference is Tarantola [Tar05] .) But SOLA, by design, does not introduce a prior. Without a prior, the observation cannot be turned into a posterior statement about the approximate property \(\mathcal{A}(m_{\mathrm{true}})\). Warning The shifted-noise pushforward is not a posterior measure. It cannot become one without a prior. And SOLA, by design, does not have one. The observation cannot update what is not there. So where does that leave us? If the Bayesian route is closed, because SOLA does not use a prior, then we need a different framework for uncertainty. We need a framework that does not require a prior, that works with a fixed true model and random observations, and that produces calibrated statements about the quantities SOLA actually targets. That framework is frequentist inference . Intuition The Bayesian asks: “given what I observed, what do I believe about the model?” The frequentist asks: “if the true model is fixed, how often would my procedure produce a correct statement?” SOLA, without a prior, is naturally suited to the second question. If you are not familiar with the frequentist framework, or if you want to see how it differs from the Bayesian approach in more detail, I have written a separate series of pages on Bayesian and Frequentist Inference . The key idea is simple: the true model is fixed but unknown, the observation is random because of noise, and uncertainty is quantified by the long-run frequency with which a procedure produces correct statements. What follows applies that framework to SOLA. SOLA as a Transformed Observation Problem In the frequentist interpretation, the true model \(m_{\mathrm{true}}\in\M\) is fixed but unknown. It is not assigned a prior measure and is not treated as a random variable. The randomness comes from the observation process. The original data equation is \[\Dobsrand = G(m_{\mathrm{true}}) + \Nrand,\] where \(\Nrand\sim\muN.\) After observation, the realized equation is \[\dobs = G(m_{\mathrm{true}}) + 
obs.\] SOLA applies a linear transformation \(\mathbf X:\D	o\Pspace\) to the data. Before observation, this gives \[\Prand = \mathbf X\Dobsrand = \mathbf X G(m_{\mathrm{true}}) + \mathbf X\Nrand.\] After observation, this gives \[\pobs = \mathbf X\dobs = \mathbf X G(m_{\mathrm{true}}) + \mathbf X
obs.\] Define the transformed noise random variable \(\etarand = \mathbf X\Nrand\) with law \(\mueta = \mathbf X_{\#}\muN.\) The realized transformed noise is \(\etaobs = \mathbf X
obs.\) Thus the transformed observation equation is \[\Prand = \mathbf X G(m_{\mathrm{true}}) + \etarand.\] The model \(m_{\mathrm{true}}\) is fixed. The transformed signal \(\mathbf X G(m_{\mathrm{true}})\) is fixed. The transformed observation \(\Prand\) is random because the transformed noise \(\etarand\) is random. If the experiment were repeated many times with the same fixed model \(m_{\mathrm{true}}\), one would obtain \[\Prand_j = \mathbf X G(m_{\mathrm{true}}) + \etarand_j, \qquad j=1,2,3,\dots.\] Each repetition would produce a different transformed observation because each repetition would have a different noise realization. Checkpoint This is the frequentist setting for SOLA. The true model is fixed. The SOLA-induced quantity \(\mathbf X G(m_{\mathrm{true}})\) is fixed. The transformed observation \(\Prand = \mathbf X\Dobsrand\) is random. The realized transformed datum \(\pobs = \mathbf X\dobs\) is what we actually observe. Confidence Sets in Property Space Suppose first that we are interested directly in the SOLA-induced approximate property \(\AX(m_{\mathrm{true}}) = \mathbf X G(m_{\mathrm{true}}).\) Then the transformed observation equation is \[\Prand = \AX(m_{\mathrm{true}}) + \etarand.\] This has the same form as the original additive-noise problem, but now in property space. If \(F_{\alpha}\subseteq\Pspace\) is a transformed-noise acceptance region satisfying \(\mueta(F_{\alpha}) = 1 - \alpha,\) then a confidence set for the approximate property is \[C_{\alpha}^{\mathbf X}(\pobs) = \left\{\mathbf p\in\Pspace : \pobs - \mathbf p \in F_{\alpha}ight\}.\] Equivalently, \(C_{\alpha}^{\mathbf X}(\pobs) = \pobs - F_{\alpha}.\) This set contains the transformed signal values \(\mathbf p\) for which the observation \(\pobs\) can be explained by an accepted transformed-noise realization. Coverage Before observation, define the random transformed confidence set \[C_{\alpha}^{\mathbf X}(\Prand) = \left\{\mathbf p\in\Pspace : \Prand - \mathbf p \in F_{\alpha}ight\}.\] Coverage in this pre-observation sense is exactly Neyman’s original construction of confidence sets [Ney37] , the construction these notes examine at length in the frequentist series. By definition, \(\AX(m_{\mathrm{true}}) \in C_{\alpha}^{\mathbf X}(\Prand)\) if and only if \(\Prand - \AX(m_{\mathrm{true}}) \in F_{\alpha}.\) But \(\Prand = \AX(m_{\mathrm{true}}) + \etarand,\) so \(\Prand - \AX(m_{\mathrm{true}}) = \etarand.\) Therefore \[\AX(m_{\mathrm{true}}) \in C_{\alpha}^{\mathbf X}(\Prand) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \etarand \in F_{\alpha}.\] Taking probabilities gives \[\Prob_{m_{\mathrm{true}}}\!\left(\AX(m_{\mathrm{true}}) \in C_{\alpha}^{\mathbf X}(\Prand)ight) = \Prob\!\left(\etarand \in F_{\alpha}ight) = \mueta(F_{\alpha}) = 1 - \alpha.\] Frequentist SOLA coverage If the true model \(m_{\mathrm{true}}\) is fixed and the noisy observation process is repeated many times, then the transformed confidence set catches the fixed transformed signal \(\mathbf X G(m_{\mathrm{true}})\) with frequency \(1 - \alpha\). This is the direct frequentist SOLA coverage statement for the approximate property \(\AX(m_{\mathrm{true}}) = \mathbf X G(m_{\mathrm{true}}).\) What SOLA Does and Does Not Provide Without a prior, SOLA can provide: Transformed observation: the actual quantity \(\pobs = \mathbf X\dobs.\) Transformed noise law: the pushforward measure \(\mueta = \mathbf X_{\#}\muN.\) Approximate property: the noiseless transformed signal \(\AX(m_{\mathrm{true}}) = \mathbf X G(m_{\mathrm{true}}).\) Frequentist confidence statements: calibrated coverage statements for confidence sets targeting \(\AX(m_{\mathrm{true}}).\) What SOLA does not automatically provide: No posterior on models. There is no posterior measure on \(m_{\mathrm{true}}\) unless a prior has been introduced. No posterior on properties. There is no posterior measure on \(\AX(m_{\mathrm{true}})\) unless a posterior on models has been constructed and pushed forward. No immunity to outliers. The transformed observation \(\pobs\) may still be affected by an unlucky realization of transformed noise. Lesson SOLA transforms the observation problem from data space to property space: \(\dobs = G(m_{\mathrm{true}}) + 
obs \;\longmapsto\; \pobs = \AX(m_{\mathrm{true}}) + \etaobs.\) After that transformation, the same conceptual choice remains: take the Bayesian route (put a prior on \(m\), condition on \(\dobs\), push the posterior through \(\AX\)), or take the frequentist route (keep \(m_{\mathrm{true}}\) fixed, push the noise through \(\mathbf X\), and build calibrated confidence procedures for the transformed quantities). This is why SOLA is naturally frequentist in this interpretation. It does not produce a posterior distribution over models or properties. It transforms the observation equation and the noise law, then uses the transformed problem to build calibrated confidence and decision procedures. The shifted-noise pushforward, the object SOLA reports by default, is not wrong, but it is not a posterior. It is a frequentist object that happens to look like one. The frequentist interpretation makes its meaning precise. References Frank P. Pijpers and Michael J. Thompson (1992). “Faster formulations of the optimally localized averages method for helioseismic inversions.” Astronomy & Astrophysics 262, L33–L36. The paper that coined SOLA. Propagated error covariance in the original SOLA formulation. title: My Take on SOLA | Adrian Mag
desc: Resolving kernels, proxy inversions, and the problem with shifted noise: a careful examination of what SOLA estimates and what its uncertainty means.
text: My Take on SOLA Resolving kernels, proxy inversions, and the problem with shifted noise. 1 The Kernel Game 2 Building SOLA 3 Averages Need Mass 4 Beyond Averages 5 Noise Enters 6 What Did SOLA Estimate? 7 Cautionary Tale 8 Inversion in Disguise 9 Uncertainty 10 What SOLA Is Good For What to expect SOLA is often introduced as a method for estimating localized averages, or more general linear properties, of an unknown model without first reconstructing the whole model. Instead of solving for everything, SOLA tries to build from the data exactly the kind of quantity one wants to report. The main purpose of these notes is to explain that idea from the ground up, and then to examine carefully what the resulting numbers mean. The idea has a distinguished lineage, and these notes stand on it. The method of optimally localized averages was created by Backus and Gilbert in a remarkable series of papers [BG67] , [BG68] , [BG70] . The subtractive variant, SOLA, the subject of these notes, was introduced for helioseismology by Pijpers and Thompson [PT92] , [PT94] , and brought into seismic tomography by Zaroli and colleagues [Zar16] , [ZKL17] . The operator-theoretic framing used throughout, and several of the critical questions these notes pursue, grew out of our own work connecting SOLA to deterministic linear inference [MKZ25] . Full references, with links, close each act. Lesson SOLA is best understood as a method for reshuffling linear data information into property-like information. The reshuffled information is real, but it must be labelled honestly. The central caution A SOLA calculation begins with target kernels. These describe the linear properties we would like to know. But the method generally returns resolving kernels. These are the linear properties that the available data can actually synthesize. If the resolving kernel equals the target kernel, then the interpretation is direct. If it does not, then the SOLA number is not the exact target property of the true model. It is the resolving-kernel property of the true model, up to observational noise. Warning The target kernel is a design request. The resolving kernel is the answer delivered by the data. How to read this document The notes are organized as a guided story. We begin with a simple integral picture, build SOLA in its cleanest form, add normalization constraints and noise, and only later ask the more delicate questions: what did SOLA estimate, what does its uncertainty mean, and what kind of prior information is needed if we want statements about the true target property? Notation and conventions Remark: Notation for operators and components We adopt the following typographic conventions throughout these notes. Finite-dimensional objects. Boldface letters denote finite-dimensional vectors and matrices (coefficient/representation objects). For example \(\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb R^N\) and \(\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb R^{N\times N}\). Infinite-dimensional objects. Non-bold (lightface) letters denote infinite-dimensional operators or functions acting on the model Hilbert space \(\M\); e.g.\ \(G:\M\to\D\), \(C_0:\M\to\M\). Components / entries. The components of a vector or the entries of a matrix are written with square brackets and subscripts: \[[\mathbf v]_i = v_i,\qquad [\mathbf A]_{ij} = A_{ij}, \qquad i,j=1,\dots,N.\] When an object is represented in a particular basis \(\{\phi_k\}_{k=1}^N\) we always mean the coordinates with respect to that basis; the matrix entries depend on the chosen basis. Inner products. Throughout these notes, all spaces are real Hilbert spaces. We write the inner product on a Hilbert space \(H\) as \((\cdot,\cdot)_H\). Recall that an inner product on a real vector space \(H\) is a map \((\cdot,\cdot)_H:H\times H\to\mathbb R\) that is (i) linear in each argument, (ii) symmetric, \((u,v)_H=(v,u)_H\), and (iii) positive definite, \((v,v)_H\ge0\) with equality iff \(v=0\). The induced norm is \(\|v\|_H=\sqrt{(v,v)_H}\). For the model space \(\M\), data space \(\D\), property space \(\Pspace\), and the space of Hilbert-Schmidt operators, we use \((\cdot,\cdot)_{\M}\), \((\cdot,\cdot)_{\D}\), \((\cdot,\cdot)_{\Pspace}\), and \((\cdot,\cdot)_{\HS}\) respectively. The angle-bracket notation \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\) is reserved for dual pairings between a space and its dual, which we do not need here since every Hilbert space is self-dual via the Riesz representation theorem. Adjoints and transposes. We reserve \(^{\top}\) for the Euclidean transpose of a finite matrix and \(^{*}\) for the Hilbert adjoint of an operator. Discrete adjoints that incorporate mass/weight matrices will be written explicitly (for example, the discrete adjoint of \(\mathbf G\) with mass matrix \(\mathbf M\) and data weight \(\mathbf W\) is \(\mathbf G^*=\mathbf M^{-1}\mathbf G^{\top}\mathbf W\)). Infinite sequences. When working with infinite coefficient sequences we use index notation \((\alpha_i)_{i\ge1}\) or \(\{\alpha_i\}_{i=1}^\infty\); for finite coefficient vectors we write \(\mathbf\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_N)^\top\) so that \([\mathbf\alpha]_i=\alpha_i\). Sources & the lineage Every act closes with the references behind its specific claims. The landmarks of the subject, all clickable, are these: George Backus and Freeman Gilbert (1967). “Numerical Applications of a Formalism for Geophysical Inverse Problems.” Geophysical Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society 13(1–3), 247–276. doi:10.1111/j.1365-246X.1967.tb02159.x George Backus and Freeman Gilbert (1968). “The Resolving Power of Gross Earth Data.” Geophysical Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society 16(2), 169–205. The founding paper: averaging kernels, unimodularity, and the question of what data can resolve. doi:10.1111/j.1365-246X.1968.tb00216.x George Backus and Freeman Gilbert (1970). “Uniqueness in the Inversion of Inaccurate Gross Earth Data.” Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A 266(1173), 123–192. Nonuniqueness and the resolution–variance trade-off. doi:10.1098/rsta.1970.0005 Frank P. Pijpers and Michael J. Thompson (1992). “Faster formulations of the optimally localized averages method for helioseismic inversions.” Astronomy & Astrophysics 262, L33–L36. The paper that coined SOLA. ADS · free scan (ADS) Frank P. Pijpers and Michael J. Thompson (1994). “The SOLA method for helioseismic inversion.” Astronomy & Astrophysics 281, 231–240. The full development: target forms, trade-offs, blind tests. ADS · free scan (ADS) Christophe Zaroli (2016). “Global seismic tomography using Backus–Gilbert inversion.” Geophysical Journal International 207(2), 876–888. SOLA at global tomography scale. doi:10.1093/gji/ggw315 Christophe Zaroli, Paula Koelemeijer, and Sophie Lambotte (2017). “Toward Seeing the Earth’s Interior Through Unbiased Tomographic Lenses.” Geophysical Research Letters 44(22). The case for interpreting estimates through resolving kernels. doi:10.1002/2017GL074996 Adrian M. Mag, Christophe Zaroli, and Paula Koelemeijer (2025). “Bridging the gap between SOLA and deterministic linear inferences in the context of seismic tomography.” Geophysical Journal International 242(1), ggaf131. Open access. The paper these notes grew alongside. doi:10.1093/gji/ggaf131 The ten acts Act 1: The Kernel Game . We begin with an unknown function observed through sensitivity kernels. The data are weighted integrals, and finite data cannot see everything. We introduce target kernels as the questions we wish the data could answer. Act 2: Building SOLA from Scratch . Combining data means combining kernels. The resolving kernel is born. We formalize the noiseless unconstrained SOLA problem and derive the normal equation. Act 3: Averages Need Mass . A localized kernel must also carry the right total mass. We introduce unimodularity, the average vector, and the constrained SOLA problem with its rank-one correction. Act 4: Beyond Averages . Not every target is an average. Derivative targets, basis coefficient targets, and contrasts each need their own resolving constraint. Act 5: Noise Enters the Room . Data are not exact. We build the noise-aware SOLA objective, balance resolution against noise amplification, and derive the noisy normal equation. Act 6: What Did SOLA Actually Estimate? . The target is the request; the resolving kernel is the answer. We confront the gap between \(\Tau(\bar m)\) and \(\mathcal{A}(\bar m)\), and learn the honest sidestep: interpret through resolving kernels. Act 7: A Synthetic Cautionary Tale . A case that looks good: resolving kernels match targets, error bars are small, and yet the SOLA estimates miss the true target properties. The nullspace explains why. Act 8: SOLA as an Inversion in Disguise . The constrained SOLA estimate can be written as the target property of a proxy model. We connect resolving kernels to classical resolution operators. Act 9: Uncertainty . The propagated covariance \(\mathbf X\mathbf C_D\mathbf X^*\) is not a posterior covariance. Without a prior, there is no Bayesian posterior. We introduce the frequentist interpretation of SOLA as a transformed observation problem with calibrated confidence sets. Act 10: What SOLA Is Good For . A fair summary of SOLA's strengths, what it should not be asked to do alone, and the final slogan: \[\text{SOLA transforms the observation problem. It does not solve the inference problem.}\]

title: Summary & Appendices | My Take on SOLA | Adrian Mag
desc: Summary of the SOLA argument and appendices on algebra of minimizers, proxy model derivation, and suggested figures.
text:
Summary & Appendices Summary of the argument, algebra of SOLA minimizers, proxy model derivation, and suggested figures. Part of My Take on SOLA . « Overview 1 The Kernel Game 2 Building SOLA 3 Averages Need Mass 4 Beyond Averages 5 Noise Enters 6 What Did SOLA Estimate? 7 Cautionary Tale 8 Inversion in Disguise 9 Uncertainty 10 What SOLA Is Good For S Summary Summary of the Argument The construction The mathematical skeleton of SOLA has three main ingredients. First, there is the forward map \(G:\M	o\D,\) which sends a model \(m\in\M\) to finite-dimensional data \(\mathbf d=G(m)\in\D\simeq\mathbb R^{N_d}.\) In components, \([G(m)]_i = (K_i,m)_{\M},\; i=1,\dots,N_d.\) The functions \(K_i\) are the sensitivity kernels. Second, there is the property map \(\Tau:\M	o\Pspace,\) which sends a model to the finite-dimensional property vector \(\mathbf p=\Tau(m)\in\Pspace\simeq\mathbb R^{N_p}.\) In components, \([\mathbf p]_k = [\Tau(m)]_k = (T_k,m)_{\M},\; k=1,\dots,N_p.\) The functions \(T_k\) are the target kernels. Third, SOLA chooses a finite-dimensional map \(\mathbf X:\D	o\Pspace\) so that \(\mathbf XG\approx \Tau.\) This is the core construction. The simplest noiseless version solves \(\mathbf X_0 = \argmin_{\mathbf X} \left\|\Tau-\mathbf XGight\|_{\HS}^2.\) With noise and resolving constraints, the basic problem becomes \[\widetilde{\mathbf X}_c = \argmin_{\mathbf X} \left\{\left\|\Tau-\mathbf XGight\|_{\HS}^2 + \Tr(\mathbf X\mathbf C_D\mathbf X^*)ight\} \quad 	ext{subject to} \quad \mathbf X\mathbf V=\mathbf W.\] Here \(\mathbf C_D\) is the data-noise covariance, and \(\mathbf X\mathbf V=\mathbf W\) collects the resolving constraints. For averages with a single calibration, this reduces to the unimodularity condition \(\mathbf X\mathbf v=\mathbf w.\) For other properties, it encodes the calibration needed for the intended interpretation. Lesson The SOLA construction is simple at heart: \(	ext{choose }\mathbf X	ext{ so that }\mathbf XG	ext{ behaves like }\Tau.\) The details decide what “behaves like” means. The interpretation Once \(\mathbf X\) has been chosen, the approximate property map is \(\mathcal{A}:=\mathbf XG:\M	o\Pspace.\) This is the map that the data combination actually synthesizes. The target map is \(\Tau:\M	o\Pspace.\) The SOLA map is \(\mathcal{A}=\mathbf XG:\M	o\Pspace.\) For the true model \( ar m\), the exact target property is \( ar{\mathbf p} = \Tau( ar m).\) The noiseless SOLA-accessible property is \(\mathcal{A}( ar m) = \mathbf XG( ar m).\) Thus the central interpretive distinction is \(\Tau( ar m) \quad	ext{versus}\quad \mathcal{A}( ar m).\) In components, \([\Tau( ar m)]_k = (T_k, ar m)_{\M},\) whereas \([\mathcal{A}( ar m)]_k = (R_k, ar m)_{\M},\) with resolving kernels \(R_k = \sum_{i=1}^{N_d} [\mathbf X]_{ki}K_i.\) Therefore the SOLA output should be interpreted through the resolving kernels \(R_k\). The target kernels \(T_k\) guide the construction, but the resolving kernels define the reported quantities. Checkpoint The target kernel is the request. The resolving kernel is the answer. The limitation The difference between the exact target property and the resolved SOLA property is \(\Tau( ar m)-\mathcal{A}( ar m) = (\Tau-\mathcal{A})( ar m).\) Hence \(\|\Tau( ar m)-\mathcal{A}( ar m)\|_{\Pspace} \le \|\Tau-\mathcal{A}\|_{\M	o\Pspace}\,\| ar m\|_{\M}.\) This inequality is useful, but it also exposes the limitation. A small resolving-target mismatch does not give a uniform property-error bound over all possible models. It becomes an error bound only when the true model is controlled. If we know, for example, that \(\| ar m\|_{\M}\le R,\) then \(\|\Tau( ar m)-\mathcal{A}( ar m)\|_{\Pspace} \le R\|\Tau-\mathcal{A}\|_{\M	o\Pspace}.\) But without such a model-side restriction, the difference can be arbitrarily large whenever \(\Tau-\mathcal{A}
eq 0\). The nullspace mechanism makes this especially clear. If \(h\in\kernel(G),\;	ext{but}\; \Tau(h)
eq\mathbf 0,\) then \(\mathcal{A}(h)=\mathbf XG(h)=\mathbf 0,\) while \(\Tau(h)
eq\mathbf 0.\) Thus the exact target property can change in directions that the SOLA map cannot see. Warning Resolving kernels can be close to target kernels and still fail to control target-property error over unrestricted model classes. The missing ingredient is control of the model. The uncertainty distinction The usual SOLA propagated covariance is \(\mathbf C_P = \mathbf X\mathbf C_D\mathbf X^*.\) This is the covariance of the propagated data-noise term \(\mathbf X oldsymbol\eta\) when \( oldsymbol\eta\sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf 0,\mathbf C_D).\) It is therefore a covariance for observational noise in the resolved SOLA quantity \(\mathcal{A}( ar m).\) It is not, by itself, a posterior covariance for the exact target property \(\Tau( ar m).\) To obtain uncertainty about \(\Tau( ar m)\), one needs model-side information. This may be a deterministic constraint set \( ar m\in B\subset\M,\) or a probabilistic prior \(m\sim\muprior.\) Lesson Propagated data-noise uncertainty is not the same thing as uncertainty about the exact target property of the true model. The frequentist interpretation The shifted-noise pushforward is not a posterior. Without a prior, the observed data cannot be turned into a statement about which models are more likely. The Bayesian route is closed. The frequentist route keeps the true model \(m_{\mathrm{true}}\) fixed and treats the observation as random. SOLA transforms the observation equation from data space to property space: \[\dobs = G(m_{\mathrm{true}}) + 
obs \;\longmapsto\; \pobs = \mathbf X G(m_{\mathrm{true}}) + \etaobs.\] The transformed noise law is \(\mueta = \mathbf X_{\#}\muN.\) Confidence sets for the approximate property \(\mathbf X G(m_{\mathrm{true}})\) are built from acceptance regions of the transformed noise, with coverage \(1-\alpha.\) Confidence for the desired property \(\Tau(m_{\mathrm{true}})\) requires additional control of resolution error. Lesson SOLA transforms the observation problem. It does not erase the distinction between Bayesian posterior probability and frequentist coverage. Without a prior, the frequentist interpretation is the natural framework for SOLA's uncertainty. The final principle The whole argument can be compressed into one line: \[ oxed{	ext{Ask with targets. Interpret with resolving kernels. Add priors when you want truth.}}\] Targets are design objects. Resolving kernels are interpretation objects. Priors or deterministic constraints are what allow claims about exact target properties of the true model. Appendix A: Algebra of SOLA Minimizers Preliminaries This appendix collects the basic algebra for the SOLA minimizers used in the main text. Let \(G:\M	o\D,\; \Tau:\M	o\Pspace,\) with finite-dimensional spaces \(\D\simeq\mathbb R^{N_d},\; \Pspace\simeq\mathbb R^{N_p}.\) Let \(\mathbf X:\D	o\Pspace\) be the SOLA matrix. The objective in the noiseless case is \(J_0(\mathbf X) = \left\|\Tau-\mathbf XGight\|_{\HS}^2.\) For compactness, define the data-space Gram operator \(\mathbf H:=GG^*:\D	o\D.\) With the conventions of these notes, \(\mathbf H\) is represented by a finite-dimensional matrix. In components, under standard choices of inner products, \([\mathbf H]_{ij} = (K_j,K_i)_{\M}.\) For the noisy case, define \(\mathbf M:=\mathbf H+\mathbf C_D=GG^*+\mathbf C_D.\) We assume the inverses appearing below exist. In practice, positive data covariance, regularized systems, or pseudoinverses may be used when exact invertibility fails. Unconstrained noiseless derivation The unconstrained noiseless SOLA problem is \(\mathbf X_0 = \argmin_{\mathbf X} \left\|\Tau-\mathbf XGight\|_{\HS}^2.\) Let \(E(\mathbf X):=\Tau-\mathbf XG.\) Then \(J_0(\mathbf X) = (E(\mathbf X),E(\mathbf X))_{\HS}.\) Perturb \(\mathbf X\) by \(\varepsilon\mathbf H_1\), where \(\mathbf H_1:\D	o\Pspace\) is an arbitrary finite-dimensional perturbation. Then \(E(\mathbf X+\varepsilon\mathbf H_1) = \Tau-(\mathbf X+\varepsilon\mathbf H_1)G = E(\mathbf X)-\varepsilon\mathbf H_1G.\) Therefore \(J_0(\mathbf X+\varepsilon\mathbf H_1) = \|E(\mathbf X)-\varepsilon\mathbf H_1G\|_{\HS}^2.\) Differentiating at \(\varepsilon=0\), \(\delta J_0(\mathbf X)[\mathbf H_1] = -2( E(\mathbf X), \mathbf H_1G)_{\HS}.\) Using the adjoint relation, \(( E(\mathbf X), \mathbf H_1G)_{\HS} = ( E(\mathbf X)G^*, \mathbf H_1)_{\HS}.\) Thus \(\delta J_0(\mathbf X)[\mathbf H_1] = -2( (\Tau-\mathbf XG)G^*, \mathbf H_1)_{\HS}.\) Stationarity for every perturbation \(\mathbf H_1\) gives \((\Tau-\mathbf XG)G^*=0.\) Hence \(\Tau G^*-\mathbf XGG^*=0,\) or \(\mathbf X\mathbf H=\Tau G^*.\) If \(\mathbf H\) is invertible, then \[ oxed{\mathbf X_0=\Tau G^*\mathbf H^{-1}.}\] Since \(\mathbf H=GG^*,\) this is often written as \(\mathbf X_0 = \Tau G^*(GG^*)^{-1}.\) Checkpoint The unconstrained noiseless minimizer is obtained by solving the normal equation \(\mathbf XGG^*=\Tau G^*.\) Constrained noiseless derivation Now impose resolving constraints \(\mathbf X\mathbf V=\mathbf W,\) where \(\mathbf V\in\D^{N_d	imes L},\; \mathbf W\in\Pspace^{N_p	imes L}.\) Introduce a Lagrange multiplier matrix \( oldsymbol\Lambda\in\Pspace^{N_p	imes L}.\) Consider the Lagrangian \(\mathcal L(\mathbf X, oldsymbol\Lambda) = \left\|\Tau-\mathbf XGight\|_{\HS}^2 + 2\Tr igl((\mathbf X\mathbf V-\mathbf W)^* oldsymbol\Lambda igr).\) The stationarity condition gives \((\Tau-\mathbf XG)G^* +  oldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf V^* = 0.\) Rearranging, \(\mathbf XGG^* = \Tau G^*- oldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf V^*.\) Using \(\mathbf H=GG^*\), \(\mathbf X = \Tau G^*\mathbf H^{-1} -  oldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf V^*\mathbf H^{-1}.\) Define \(\mathbf X_0:=\Tau G^*\mathbf H^{-1},\) and \(\mathbf U:=\mathbf H^{-1}\mathbf V.\) Since \(\mathbf H\) is self-adjoint, \(\mathbf V^*\mathbf H^{-1}=\mathbf U^*.\) Therefore \(\mathbf X = \mathbf X_0- oldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf U^*.\) Now impose the constraint: \(\mathbf X\mathbf V=\mathbf W.\) Substituting, \((\mathbf X_0- oldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf U^*)\mathbf V = \mathbf W.\) Thus \(\mathbf X_0\mathbf V -  oldsymbol\Lambda\,\mathbf U^*\mathbf V = \mathbf W.\) Define \( oldsymbol\Gamma := \mathbf U^*\mathbf V = \mathbf V^*\mathbf H^{-1}\mathbf V.\) Then \( oldsymbol\Lambda = (\mathbf X_0\mathbf V-\mathbf W) oldsymbol\Gamma^{-1}.\) Therefore \[ oxed{\mathbf X_c = \mathbf X_0 - (\mathbf X_0\mathbf V-\mathbf W) oldsymbol\Gamma^{-1}\mathbf U^*}\] with \(\mathbf X_0=\Tau G^*\mathbf H^{-1},\; \mathbf U=\mathbf H^{-1}\mathbf V,\;  oldsymbol\Gamma=\mathbf V^*\mathbf U.\) The single-constraint formula drops out when \(\mathbf V=\mathbf v,\;\mathbf W=\mathbf w,\; oldsymbol\Gamma= eta,\;\mathbf U=\mathbf u,\) giving \(\mathbf X_c = \mathbf X_0 -  rac{\mathbf X_0\mathbf v-\mathbf w}{ eta}\mathbf u^*.\) Lesson The constrained noiseless solution is the unconstrained solution plus a rank-one correction that enforces the resolving constraint. Unconstrained noisy derivation The noise-aware objective is \(J(\mathbf X) = \left\|\Tau-\mathbf XGight\|_{\HS}^2 + \Tr(\mathbf X\mathbf C_D\mathbf X^*).\) The first variation of the first term is the same as before: \(-2( (\Tau-\mathbf XG)G^*, \mathbf H_1)_{\HS}.\) For the noise term, using the standard trace derivative, \(\delta \Tr(\mathbf X\mathbf C_D\mathbf X^*)[\mathbf H_1] = 2( \mathbf X\mathbf C_D, \mathbf H_1)_{\HS},\) assuming \(\mathbf C_D\) is self-adjoint. Thus stationarity gives \(-(\Tau-\mathbf XG)G^*+\mathbf X\mathbf C_D=0.\) Equivalently, \(\Tau G^*-\mathbf XGG^* = \mathbf X\mathbf C_D.\) Hence \(\Tau G^* = \mathbf X(GG^*+\mathbf C_D).\) Define \(\mathbf M:=GG^*+\mathbf C_D.\) Then \(\mathbf X\mathbf M=\Tau G^*.\) If \(\mathbf M\) is invertible, \[ oxed{\widetilde{\mathbf X}_0=\Tau G^*\mathbf M^{-1}.}\] Checkpoint The noisy unconstrained solution is obtained from the noiseless solution by replacing \(GG^*\) with \(GG^*+\mathbf C_D\). Constrained noisy derivation Finally, impose the resolving constraints \(\mathbf X\mathbf V=\mathbf W\) on the noisy objective. Use the Lagrangian \(\mathcal L(\mathbf X, oldsymbol\Lambda) = \left\|\Tau-\mathbf XGight\|_{\HS}^2 + \Tr(\mathbf X\mathbf C_D\mathbf X^*) + 2\Tr igl((\mathbf X\mathbf V-\mathbf W)^* oldsymbol\Lambda igr).\) The stationarity condition is \(-(\Tau-\mathbf XG)G^* + \mathbf X\mathbf C_D +  oldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf V^* = 0.\) Rearranging, \(\mathbf X(GG^*+\mathbf C_D) = \Tau G^*- oldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf V^*.\) Using \(\mathbf M:=GG^*+\mathbf C_D,\) we obtain \(\mathbf X = \Tau G^*\mathbf M^{-1} -  oldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf V^*\mathbf M^{-1}.\) Define \(\widetilde{\mathbf X}_0:=\Tau G^*\mathbf M^{-1},\; \mathbf U:=\mathbf M^{-1}\mathbf V.\) Since \(\mathbf M\) is self-adjoint, \(\mathbf V^*\mathbf M^{-1}=\mathbf U^*.\) Therefore \(\mathbf X = \widetilde{\mathbf X}_0- oldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf U^*.\) Apply the constraint: \((\widetilde{\mathbf X}_0- oldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf U^*)\mathbf V=\mathbf W.\) Hence \(\widetilde{\mathbf X}_0\mathbf V- oldsymbol\Lambda\,\mathbf U^*\mathbf V=\mathbf W.\) Define \( oldsymbol\Gamma := \mathbf U^*\mathbf V = \mathbf V^*\mathbf M^{-1}\mathbf V.\) Then \( oldsymbol\Lambda = (\widetilde{\mathbf X}_0\mathbf V-\mathbf W) oldsymbol\Gamma^{-1}.\) Thus \[ oxed{\widetilde{\mathbf X}_c = \Tau G^*\mathbf M^{-1} - (\Tau G^*\mathbf U-\mathbf W) oldsymbol\Gamma^{-1}\mathbf U^*}\] where \(\mathbf M=GG^*+\mathbf C_D,\; \mathbf U=\mathbf M^{-1}\mathbf V,\;  oldsymbol\Gamma=\mathbf V^*\mathbf U.\) The single-constraint formula drops out when \(\mathbf V=\mathbf v,\;\mathbf W=\mathbf w,\; oldsymbol\Gamma= eta,\;\mathbf U=\mathbf u,\) giving \(\widetilde{\mathbf X}_c = \Tau G^*\mathbf M^{-1} -  rac{\Tau G^*(\mathbf u)-\mathbf w}{ eta}\mathbf u^*.\) Lesson The constrained noisy solution is the noise-aware SOLA operator plus the correction needed to enforce the resolving constraint. Appendix B: Proxy Model Derivation Factorization of the constrained operator This appendix explains why the constrained SOLA estimate can sometimes be written as the target property of a proxy model. Start from the constrained noisy SOLA operator \(\widetilde{\mathbf X}_c = \Tau G^*\mathbf M^{-1} - (\Tau G^*\mathbf U-\mathbf W) oldsymbol\Gamma^{-1}\mathbf U^*,\) with \(\mathbf M=GG^*+\mathbf C_D,\; \mathbf U=\mathbf M^{-1}\mathbf V,\;  oldsymbol\Gamma=\mathbf V^*\mathbf U.\) Apply \(\widetilde{\mathbf X}_c\) to the observed data \(\widetilde{\mathbf d}\): \(\widetilde{\mathbf X}_c\widetilde{\mathbf d} = \Tau G^*\mathbf M^{-1}\widetilde{\mathbf d} - (\Tau G^*\mathbf U-\mathbf W) oldsymbol\Gamma^{-1}\mathbf U^*\widetilde{\mathbf d}.\) Define the coefficient vector \(\mathbf c :=  oldsymbol\Gamma^{-1}\mathbf U^*\widetilde{\mathbf d}\in\mathbb R^L.\) Then \(\widetilde{\mathbf X}_c\widetilde{\mathbf d} = \Tau G^*\mathbf M^{-1}\widetilde{\mathbf d} - (\Tau G^*\mathbf U-\mathbf W)\mathbf c.\) Now suppose there exist models \(f_1,\dots,f_L\in\M\) such that \(G(f_\ell)=\mathbf v_\ell,\; \Tau(f_\ell)=\mathbf w_\ell,\; \ell=1,\dots,L.\) Then \(\mathbf W\mathbf c = \Tau\!\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^L c_\ell f_\ellight)\) and \(\Tau G^*\mathbf U\,\mathbf c = \Tau\!\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^L c_\ell\, G^*\mathbf u_\ellight).\) Therefore \(\widetilde{\mathbf X}_c\widetilde{\mathbf d} = \Tau\!\left( G^*\mathbf M^{-1}\widetilde{\mathbf d} + \sum_{\ell=1}^L c_\ell igl(f_\ell - G^*\mathbf u_\ell igr) ight).\) This gives the proxy model formula. Construction of the proxy model Define \(\hat m := G^*\mathbf M^{-1}\widetilde{\mathbf d} + \sum_{\ell=1}^L c_\ell igl(f_\ell - G^*\mathbf u_\ell igr),\; \mathbf c= oldsymbol\Gamma^{-1}\mathbf U^*\widetilde{\mathbf d}.\) Then \[ oxed{\widetilde{\mathbf X}_c\widetilde{\mathbf d}=\Tau(\hat m).}\] Thus the constrained SOLA estimate can be interpreted as the exact target property of the proxy model \(\hat m\). The first part, \(G^*\mathbf M^{-1}\widetilde{\mathbf d},\) is a noise-weighted back-projection of the data. The second part, \(\sum_{\ell=1}^L c_\ell igl(f_\ell - G^*\mathbf u_\ell igr),\) is the correction associated with the resolving constraints. Warning The proxy model \(\hat m\) is an algebraic representative. It is not automatically the true model. The conditions \(G(f_\ell)=\mathbf v_\ell,\; \Tau(f_\ell)=\mathbf w_\ell\) mean that each \(f_\ell\) realizes both the data-side calibration vector and the property-side desired response for the \(\ell\)th constraint. Such functions exist if each \((\mathbf v_\ell,\mathbf w_\ell)\) lies in the range of the combined map \( egin{bmatrix} G\ \Tau \end{bmatrix}.\) If any \(f_\ell\) is not unique, the proxy model is not unique either. If \(f_\ell\) and \(f_\ell'\) both satisfy the conditions for a given \(\ell\), then \(f_\ell-f_\ell'\in\kernel(G)\cap\kernel(\Tau).\) Changing \(f_\ell\) by such a direction changes \(\hat m\), but not the SOLA estimate \(\Tau(\hat m).\) Lesson The proxy model is useful for interpretation, but it should not be mistaken for a uniquely recovered physical model. Connection with null-space components The proxy formula becomes especially transparent in the noiseless constrained case. Set \(\mathbf C_D=\mathbf 0,\; \mathbf M=GG^*.\) Then \(\mathbf u_\ell=(GG^*)^{-1}\mathbf v_\ell.\) Since \(\mathbf v_\ell=G(f_\ell),\) we have \(G(G^*\mathbf u_\ell) = GG^*(GG^*)^{-1}\mathbf v_\ell = \mathbf v_\ell.\) Therefore \(G igl(G^*\mathbf u_\ell-f_\ell igr) = \mathbf 0.\) So in the noiseless constrained case, \(G^*\mathbf u_\ell-f_\ell\in\kernel(G)\) for each \(\ell\). The proxy model is then \(\hat m = G^*(GG^*)^{-1}\widetilde{\mathbf d} + \sum_{\ell=1}^L c_\ell igl(f_\ell - G^*\mathbf u_\ell igr).\) It is the minimum-norm style back-projection \(G^*(GG^*)^{-1}\widetilde{\mathbf d}\) plus a sum of nullspace corrections chosen to enforce the resolving constraints at the property level. This is why SOLA can be viewed as an inversion in disguise. It may not explicitly reconstruct a model as its primary output, but its constrained estimate can often be represented as the target property of a particular proxy model. In the noisy case, the corrections are not generally exact \(G\)-nullspace directions, because \(\mathbf M=GG^*+\mathbf C_D.\) Then \(GG^*\mathbf u_\ell = \mathbf v_\ell-\mathbf C_D\mathbf u_\ell,\) and therefore \(G(G^*\mathbf u_\ell-f_\ell) = -\mathbf C_D\mathbf u_\ell.\) So the corrections belong to the noise-weighted geometry of the problem rather than the exact nullspace of \(G\). Checkpoint Noise-free constrained SOLA has a clean nullspace-proxy interpretation. Noise-aware SOLA has a related proxy interpretation, but the geometry is modified by \(\mathbf C_D\). Appendix C: Suggested Figures Figures for Acts I–III Figure 1: The unknown model behind a curtain. Show a smooth unknown function \(m(r)\) on \([0,1]\). Partially obscure it with a translucent curtain or dashed style. Message: the model exists, but it is not observed directly. Figure 2: Sensitivity kernels as listening devices. Plot several sensitivity kernels \(K_i(r)\) on the same axis. Use light transparent curves so their family structure is visible. Optional annotation: \([\mathbf d]_i=\int_\Omega K_i(r)m(r)\dd r.\) Message: each datum listens to the model through a different kernel. Figure 3: Data as integrals. Show one sensitivity kernel \(K_i(r)\), the model \(m(r)\), and their product \(K_i(r)m(r)\). Shade the area under the product curve. Message: the datum is one number obtained by integrating the product. Figure 4: The target kernel as the desired question. Plot a localized target kernel \(T(r)\). Show it centred at some location \(r_0\). Annotate: \([\mathbf p]_1=\int_\Omega T(r)m(r)\dd r.\) Message: the target kernel encodes the property we wish the data could measure. Figure 5: Weighted kernels becoming a resolving kernel. Show several kernels \(K_i\) with weights \(x_i\). Then show the weighted sum \(R=\sum_i x_iK_i.\) Overlay the target kernel \(T\). Message: choosing data weights is choosing a resolving kernel. Figure 6: Same shape, wrong mass. Plot two similar-looking kernels with different total area. Shade their areas differently. Annotate: \(\int R(r)\dd r
eq 1.\) Message: visual localization is not enough for an average. Figure 7: Unimodularity correction. Show an unconstrained resolving kernel and the constrained resolving kernel. Indicate that the constrained version satisfies \(\int_\Omega R_k(r)\dd r=1.\) Message: the constraint calibrates the resolving kernel. Figures for Acts IV–VI Figure 8: Different target types. Show three target kernels: (a) a positive localized average; (b) a derivative-like target with positive and negative lobes; (c) an oscillatory basis coefficient target. Message: not all targets are averages, so not all constraints should be unit-mass constraints. Figure 9: Resolving constraints as calibration tests. Show a test model \(q\), the data response \(G(q)=\mathbf v\), and the desired property response \(\Tau(q)=\mathbf w\). Then show the constraint \(\mathbf X\mathbf V=\mathbf W.\) Message: resolving constraints enforce correct behavior on selected test directions. Figure 10: Resolution-noise trade-off slider. Make a schematic with a slider. Left side: broad stable resolving kernel with small error bars. Right side: sharp resolving kernel with large error bars. Message: sharper resolution can amplify noise. Figure 11: Propagated covariance. Show data error bars being pushed through \(\mathbf X\) to property error bars. Annotate: \(\mathbf C_P=\mathbf X\mathbf C_D\mathbf X^*.\) Message: this is propagated data-noise uncertainty. Figure 12: Target versus resolving kernel. Overlay \(T_k\) and \(R_k\). Highlight their difference \(T_k-R_k.\) Message: the mismatch direction is where interpretation can leak. Figure 13: Every map point has its own kernel. Show a row of SOLA map values. Under each value, show its associated resolving kernel. Message: a SOLA map is a map of values plus a map of kernels. Figures for Acts VII–X Figure 14: Synthetic cautionary example setup. Panel 1: sensitivity kernels \(K_i\). Panel 2: target kernels \(T_k\). Panel 3: observed data \(\widetilde{\mathbf d}\) with \(\pm1\sigma\) bars. Message: the example begins as a normal SOLA calculation. Figure 15: Good-looking resolving kernels. Overlay resolving kernels \(R_k\) on target kernels \(T_k\). Make the match look visually persuasive. Message: standard diagnostics may look good. Figure 16: The apparent failure. Plot SOLA estimates \([\widetilde{\mathbf p}]_k\) with \(\pm2\sigma\) bands. Overlay true target properties \([ ar{\mathbf p}]_k=[\Tau( ar m)]_k.\) Message: the target-property interpretation can fail dramatically. Figure 17: Nullspace cartoon. Show model space as a plane or room. Show data-visible directions and data-invisible directions. Mark a direction \(h\) with \(G(h)=\mathbf 0,\; \Tau(h)
eq\mathbf 0.\) Message: some directions are invisible to data but visible to target properties. Figure 18: Proxy model diagram. Show two paths: \(\widetilde{\mathbf d} \xrightarrow{\;\widetilde{\mathbf X}_c\;} \widetilde{\mathbf p}\) and \(\widetilde{\mathbf d} \longmapsto \hat m \xrightarrow{\;\Tau\;} \widetilde{\mathbf p}.\) Message: SOLA can be interpreted directly or through a proxy model. Figure 19: Resolution operator versus resolving kernel. Show classical inversion: \(m\mapsto \mathcal Rm.\) Show SOLA: \(T_k\mapsto R_k=\mathcal R^*T_k.\) Message: resolution operators and resolving kernels are related views of the same filtering phenomenon. Figure 20: Shifted noise versus observation model. Left panel: a Gaussian cloud centred at \(\widetilde{\mathbf d}\). Right panel: a family of Gaussian clouds centred at \(G(m)\) for different \(m\). Message: shifted noise is observation-centred, the observation model is model-centred. Figure 21: Frequentist SOLA. Show: \(\dobs = G(m_{\mathrm{true}}) + 
obs \;\longmapsto\; \pobs = \mathbf X G(m_{\mathrm{true}}) + \etaobs.\) Show confidence set: \(C_{\alpha}^{\mathbf X}(\pobs) = \pobs - F_{\alpha}\) with coverage \(1-\alpha.\) Message: SOLA transforms the observation problem; the frequentist framework gives calibrated confidence without a prior. Figure 22: Final summary graphic. Three columns: (1) Ask with targets: \(T_k.\) (2) Interpret with resolving kernels: \(R_k.\) (3) Add priors when you want truth: \( ar m\in B\) or \(m\sim\muprior.\) Message: the whole document in one picture. ← Act 10: What SOLA Is Good For Back to Overview →

title: Act I: A Familiar Problem | Think First, Discretize Later | Adrian Mag
desc: Act I of Think First, Discretize Later: A simple inverse problem that looks fine on the surface but hides a silent trap.
text:
Act I: A Familiar Problem A simple inverse problem that looks fine, until you look deeper. Part of Think First, Discretize Later . « Overview 1 Familiar Problem 2 Something Is Wrong 3 What Problem? 4 Functional Analysis 5 Data & Adjoint 6 The Prior 7 The Repair 8 The Verdict S Summary A Simple Inverse Problem The continuous story we have not yet taken seriously We begin with a deliberately modest inverse problem. There is an unknown object, which we call the model , and there are finitely many noisy observations of that model. The observations do not reveal the model directly. Instead, each datum is obtained by applying a known measurement rule to the model and then corrupting the result with noise. At first, we will treat this problem in the most computationally convenient way: we will discretize the model immediately, represent it using basis functions, turn the forward map into a matrix, and compute a finite-dimensional Gaussian posterior. This is the obvious route. It is also the route that will eventually betray us. The purpose of this first act is not to do things correctly. The purpose is to do something plausible, watch it appear to work, and then prepare the stage for the moment when the cracks start to show. The unknown model Let the physical domain be an interval \[ \Omega = [0,L]. \] The unknown model is a function \[ m : \Omega 	o \R. \] For example, \(m(x)\) might describe a material property as a function of depth, position, or time. At this stage we will not ask too carefully what kind of function \(m\) is allowed to be. Is it continuous? Square-integrable? Smooth? Does it satisfy boundary conditions? Does it have derivatives? For now, we only say \[ m \in 	ext{some space of functions on } \Omega. \] This vagueness is intentional. It reflects the way many inverse problems first appear in practice. We know that there is a function we want to infer, and we know that our data depend on it. The exact mathematical home of that function is often postponed until later. Warning The phrase "some space of functions" is not harmless. It is a modelling choice waiting to happen. If we do not make it explicitly, the discretization will make it for us. The observations Suppose we have \(N_d\) observations, \[ [\obs]_1,\ldots,[\obs]_{N_d} \in \R. \] We collect them into a data vector \[ \obs =  egin{pmatrix} [\obs]_1 \ \vdots \ [\obs]_{N_d} \end{pmatrix} \in \R^{N_d}. \] Each observation is a noisy measurement of the unknown function. A typical example has the form \[ [\obs]_i = \int_{\Omega} K_i(x)\,m(x)\,dx + [
oise]_i, \qquad i=1,\ldots,N_d, \] where \(K_i\) is a known sensitivity kernel and \([
oise]_i\) is observational noise. The sensitivity kernel \(K_i\) tells us which parts of the model influence the \(i\)th datum. If \(K_i\) is concentrated near some point, then the datum is mostly sensitive to the model near that point. If \(K_i\) is broad, then the datum blends information over a wider region. Intuition Each datum is a weighted average of the model, plus noise. The kernels \(K_i\) are the weights. They decide what the experiment can see and what it must leave hidden. The forward operator We define the forward operator \[ G : \M 	o \R^{N_d} \] componentwise by \[ [G(m)]_i = \int_{\Omega} K_i(x)\,m(x)\,dx, \qquad i=1,\ldots,N_d. \] Here \(\M\) denotes the model space, although we have not yet chosen it carefully. This is one of the central tensions of the story: we already know how to write down the measurements, but we have not yet decided what mathematical universe the unknown belongs to. The map \(G\) is linear: \[ G(\alpha m_1 +  eta m_2) = \alpha G(m_1) +  eta G(m_2), \] for scalars \(\alpha, eta \in \R\) and models \(m_1,m_2 \in \M\). This linearity is important. It means that we are studying a linear inverse problem . The difficulty will not come from nonlinearity. The difficulty will come from a quieter source: the interaction between infinite-dimensional unknowns, finite-dimensional data, priors, and discretization. Remark We adopt the following typographic conventions throughout these notes. Finite-dimensional objects. Boldface letters denote finite-dimensional vectors and matrices (coefficient/representation objects). For example \(\mathbf{v}\in\R^N\) and \(\mathbf{A}\in\R^{N	imes N}\). Infinite-dimensional objects. Non-bold (lightface) letters denote infinite-dimensional operators or functions acting on the model Hilbert space \(\M\); e.g. \(G:\M	o\D\), \(C_0:\M	o\M\). Components / entries. The components of a vector or the entries of a matrix are written with square brackets and subscripts: \([\mathbf v]_i = v_i\), \([\mathbf A]_{ij} = A_{ij}\). When an object is represented in a particular basis \(\{\phi_k\}_{k=1}^N\) we always mean the coordinates with respect to that basis. Adjoints and transposes. We reserve \(^{	op}\) for the Euclidean transpose of a finite matrix and \(^{*}\) for the Hilbert adjoint of an operator. Discrete adjoints that incorporate mass/weight matrices will be written explicitly. Infinite sequences. When working with infinite coefficient sequences we use index notation \((\alpha_i)_{i\ge1}\); for finite coefficient vectors we write \(\mathbf\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_N)^{	op}\) so that \([\mathbf\alpha]_i=\alpha_i\). Bar and tilde. A bar denotes the true model: \( ar{m}\) is the true model, \( ar{\mathbf{d}}=G ar{m}\) is the noise-free data. A tilde denotes posterior or observed quantities: \(	ilde{\mathbf{d}}\) is the observed data, \(	ilde{m}_N^{\obs}\) is the posterior mean function, \(	ilde{\mathbf{u}}_N^{\obs}\) are the posterior mean coefficients. Gaussian observational noise We assume that the noise vector \[ 
oise =  egin{pmatrix} [
oise]_1 \ \vdots \ [
oise]_{N_d} \end{pmatrix} \] is Gaussian: \[ 
oise \sim \N(0,\Cd), \] where \(\Cd \in \R^{N_d 	imes N_d}\) is symmetric positive definite. The covariance matrix \(\Cd\) encodes the size and correlation structure of the observational errors. If \[ \Cd = \sigma_D^2 \mathbf{I}_{N_d}, \] then the noise components are independent and have the same variance \(\sigma_D^2\). More generally, off-diagonal entries of \(\Cd\) allow different data errors to be correlated. Thus, the data model is \[ \obs = G(m) + 
oise, \qquad 
oise \sim \N(0,\Cd). \] The inverse problem in its most innocent form The data equation The inverse problem begins with the equation \[ \obs = G m + 
oise. \] Here \[ \obs \in \D, \qquad m \in \M, \qquad 
oise \sim \N(0,\Cd), \] where, for this first example, \[ \D = \R^{N_d}. \] This equation is compact, but it contains almost the entire drama. The unknown \(m\) belongs to a function space. The data \(\obs\) belong to a finite-dimensional space. The forward map \(G\) compresses a function into finitely many numbers. Noise is then added. The inverse problem asks us to travel in the opposite direction: \[ \obs \quad \leadsto \quad m. \] But the arrow is not reversible. Many different functions can give essentially the same data. What we want to infer In a deterministic inverse problem, we might ask for a single best model \(m^\dagger\) satisfying \[ G m^\dagger \approx \obs. \] In a Bayesian inverse problem, we ask for something richer: a probability distribution over possible models after observing the data. That is, we want the posterior measure \[ \post = \mathbb{P}(m \in \cdot \mid \obs). \] This posterior should tell us not only which models fit the data well, but also how uncertain we remain. The posterior mean may summarize the central tendency, but the posterior covariance, credible intervals, and samples reveal the spread. Lesson The output of a Bayesian inverse problem is not just a curve. It is a probability measure on possible curves. Why the problem is indirect The difficulty is that the data are finite and indirect. Each datum is only a projection, average, or blurred measurement of the model. If the model is a function, then it has infinitely many degrees of freedom, while the data vector has only \(N_d\) components. Even before noise enters, the equation \[ \obs = G m \] usually has many solutions or no exact solution. With noise, exact equality is not the right goal anyway. Instead, we must combine three ingredients: the information supplied by the data; the uncertainty in the observations; prior information about plausible models. The Bayesian framework gives us a systematic way to combine these ingredients. But only if the ingredients themselves are chosen coherently. Intuition The data do not show us the model directly. They show us shadows of the model cast through the forward operator. Discretizing First Choosing hat functions Now we take the computational shortcut. Instead of first deciding what the function space \(\M\) really is, we immediately introduce a finite-dimensional basis. This is natural, practical, and familiar. It is also the seed of the problem. A mesh on the physical domain Let \[ 0 = x_1 < x_2 < \cdots < x_N = L \] be a mesh on \(\Omega = [0,L]\). For simplicity, we may imagine a uniform mesh with spacing \[ h =  rac{L}{N-1}. \] The mesh converts the continuous domain into finitely many nodes. We will represent the unknown model by its coefficients relative to basis functions associated with these nodes. Piecewise-linear basis functions Let \[ \{\phi_j\}_{j=1}^N \] be the standard piecewise-linear hat functions associated with the mesh. Thus \[ \phi_j(x_i) = \delta_{ij}, \] and each \(\phi_j\) is supported only near the node \(x_j\). The hat functions form a basis for the finite-dimensional space \[ \M_N = \operatorname{span}\{\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_N\}. \] Every function in \(\M_N\) is continuous and piecewise linear. At this point, the discretization feels like a harmless approximation. We are not solving for an arbitrary function anymore. We are solving for a function inside \(\M_N\). The finite-dimensional approximation We write \[ m_N(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{N} [\mathbf{u}]_j \phi_j(x). \] The unknown function has now been replaced by the coefficient vector \[ \mathbf{u} =  egin{pmatrix} [\mathbf{u}]_1 \ \vdots \ [\mathbf{u}]_N \end{pmatrix} \in \R^N. \] The coefficient \([\mathbf{u}]_j\) controls the amplitude of the \(j\)th hat function. Since \(\phi_j(x_i)=\delta_{ij}\), for nodal hat functions the coefficient \([\mathbf{u}]_j\) is also the value of the approximate function at node \(x_j\): \[ m_N(x_j) = [\mathbf{u}]_j. \] This makes the representation easy to interpret. It also quietly encourages us to think of \(\mathbf{u}\) as the actual unknown, rather than as a coordinate vector representing a function. Warning A coefficient vector is not the same thing as a function. The vector \(\mathbf{u}\) becomes a function only after we choose the basis that interprets it. F1b, Basis and discretization. The \(N=30\) hat functions \(\phi_j\) and the true model \( ar{m}\) projected onto them, with nodal coefficients \([\mathbf{u}]_j\). F1, The setup. The true model \( ar{m}\), the sensitivity kernels \(K_i\), and the twenty noisy data points. Turning the forward map into a matrix Data predicted by basis functions For each basis function \(\phi_j\), we can compute its contribution to each datum: \[ [\Gb]_{ij} = [G(\phi_j)]_i. \] In the integral-kernel example, this means \[ [\Gb]_{ij} = \int_{\Omega} K_i(x)\,\phi_j(x)\,dx. \] Therefore, if \[ m_N(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{N} [\mathbf{u}]_j\phi_j(x), \] then linearity gives \[ [G(m_N)]_i = \sum_{j=1}^N [\mathbf{u}]_j G_i\phi_j = \sum_{j=1}^N [\Gb]_{ij}[\mathbf{u}]_j. \] In vector form, \[ G(m_N) = \Gb\mathbf{u}, \] where \[ \Gb \in \R^{N_d 	imes N}. \] F1c, The discrete forward matrix. Each entry \([\Gb]_{ij}\) measures how strongly the \(j\)th hat function contributes to the \(i\)th datum. The naive matrix problem The continuous-looking inverse problem has now become the finite-dimensional linear model \[ \obs = \Gb \mathbf{u} + 
oise, \] with \[ 
oise \sim \N(0,\Cd). \] This is a standard Bayesian linear regression problem. Everything appears to be finite-dimensional. Everything appears to be familiar. We have a design matrix \(\Gb\), unknown coefficients \(\mathbf{u}\), data \(\obs\), and Gaussian noise. At this stage, it is tempting to forget the function \(m\) entirely and simply declare victory over the infinite-dimensional problem. The beast has been put in a matrix-shaped cage. But we will soon find out the beast cannot be contained, it is after all an infinite-dimensional beast. A Gaussian prior on coefficients The tempting choice To complete the Bayesian formulation, we need a prior distribution on the unknown coefficients.
