The most tempting choice is \[ \mathbf{u} \sim \N(0,\sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_N). \] Equivalently, \[ \mathbf{C}_N = \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_N. \] This says that the coefficients are independent, centred Gaussian random variables: \[ [\mathbf{u}]_j \sim \N(0,\sigma^2), \qquad j=1,\ldots,N, \] with no prior correlation between different nodes. More generally, we may allow a nonzero prior mean \[ \mathbf{u}_0 \in \R^N \] and write \[ \mathbf{u} \sim \N(\mathbf{u}_0,\mathbf{C}_N). \] For the naive example, however, the important case is \[ \mathbf{C}_N = \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_N. \] Why this looks reasonable at first glance The prior \(\N(0,\sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_N)\) looks reasonable for several reasons. First, it is simple. It introduces only one scale parameter, \(\sigma\), which controls the typical size of the coefficients. Second, it is symmetric in the coefficients. No node is preferred over any other node. Third, it is computationally convenient. The covariance matrix is diagonal, easy to store, easy to invert, and easy to sample from. Fourth, it resembles a familiar finite-dimensional default: when we do not know much about a vector, we often place an isotropic Gaussian prior on it. These arguments are not silly. In a genuinely finite-dimensional problem, they may be defensible. The trouble begins when this prior is used as a stand-in for a probability distribution over functions and then carried through mesh refinement. Intuition A diagonal prior says that every coefficient is allowed to wiggle independently. As the mesh becomes finer, we add more wiggles. Unless their size is controlled in a way that depends on the function space, the wiggles do not politely vanish. They accumulate. F1d, Prior samples. Draws from the naive prior \(\mathbf{u}\sim\N(0,\sigma^2\mathbf{I}_N)\), shown both as coefficient vectors and as reconstructed functions \(m_N^{(s)}(z)\). The naive posterior Finite-dimensional Gaussian conditioning We now have the finite-dimensional Bayesian linear model \[ \mathbf{u} \sim \N(\mathbf{u}_0,\mathbf{C}_N), \] and \[ \obs\mid \mathbf{u} \sim \N(\Gb\mathbf{u},\Cd). \] Because both the prior and the noise are Gaussian, the posterior distribution of \(\mathbf{u}\) given \(\obs\) is also Gaussian: \[ \mathbf{u}\mid \obs \sim \N(	ilde{\mathbf{u}}_N^{\obs},\mathbf{C}_N^{\obs}). \] This is one of the great computational conveniences of linear Gaussian inverse problems. The posterior is available in closed form. No sampling method is needed to obtain the posterior mean or covariance. Posterior covariance The posterior covariance is \[ \mathbf{C}_N^{\obs} = \mathbf{C}_N - \mathbf{C}_N \Gb^{\T} \left( \Gb \mathbf{C}_N \Gb^{\T} + \Cd ight)^{-1} \Gb \mathbf{C}_N. \] The matrix \[ \Gb \mathbf{C}_N \Gb^{\T} + \Cd \] is the covariance of the predicted data, including both prior uncertainty pushed through the forward model and observational noise. The term \[ \mathbf{C}_N \Gb^{\T} \left( \Gb \mathbf{C}_N \Gb^{\T} + \Cd ight)^{-1} \Gb \mathbf{C}_N \] is the amount of prior covariance removed by observing the data. In directions where the data are informative, the posterior uncertainty shrinks. In directions that the data cannot see, the posterior remains close to the prior. This last sentence is the fuse. If the prior is badly behaved in the unseen directions, then the posterior inherits that bad behaviour. Posterior mean The posterior mean is \[ 	ilde{\mathbf{u}}_N^{\obs} = \mathbf{u}_0 + \mathbf{C}_N \Gb^{\T} \left( \Gb \mathbf{C}_N \Gb^{\T} + \Cd ight)^{-1} \left( \obs - \Gb\mathbf{u}_0 ight). \] The term \(\obs - \Gb\mathbf{u}_0\) is the data residual relative to the prior mean. The operator \[ \mathbf{C}_N \Gb^{\T} \left( \Gb \mathbf{C}_N \Gb^{\T} + \Cd ight)^{-1} \] maps this residual back into coefficient space. For the zero-mean isotropic prior \(\mathbf{C}_N=\sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_N\), this becomes \[ 	ilde{\mathbf{u}}_N^{\obs} = \sigma^2 \Gb^{\T} \left( \sigma^2 \Gb\Gb^{\T} + \Cd ight)^{-1} \obs. \] Everything here is finite-dimensional and computable. We can assemble \(\Gb\), choose \(\mathbf{C}_N\) and \(\Cd\), compute the posterior mean, and reconstruct a function from the coefficient vector. The first plot: it looks fine Reconstructing the posterior mean Once the posterior mean coefficients \(	ilde{\mathbf{u}}_N^{\obs}\) are computed, we convert them back into a function: \[ 	ilde{m}_N^{\obs}(x) = \sum_{j=1}^N 	ilde{u}_{N,j}^{\obs} \phi_j(x). \] This reconstructed posterior mean is the curve we would naturally plot against the true model. It is smooth enough to look respectable, flexible enough to follow the main features of the truth, and stable enough that nothing appears obviously broken. In a practical workflow, this is often the first moment of relief: the code runs, the matrix dimensions agree, the posterior mean has the right shape, and the curve seems to pass the eye test. F2, Naive recovery on hats. The posterior mean under a \(\sigma_m^2\mathbf{I}\) prior tracks \( ar{m}\). Nothing looks wrong, yet. Comparing the mean with the truth Suppose the true model is \(m_{\mathrm{true}}\). Then the synthetic data are generated by \[ \obs = G m_{\mathrm{true}} + 
oise. \] After computing \(	ilde{m}_N^{\obs}\), we compare \[ 	ilde{m}_N^{\obs}(x) \quad 	ext{with} \quad m_{\mathrm{true}}(x). \] If the observations are informative enough and the noise level is moderate, the posterior mean may recover the broad features of the truth. Peaks may appear in approximately the right places. Long-wavelength structure may be captured. The result may look scientifically plausible. This is the dangerous part. The posterior mean can look sensible even when the posterior distribution is not. The false comfort of a plausible curve The posterior mean is only one summary of the posterior. It does not tell us whether typical posterior samples are reasonable. It does not tell us whether posterior uncertainty is controlled under mesh refinement. It does not tell us whether the finite-dimensional posterior is approaching a meaningful infinite-dimensional object. A plausible mean can therefore hide a pathological posterior. The reason is simple: the data constrain only a finite number of directions. If the number of basis functions \(N\) is larger than the number of observations \(N_d\), then there are directions in coefficient space that are weakly constrained or entirely invisible to the data. In those directions, the posterior covariance is controlled mostly by the prior. If the prior was chosen without reference to a continuous function-space model, there is no reason to expect that uncertainty to behave sensibly as \(N\) increases. Checkpoint At this stage, the posterior mean may look acceptable. The trap is that a reasonable-looking mean can hide an unreasonable posterior measure. What we have done so far Let us summarize the naive workflow. We began with an unknown function \(m\) on a domain \(\Omega\). We introduced data through a linear forward map \(G\). We discretized the model immediately using hat functions. We replaced the function \(m\) by coefficients \(\mathbf{u}\). We replaced the forward operator by a matrix \(\Gb\). We placed a Gaussian prior directly on the coefficients. We computed the finite-dimensional Gaussian posterior. We reconstructed and plotted the posterior mean. (None of this is a straw man: discretize first, then estimate coefficients, is exactly the workflow the standard inverse-theory textbooks teach, see, e.g., Menke [Men18] . The next act asks what it quietly assumes.) Nothing in this list looks outrageous. That is precisely why the example is useful. The mistake is not dramatic. It does not announce itself by crashing the code or producing nonsense immediately. It hides behind a plausible curve. Lesson The first act ends with a posterior mean that looks alright. The second act begins by asking what the posterior itself is doing. References William Menke (2018). Geophysical Data Analysis: Discrete Inverse Theory , 4th edition. Elsevier. The discretize-first workflow, as the textbooks teach it. doi:10.1016/C2016-0-05203-8 ← Overview Act II: Something Is Wrong →

title: Act II: Something Is Wrong | Think First, Discretize Later | Adrian Mag
desc: Act II of Think First, Discretize Later: Sampling the naive posterior reveals that uncertainty explodes under mesh refinement.

title: Act III: What Problem Are We Actually Solving? | Think First, Discretize Later | Adrian Mag
desc: Act III of Think First, Discretize Later: Stepping back to define the function-space inverse problem before discretizing.

title: Act IV: A Guided Detour Through Functional Analysis | Think First, Discretize Later | Adrian Mag
desc: Act IV of Think First, Discretize Later: A guided climb through functional analysis, from sets to Hilbert spaces.
text:
Act IV: A Guided Detour Through Functional Analysis From sets to Hilbert spaces, each layer of structure makes more of the inverse problem meaningful. Part of Think First, Discretize Later . « Overview 1 Familiar Problem 2 Something Is Wrong 3 What Problem? 4 Functional Analysis 5 Data & Adjoint 6 The Prior 7 The Repair 8 The Verdict S Summary A Zoo of Spaces Why there are so many spaces We have reached the point where the inverse problem can no longer be treated as a matrix problem wearing a function-shaped hat. We must decide where the unknown model lives. This forces us into the world of functional analysis. At first glance, functional analysis looks like a zoo. There are sets, topological spaces, metric spaces, vector spaces, normed spaces, Banach spaces, inner-product spaces, Hilbert spaces, Sobolev spaces, spaces of distributions, spaces of continuous functions, spaces of measures, and many others. This abundance is not mathematical decoration. Each type of space carries a different kind of structure. Each structure allows us to ask different questions. For inverse problems, the relevant questions include: What objects are admissible models? What does it mean for two models to be close? What does it mean for a sequence of models to converge? Can we add perturbations to a model? Can we measure the size of a perturbation? Can we define angles, orthogonality, projections, and adjoints? Can we place a Gaussian prior on the space? Different spaces answer these questions with different levels of richness. The path through this chapter is therefore not a catalogue for its own sake. It is a guided climb: each step adds just enough structure to make more of the inverse problem meaningful. Intuition A space is not only a container for objects. It is a rulebook for what we are allowed to do with those objects. F4a, The structure ladder. Click any rung to see what that level of structure makes possible. Each rung inherits everything below it. Set membership: \(m \in \M\) Topological space continuity, convergence (without distance) Metric space distance: \(d(m_1, m_2)\) Vector space perturbations, linear combinations: \(m + \delta m\) Normed space size: \(\|m\|\), Lipschitz continuity Banach space complete limits: Cauchy \(\Rightarrow\) convergent Inner-product space angles, orthogonality, projections: \(\langle u, v angle\) Hilbert space adjoints, spectral theory, Gaussian measures, covariance operators Sets Membership The simplest mathematical structure is a set. A set is just a collection of objects. If \(X\) is a set and \(x\) is one of its elements, we write \(x \in X\). For example, we might write \(m \in \M\) to say that \(m\) is an admissible model. At the level of sets, the only basic question is membership: \(	ext{Is this object allowed or not?}\) A set tells us which objects belong to our model universe, but nothing more. For example, suppose \[ \M = \{m:\Omega	o\R\}. \] This says that every real-valued function on \(\Omega\) is admissible. But it does not tell us whether one function is close to another, whether a sequence of functions converges, whether small perturbations make sense, or whether Gaussian probability measures can be placed on \(\M\). No geometry yet A bare set has no geometry. There is no distance, no notion of size, no notion of angle, and no notion of convergence. If \(m_1,m_2\in \M\), a set alone does not allow us to ask whether \(m_1\) is close to \(m_2\), nor whether \(m_n 	o m\). This is too little structure for inverse problems. In inverse problems, we need to compare models, perturb models, approximate models, and study the behaviour of sequences of approximations. Lesson A set tells us what objects are allowed. It does not tell us how those objects relate to one another. Topological spaces Open sets The next layer of structure is topology. A topological space is a set \(X\) together with a collection of subsets called open sets. We write this collection as \(\mathcal{T}\). The pair \((X,\mathcal{T})\) is called a topological space. The open sets tell us what it means for points to be near one another, but in a very flexible way. A topology does not necessarily come from a distance. It only tells us which subsets count as neighbourhoods. The collection \(\mathcal{T}\) must satisfy: \(\varnothing \in \mathcal{T}\) and \(X\in\mathcal{T}\); arbitrary unions of open sets are open; finite intersections of open sets are open. These rules are abstract, but the goal is familiar: topology lets us talk about continuity and convergence without first committing to a particular formula for distance. Continuity If \(X\) and \(Y\) are topological spaces, a map \(F:X	o Y\) is continuous if the inverse image of every open set in \(Y\) is open in \(X\). That is, if \(U\subset Y\) is open, then \(F^{-1}(U) = \{x\in X : F(x)\in U\}\) must be open in \(X\). For inverse problems, continuity matters because the forward map should not behave like a mathematical trapdoor. If two models are close, their predicted data should also be close: \[ m_n 	o m \quad\Longrightarrow\quad G m_n 	o G m. \] Convergence without distances A topology gives a notion of convergence. We can say that a sequence \(x_1,x_2,x_3,\ldots\) converges to \(x\) if, eventually, the sequence lies in every neighbourhood of \(x\). The important point is that convergence can be discussed without a distance function. This is useful in many areas of analysis, especially when dealing with weak convergence, distributions, and probability measures. However, for the present story, topology alone is still too sparse. We will want to measure sizes of perturbations, define covariance operators, and discuss Gaussian priors. For this, it is usually helpful to have more structure. Intuition Topology tells us when things approach each other, but it does not necessarily tell us how far apart they are. Metric spaces Distances A metric space is a set \(X\) equipped with a distance function \(d:X	imes X	o [0,\infty)\). For \(x,y,z\in X\), the metric must satisfy: \(d(x,y)\geq 0\); \(d(x,y)=0\) if and only if \(x=y\); \(d(x,y)=d(y,x)\); \(d(x,z)\leq d(x,y)+d(y,z)\). The last condition is the triangle inequality. A metric allows us to quantify closeness: \(d(x,y) \ll 1\). In inverse problems, metrics let us ask whether reconstructed models are close to one another, whether approximations converge, and whether the posterior changes continuously when the data are perturbed. Convergence by distance In a metric space, convergence has a very concrete meaning: \(x_n 	o x\) if \(d(x_n,x)	o 0\). For example, if \(X=C([0,L])\), we may define the uniform distance \(d(f,g) = \sup_{x\in[0,L]} |f(x)-g(x)|\). Then \(f_n 	o f\) means uniform convergence. Alternatively, if \(X=L^2(\Omega)\), we may define \(d(f,g) = \left( \int_\Omega |f(x)-g(x)|^2\,dx ight)^{1/2}\). Then convergence means convergence in mean-square size. These two notions of convergence are different. Choosing a space means choosing which distinctions matter. Warning There is no single universal notion of closeness between functions. The chosen space decides what kind of closeness is being measured. Vector spaces Addition and scalar multiplication A vector space is a set \(V\) whose elements can be added and multiplied by scalars. If \(u,v\in V\) and \(\alpha, eta\in\R\), then \(\alpha u+ eta v \in V\). Examples include \(\R^N\), \(L^2(\Omega)\), \(C([0,L])\), \(H^1(\Omega)\). If \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) are models, vector space structure lets us form \(m_1+m_2\), \(\alpha m_1\), \(m_1-m_2\). The difference \(m_1-m_2\) is especially important, it represents a perturbation, an update, or an error. Perturbations In inverse problems, we often reason in terms of perturbations: \(m = m_0+\delta m\). Here \(m_0\) is a reference model and \(\delta m\) is an update. This expression only makes sense if the model space has a linear structure. Linear structure is also what allows us to describe Gaussian priors by adding a random perturbation to a mean: \(m = m_0 + \xi\), where \(\xi\) is a centred random element. Intuition Vector spaces are natural when models can be nudged, corrected, averaged, and superposed. Linear inverse problems A linear inverse problem is built around a linear forward map \(G:\M	o\D\). Linearity means \(G(\alpha m_1+ eta m_2) = \alpha G m_1+ eta G m_2\). This structure is powerful. It allows us to understand how perturbations in the model produce perturbations in the data: \(\delta y = G \delta m\). It also allows Gaussian priors and Gaussian noise to produce Gaussian posteriors, provided the rest of the formulation is coherent. But vector spaces alone are still not enough. They let us add models, but they do not tell us how large a model is, how far apart two models are, or what it means for an infinite sequence of approximations to converge. For that, we need norms. Manifolds When the unknown does not live in a vector space Not every meaningful model space is naturally a vector space. Sometimes the unknown lives on a curved space called a manifold. Examples include: directions on a sphere; rotations in three dimensions; positive-definite matrices; shapes or interfaces; diffeomorphisms; fields constrained to have fixed magnitude. In such cases, adding two models may not make sense. The model space is curved, not linear. Tangent spaces Even when the model space is a manifold, local perturbations often live in a linear space called a tangent space. If \(m\) is a point on a manifold \(\mathcal{M}\), the tangent space at \(m\) is written \(T_m\mathcal{M}\). Elements of \(T_m\mathcal{M}\) represent infinitesimal perturbations around \(m\). In this document, we will not go in that direction. Our goal is already rich enough: to understand why even linear inverse problems can go wrong if we discretize before choosing the function-space formulation. Remark Manifolds are important, but this document stays in the linear world. Our unknowns will live in vector spaces. Adding Structure One Layer at a Time From set to vector space We now rebuild the model space slowly. The aim is to understand why each layer of structure is useful and what it buys us. A bare set tells us which objects are allowed. A vector space tells us that objects can be added, scaled, and perturbed. This is the first major step toward linear inverse problems. Linear combinations allow us to construct approximations by basis expansion: \(m_N = \sum_{j=1}^N [\mathbf{u}]_j\phi_j\), form averages \( ar{m} = \E[m]\), and study fluctuations \(m- ar{m}\). These operations are essential in Gaussian Bayesian inversion. Lesson Linear spaces are the natural habitat of additive perturbations. If our inference problem is about updates, differences, and superposition, linear structure is not decoration. It is the grammar. From vector space to normed space A vector space lets us add and scale. But it still does not tell us how large a model is. To measure size, we introduce a norm. A normed space is a vector space \(V\) equipped with a function \(
orm{\cdot}:V	o[0,\infty)\) such that, for all \(u,v\in V\) and \(\alpha\in\R\): \(
orm{u}\geq 0\); \(
orm{u}=0\) if and only if \(u=0\); \(
orm{\alpha u}=|\alpha|\,
orm{u}\); \(
orm{u+v}\leq 
orm{u}+
orm{v}\). Measuring size In \(L^2(\Omega)\), \(
orm{m}_{L^2} = \left( \int_\Omega |m(x)|^2\,dx ight)^{1/2}\). This norm measures the root-mean-square size of a function. In \(H^1(\Omega)\), \(
orm{m}_{H^1} = \left( \int_\Omega |m(x)|^2\,dx + \int_\Omega |m'(x)|^2\,dx ight)^{1/2}\). This norm measures both the size of the function and the size of its derivative. Thus, choosing a norm is not neutral. It decides which features of a model are expensive. F4b, Different norms see different things. Choose a perturbation \(\delta m\). The same function looks small under \(\|\cdot\|_{L^2}\) but large under \(\|\cdot\|_{H^1}\) when it oscillates rapidly, because \(H^1\) also measures the derivative. sin(2πx), low freq sin(20πx), high freq localized bump Convergence A norm automatically defines a distance: \(d(m_1,m_2) = 
orm{m_1-m_2}\). Therefore, it gives a notion of convergence: \(m_n 	o m\) if \(
orm{m_n-m}	o 0\). This is crucial for discretization. When we say that finite-dimensional approximations converge to a function-space model, we must mean convergence in some norm: \(
orm{m_N-m}_{\M}	o 0\). Different norms give different meanings to this statement. Warning A discretization cannot be called convergent until we say which norm or topology defines convergence. From normed space to Banach space Normed spaces are useful, but one more property is often essential: completeness. A complete normed vector space is called a Banach space. A sequence \((m_n)\) in a normed space is called Cauchy if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists an index \(N_\varepsilon\) such that \(
orm{m_n-m_k} < \varepsilon\) whenever \(n,k\geq N_\varepsilon\). A normed space is complete if every Cauchy sequence has a limit in the space. Completeness prevents sequences from slipping out of the space through invisible cracks. Intuition Completeness means that if a sequence behaves as though it is converging, the limit has not been exiled from the space. From Banach space to inner-product space A Banach space gives us size and convergence. But for many parts of linear inverse theory, we want more: angles, orthogonality, projections, and adjoints. These come from an inner product. An inner product on a real vector space \(V\) is a map \(\inner{\cdot}{\cdot}:V	imes V	o\R\) such that, for \(u,v,w\in V\) and \(\alpha, eta\in\R\): \(\inner{u}{v}=\inner{v}{u}\); \(\inner{\alpha u+ eta v}{w} = \alpha\inner{u}{w}+ eta\inner{v}{w}\); \(\inner{u}{u}\geq 0\); \(\inner{u}{u}=0\) if and only if \(u=0\). An inner product defines a norm by \(
orm{u} = \sqrt{\inner{u}{u}}\). Angles and orthogonality In \(L^2(\Omega)\), \(\inner{f}{g}_{L^2} = \int_\Omega f(x)g(x)\,dx\). Two elements are orthogonal if \(\inner{u}{v} = 0\). Orthogonality is indispensable in approximation theory. The best approximation to \(m\in\M\) in a subspace \(\M_N\) is characterized by: \(\inner{m-P_Nm}{v_N}_{\M}=0\) for all \(v_N\in\M_N\). Projection The orthogonal projection \(P_Nm\) is the element of \(\M_N\) closest to \(m\): \(P_Nm = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{v_N\in\M_N} 
orm{m-v_N}_{\M}\). The error \(m-P_Nm\) is orthogonal to the approximation space. From inner-product space to Hilbert space An inner-product space becomes a Hilbert space when it is complete with respect to the norm induced by the inner product. Thus, a Hilbert space is an inner-product space in which every Cauchy sequence converges. Hilbert spaces are especially useful because they provide: a norm for measuring size; a topology for discussing convergence; an inner product for geometry; orthogonality; projections onto closed subspaces; adjoints of bounded linear operators; spectral theory for many important operators; a natural language for covariance operators; a convenient setting for Gaussian measures. For linear inverse problems, the adjoint is particularly important. If \(G:\M	o\D\) is a bounded linear map between Hilbert spaces, its adjoint \(G^{\adj}:\D	o\M\) is defined by \(\inner{G m}{d}_{\D} = \inner{m}{G^{\adj} d}_{\M}\). This definition depends on the inner products of both spaces. It is not merely a transpose. The transpose appears only after coordinates and Euclidean geometries have been chosen. Lesson Hilbert spaces are not the only possible model spaces, but they are often the simplest setting where geometry, projection, adjoints, and Gaussian priors can speak the same language. Hilbert Spaces We Actually Use \(L^2\) spaces The space \(L^2(\Omega)\) consists of square-integrable functions: \[ L^2(\Omega) = \left\{ f : \Omega 	o \R : \int_\Omega |f(x)|^2\,dx < \infty ight\}. \] The inner product is \(\inner{f}{g}_{L^2} = \int_\Omega f(x)g(x)\,dx\), and the norm is \(
orm{f}_{L^2} = \left( \int_\Omega |f(x)|^2\,dx ight)^{1/2}\). For the toy inverse problem, the \(L^2\) setting is natural if \(K_i\in L^2(\Omega)\). Then, by Cauchy-Schwarz, \(|[G(m)]_i| \leq 
orm{K_i}_{L^2} 
orm{m}_{L^2}\). However, \(L^2(\Omega)\) does not directly encode smoothness, and pointwise values are not fundamental. If the data require pointwise values, \(L^2\) may not be the right model space. Warning Choosing \(L^2\) says that average-square size matters. It does not say that functions are smooth, continuous, or pointwise meaningful. Sobolev spaces Weak derivatives Sobolev spaces add controlled derivatives to the story. A function \(f\) has a weak derivative \(g\) if integration by parts behaves as though \(g\) were the derivative of \(f\): \(\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi'(x)\,dx = -\int_\Omega g(x)\varphi(x)\,dx\) for every sufficiently smooth test function \(\varphi\). (Everything in this zoo, from normed spaces to the Sobolev scale, is developed rigorously and readably in Brezis [Bre11] , the reference to keep at hand for this act.) Smoothness as square-integrability of derivatives For an integer \(k\geq 0\), the Sobolev space \(H^k(\Omega)\) is \[ H^k(\Omega) = \left\{ f \in L^2(\Omega) : D^\alpha f \in L^2(\Omega),\ |\alpha|\leq k ight\}. \] The \(H^k\) norm is \(
orm{f}_{H^k}^2 = \sum_{|\alpha|\leq k} 
orm{D^\alpha f}_{L^2}^2\). In Bayesian inversion, this connects directly to the prior. A prior covariance operator can be chosen so that samples have a particular Sobolev regularity. Intuition Sobolev spaces turn smoothness into bookkeeping. The derivatives that must be square-integrable are the entries in the ledger. F4c, Sobolev spaces as smoothness filters. Drag the slider to change the Sobolev order \(s\). The \(H^s\) norm weights each Fourier coefficient \(a_j\) by \((1+j^2)^{s}\), so high frequencies are penalized. Typical draws from an \(H^s\)-based prior scale their coefficients by \((1+j^2)^{-s/2}\), which suppresses high frequencies. As \(s\) increases, both effects strengthen, the space demands more smoothness. s = 0 (\(H^0 = L^2\) ↔ \(H^4\)) Boundary conditions Boundary conditions are often treated as numerical details. In a function-space formulation, they are part of the mathematical model. Dirichlet conditions fix the value of the function at the boundary, e.g. \(f(0)=0\), \(f(L)=0\). Neumann conditions fix the derivative, e.g. \(f'(0)=0\), \(f'(L)=0\). Mixed conditions combine different types at different parts of the boundary. If a prior covariance is built from a differential operator like \(\kappa^2 I - \Delta\), then the boundary conditions used to define \(\Delta\) affect the covariance, and therefore affect the prior measure. Warning Boundary conditions are not numerical decoration. They are part of the mathematical model and, often, part of the prior. F4d, Boundary conditions change the space. Select a boundary condition to see the first four eigenfunctions of \(-\Delta\). The eigenfunctions, and therefore any covariance built from them, depend on this choice. Boundary condition Dirichlet: f(0)=f(L)=0 Neumann: f'(0)=f'(L)=0 Mixed: f(0)=0, f'(L)=0 Choosing a model space There is no universal answer. The model space is a modelling decision. It must reflect the physical problem, the data, the forward map, and the kind of prior information we are willing to assert. The key questions are: What physical quantities should be finite? How smooth should the model be? What boundary behaviour is meaningful? What should count as a small perturbation? The chosen geometry determines which perturbations are considered mild and which are considered large. This matters for regularization, prior modelling, posterior covariance, and adjoints. Lesson Choosing a model space is choosing what kind of object the unknown is, what kind of perturbations are meaningful, and what kind of uncertainty can be placed on the problem. The moral of Act IV The functional-analytic detour was not a luxury expedition. It was necessary cartography. We began with sets, which only provide membership. We added topology, which allows continuity and convergence. We added metrics and norms, which measure distance and size. We added completeness, producing Banach spaces. We added inner products, giving angles, orthogonality, projections, and adjoints. With completeness and an inner product together, we arrived at Hilbert spaces. For linear Bayesian inverse problems, Hilbert spaces are often the sweet spot. They are structured enough to support the geometry we need, but familiar enough to connect cleanly to computation. Checkpoint The next act turns from the model space to the data space and the forward operator. In particular, we will see why the adjoint \(G^{\adj}\) is determined by the inner products on both spaces, and why replacing it by a transpose can quietly change the problem. References Haim Brezis (2011). Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations . Springer. The functional-analysis ladder of this act, including Sobolev spaces, done properly. doi:10.1007/978-0-387-70914-7 ← Act III: What Problem? Act V: Data & Adjoint →

title: Act V: The Data Space and the Adjoint | Think First, Discretize Later | Adrian Mag
desc: Act V of Think First, Discretize Later: The data space, the forward operator, and why the adjoint is not just a transpose.
text:
Act V: The Data Space and the Adjoint The adjoint is defined by inner products, not by a matrix transpose. Part of Think First, Discretize Later . « Overview 1 Familiar Problem 2 Something Is Wrong 3 What Problem? 4 Functional Analysis 5 Data & Adjoint 6 The Prior 7 The Repair 8 The Verdict S Summary The Data Space Finite-dimensional data In the toy inverse problem, the data consist of finitely many real numbers: \[ \obs =  egin{pmatrix} [\obs]_1 \ \vdots \ [\obs]_{N_d} \end{pmatrix}. \] Thus, the natural data space is \(\D = \R^{N_d}\). This is already a major simplification. The model may live in an infinite-dimensional function space, but the observations live in a finite-dimensional vector space. The forward map therefore compresses a model into finitely many numbers: \(G : \M 	o \R^{N_d}\). The data equation is \[ \obs = G m + 
oise, \qquad 
oise \sim \N(0,\Cd). \] At first glance, finite-dimensional data seem completely harmless. But even here, a modelling choice remains hidden: we must decide how to measure lengths, angles, and residuals in the data space. Intuition The data space may be finite-dimensional, but it still has geometry. Ignoring that geometry is how a transpose sneaks into places where an adjoint was supposed to stand. Why finite dimensions are easier All norms induce the same topology On \(\R^{N_d}\), many different norms can be defined. In finite dimensions, all norms induce the same topology. This means that they give the same notion of convergence. This is not true in infinite-dimensional spaces. Remark Although all norms on \(\R^{N_d}\) induce the same topology, they do not define the same geometry. They may measure length and angle differently. For inverse problems, this distinction matters. Completeness is automatic Every finite-dimensional normed vector space is complete. Therefore, data-space limits do not escape the space. This makes the data side of the inverse problem much easier than the model side. Linear maps are continuous Every linear map between finite-dimensional normed spaces is continuous. When the model space is infinite-dimensional, this automatic continuity is no longer guaranteed. A linear map \(G:\M	o\D\) must be checked. Since \(\D=\R^{N_d}\) is finite-dimensional, checking continuity of \(G\) often reduces to checking the continuity of its individual components. For example, if \(G_i m = \int_\Omega K_i(x)\,m(x)\,dx\) and \(\M=L^2(\Omega)\), \(K_i\in L^2(\Omega)\), then by Cauchy-Schwarz, \(|G_i m| \leq 
orm{K_i}_{L^2}
orm{m}_{L^2}\). But geometry still matters Choosing an inner product A general inner product on \(\R^{N_d}\) can be written as \(\inner{a}{b}_{\D} = a^{	op} \Wb_D b\), where \(\Wb_D\in\R^{N_d	imes N_d}\) is symmetric positive definite. If \(\Wb_D=\mathbf{I}_{N_d}\), this is the usual Euclidean inner product. This choice affects the adjoint of the forward map. In particular, if the model space also has a non-Euclidean geometry, then the adjoint is not represented by the ordinary matrix transpose. Warning In finite dimensions, the transpose and the adjoint coincide only when the coordinate bases are orthonormal for the inner products being used. Noise covariance and data weighting The observational noise is modelled as \(
oise \sim \N(0,\Cd)\). The inverse covariance \(\Cd^{-1}\) is called the precision matrix. It weights the data residual \(r(m)=\obs-G m\). The usual Gaussian likelihood contains the quadratic form \(r(m)^{	op} \Cd^{-1} r(m)\). A residual in a noisy datum is less serious than the same residual in a highly accurate datum. Intuition The covariance says how the noise wiggles. The precision says how strongly each residual is judged. Interactive: The Data Ellipse σ₁ 1.0 σ₂ 0.8 ρ (correlation) 0.0 F5d, The data ellipse. The noise covariance \(\Cd\) defines an ellipse in data space. Its shape depends on the variances \(\sigma_1^2, \sigma_2^2\) and the correlation \(ho\). The misfit contours \(r^{\T}\Cd^{-1}r = 	ext{const}\) are concentric ellipses aligned with the covariance. Residuals are judged relative to the noise geometry, not by raw Euclidean length. Whitened and unwhitened data Sometimes it is convenient to transform the data so that the noise becomes standard Gaussian. Assume \(\Cd = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^{	op}\), where \(\mathbf{L}\) is invertible. Define the whitened residual \(\widetilde{r}(m) = \mathbf{L}^{-1}(\obs-G m)\). Then \(
orm{\widetilde{r}(m)}_2^2 = r^{	op} \Cd^{-1} r\). Whitening is often computationally useful, but it is not magic. It is a change of coordinates in data space. The underlying statistical model is the same. F5g, Whitening as coordinate change. In the original data space (left), the noise covariance \(\Cd\) produces a tilted ellipse, and the misfit \(r^{\T}\Cd^{-1}r\) is measured by an anisotropic metric. After whitening \(\widetilde{r} = L^{-1}r\) (right), the ellipse becomes a circle, and the same misfit is just \(\|\widetilde{r}\|_2^2\). The statistical model is unchanged; only the coordinates differ. The data misfit The data misfit measures how well a model predicts the observed data. For Gaussian observational noise, the natural quadratic misfit is \(
orm{r(m)}_{\Cd^{-1}}^2\), and the likelihood is \(\pi(\obs\mid m) \propto \exp\left( - rac{1}{2} (\obs-G m)^{	op} \Cd^{-1}(\obs-G m) ight)\). The Bayesian update is driven by the potential \(\Phi(m;\obs) =  rac{1}{2} 
orm{\obs-G m}_{\Cd^{-1}}^2\). Lesson The data misfit is not merely a least-squares penalty. It is the negative log likelihood produced by the noise model. The Forward Operator and Its Adjoint The forward map The forward map sends a model to predicted data: \(G : \M 	o \D\). For the toy problem, \([G m]_i = \int_\Omega K_i(x)\,m(x)\,dx\). If \(\M\) is a Hilbert space and \(\D\) is equipped with an inner product, then \(G\) has an adjoint, provided \(G\) is bounded. The adjoint tells us how data-space residuals are pulled back into model space. The adjoint is not just a transpose Definition of the adjoint Let \(\M\) and \(\D\) be Hilbert spaces with inner products \(\inner{\cdot}{\cdot}_{\M}\) and \(\inner{\cdot}{\cdot}_{\D}\). The adjoint of a bounded linear operator \(G:\M	o\D\) is the unique bounded linear operator \(G^{\adj}:\D	o\M\) satisfying \[ \inner{G m}{d}_{\D} = \inner{m}{G^{\adj} d}_{\M} \] for all \(m\in\M\), \(d\in\D\). (The mismatch between the matrix transpose and the true adjoint is a well-documented trap wherever continuous problems are discretized; the PDE-constrained optimization literature treats it under the heading of adjoint consistency and “optimize-then-discretize” [HPUU09] .) This equation is the definition. It is not a computational trick. It says that the same pairing can be evaluated either by pushing the model forward into data space or by pulling the data vector back into model space. Intuition The forward map asks: "What data does this model predict?" The adjoint asks: "What model-space direction is suggested by this data-space quantity?" F5a, The adjoint is defined by a balance. The defining identity \(\inner{G m}{d}_{\D} = \inner{m}{G^{\adj} d}_{\M}\) says: you can either push \(m\) forward into data space and pair it with \(d\), or pull \(d\) back into model space and pair it with \(m\). The adjoint is the operator that makes both sides agree. It is not born by flipping a matrix; it is born from the two geometries. Why inner products determine the adjoint The adjoint depends on the inner products. Change the inner product, and the adjoint changes. Suppose the data-space inner product is \(\inner{a}{b}_{\D}=a^{	op} \Wb_D b\), and the model-space inner product is \(\inner{u}{v}_{\M}=u^{	op} \Mb v\). Let the forward map be represented by a matrix \(\Gb\in\R^{N_d	imes N}\). The adjoint matrix \(A\) must satisfy \(\inner{\Gb u}{d}_{\D} = \inner{u}{Ad}_{\M}\) for all \(u,d\). The left-hand side is \((\Gb u)^{\T} \Wb_D d = u^{	op} \Gb^{\T} \Wb_D d\). The right-hand side is \(u^{	op} \Mb A d\). Therefore, \(\Mb A = \Gb^{\T} \Wb_D\), and \[ A = \Mb^{-1}\Gb^{\T} \Wb_D. \] Only when \(\Mb=\mathbf{I}_N\) and \(\Wb_D=\mathbf{I}_{N_d}\) does this reduce to \(\Gb^{\T}\). Matrix transpose versus Hilbert adjoint The transpose is a coordinate operation. The Hilbert adjoint is a geometric operation. In Euclidean coordinates with orthonormal bases, these two operations coincide. That coincidence is useful, but it is also dangerous. If the basis functions in the model space are not orthonormal, then the coefficient vectors do not inherit the Euclidean inner product. With basis functions \(\{\phi_j\}\), the inner product between two functions is \(\inner{m_N}{n_N}_{\M} = \mathbf{u}^{	op} \Mb\mathbf{v}\), not generally \(\mathbf{u}^{	op}\mathbf{v}\). Warning Using \(\Gb^{\T}\) as the adjoint when the basis is not orthonormal means silently using the wrong geometry. Euclidean coordinates orthonormal bases: \(\Mb=\mathbf{I},\ \Wb_D=\mathbf{I}\) \(\inner{u}{v} = u^{\T}v\) \(\inner{a}{b} = a^{\T}b\) \(G^{\adj} = G^{\T}\) transpose = adjoint ✓ the coincidence of orthonormal worlds useful, but dangerous to generalise General geometry non-orthonormal bases: \(\Mb
eq\mathbf{I},\ \Wb_D
eq\mathbf{I}\) \(\inner{u}{v}_{\M} = u^{\T}\Mb\,v\) \(\inner{a}{b}_{\D} = a^{\T}\Wb_D\,b\) \(G^{\adj}_{\mathrm{disc}} = \Mb^{-1}\Gb^{\T}\Wb_D\) transpose ≠ adjoint ✗ Gram matrices carry the geometry ignoring them silently changes the problem F5b, Transpose versus adjoint. In Euclidean coordinates with orthonormal bases (left), the adjoint coincides with the transpose. In general geometry (right), the adjoint acquires Gram matrix factors \(\Mb^{-1}\) and \(\Wb_D\). The transpose only wins in Euclidean costume. The role of Gram matrices Non-orthonormal bases A basis \(\{\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_N\}\) is orthonormal in \(\M\) if \(\inner{\phi_i}{\phi_j}_{\M} = \delta_{ij}\). Most finite element bases are not orthonormal. Hat functions overlap with neighbouring hat functions, so their inner products are not zero for neighbouring indices. (In the finite element world the Gram matrix is the mass matrix , and its role in transporting inner products to coefficient space is classical, see Brenner and Scott [BS08] .) The model-space Gram matrix The model-space Gram matrix is defined by \([\Mb]_{ij} = \inner{\phi_i}{\phi_j}_{\M}\). For \(\M=L^2(\Omega)\), this is the familiar finite element mass matrix: \([\Mb]_{ij} = \int_\Omega \phi_i(x)\phi_j(x)\,dx\). For \(\M=H^1(\Omega)\), the Gram matrix becomes \([\Mb]_{ij} = \int_\Omega \phi_i(x)\phi_j(x)\,dx + \int_\Omega \phi_i'(x)\phi_j'(x)\,dx\). Thus, the same basis functions produce different Gram matrices depending on the chosen model-space geometry. Intuition The Gram matrix is the memory of the function-space geometry after we choose coordinates. Interactive: Gram Matrix as Geometry Memory Hover over matrix entries to highlight basis function pairs F5c, The Gram matrix is geometry memory. Three overlapping hat functions \(\phi_1, \phi_2, \phi_3\) on an interval. The Gram matrix \(M_{ij} = \int \phi_i\phi_j\,dx\) has nonzero off-diagonal entries because neighbouring hats overlap. The coefficient dot product \(\mathbf{u}^{\T}\mathbf{v}\) ignores this overlap; the function-space inner product \(\mathbf{u}^{\T}\Mb\mathbf{v}\) remembers it. The data-space Gram matrix Similarly, the data-space inner product may be written as \(\inner{a}{b}_{\D} = a^{	op} \Wb_D b\). The matrix \(\Wb_D\) is the Gram matrix of the data-space coordinate basis. In many finite-dimensional data problems, we choose Euclidean data coordinates and therefore take \(\Wb_D=\mathbf{I}_{N_d}\). But this is still a choice, not an inevitability. The discrete adjoint The discrete adjoint is the matrix \[ G^{\adj}_{\mathrm{disc}} = \Mb^{-1}\Gb^{\T} \Wb_D. \] This formula is one of the simplest places where the naive discretization betrays itself. If we use \(\Gb^{\T}\) instead of \(\Mb^{-1}\Gb^{\T} \Wb_D\), then we are not using the adjoint corresponding to the chosen model and data spaces. Proposition Let \(\Gb:\R^N	o\R^{N_d}\) be represented by a matrix \(\Gb\). Equip \(\R^N\) with the inner product \(\inner{u}{v}_{\M}=u^{	op} \Mb v\), where \(\Mb\) is symmetric positive definite, and equip \(\R^{N_d}\) with \(\inner{a}{b}_{\D}=a^{	op} \Wb_D b\), where \(\Wb_D\) is symmetric positive definite. Then the adjoint of \(\Gb\) with respect to these inner products is represented by \[ G^{\adj}_{\mathrm{disc}} = \Mb^{-1}\Gb^{\T} \Wb_D. \] The adjoint \(G^{\adj}_{\mathrm{disc}}\) is defined by \(\inner{\Gb u}{d}_{\D} = \inner{u}{G^{\adj}_{\mathrm{disc}}d}_{\M}\) for all \(u\in\R^N\) and \(d\in\R^{N_d}\). Expanding both inner products gives \(u^{	op} \Gb^{\T} \Wb_D d = u^{	op} \Mb G^{\adj}_{\mathrm{disc}} d\). Since this holds for all \(u\) and \(d\), we have \(\Gb^{\T} \Wb_D = \Mb G^{\adj}_{\mathrm{disc}}\). Multiplying by \(\Mb^{-1}\) gives \(G^{\adj}_{\mathrm{disc}} = \Mb^{-1}\Gb^{\T} \Wb_D\). Interactive: Adjoint Calculator Model Gram matrix M: Identity (orthonormal) Mass matrix (hat functions) Anisotropic (stretched) Data Gram matrix W_D: Identity (Euclidean) Weighted (unequal variances) Correlated (tilted) Forward matrix G: Row sampler [1, 0.5] Column sampler [1; 0.3] Mixed [0.8, 0.6; 0.2, 0.9] F5e, Interactive adjoint calculator. Choose the model Gram matrix \(\Mb\), the data Gram matrix \(\Wb_D\), and the forward matrix \(\Gb\). The plot shows the data vector \(d\) (orange) and two pullback arrows in model space: \(G^{\T} d\) (red, wrong) and \(\Mb^{-1}\Gb^{\T}\Wb_D d\) (green, correct). When both Gram matrices are identity, the arrows coincide. Otherwise, they point in visibly different directions. The geometry-aware discretization What changes In the naive discretization, posterior formulas use \(\Gb^{\T}\). This is correct only when the relevant adjoint is represented by \(\Gb^{\T}\), which requires orthonormal coordinates. With non-orthonormal basis functions, the geometry-aware adjoint is \(G^{\adj}_{\mathrm{disc}} = \Mb^{-1}\Gb^{\T} \Wb_D\). The posterior formulas must be interpreted as discretizations of the function-space formulas: \[ C^{\obs} = C_0 - C_0 G^{\adj} \left( G C_0 G^{\adj} + \Cd ight)^{-1} G C_0, \] \[ m^{\obs} = m_0 + C_0 G^{\adj} \left( G C_0 G^{\adj} + \Cd ight)^{-1} (\obs-G m_0). \] The object to discretize is \(G^{\adj}\), not the symbol \(\Gb^{\T}\). Function-space object Discrete representation \(G\) \(\Gb\) \(G^{\adj}\) \(\Mb^{-1}\Gb^{\T}\Wb_D\) \(\inner{\cdot}{\cdot}_{\M}\) \(\Mb\) \(\inner{\cdot}{\cdot}_{\D}\) \(\Wb_D\) \(C_0\) (covariance operator) \(C_{0,N}\) (operator matrix in basis \(\{\phi_j\}\)) F5h, Translation table: function-space to discrete. The target is the operator formula on the left. The discrete ingredients on the right are what enter a computation. The adjoint \(G^{\adj}\) becomes \(\Mb^{-1}\Gb^{\T}\Wb_D\), not \(\Gb^{\T}\), unless both Gram matrices are identity. The entry \(C_{0,N}\) is the matrix of the covariance operator \(C_0\) in the chosen basis; in a non-orthonormal basis it is not the same as the covariance matrix of the coefficient vector \(\mathbf{u}\), which involves mass-matrix weighting. What stays invariant A geometry-aware discretization keeps the continuous problem fixed. Changing the basis should not change the mathematical problem. This is the point of including Gram matrices. They ensure that coordinate vectors remember the geometry of the functions they represent. Intuition The coordinates may change costume. The function-space problem should remain the same actor. Why this prevents changing the problem by accident When we use the wrong adjoint, we are not merely making a small algebraic mistake. We are changing the inverse problem. The adjoint appears in posterior mean formulas, posterior covariance formulas, gradient calculations, normal equations, data-to-model backprojection, and covariance updates. If the adjoint is wrong, then residuals are pulled back into the wrong model-space directions. The posterior mean can shift. The uncertainty can be misrepresented. The discretized problem can stop approximating the intended continuous problem. F5f, Residual pullback: transpose vs. adjoint. The residual \(r = \obs - G m\) lives in data space. Pulling it back into model space via \(G^{\T}\) (left) ignores the Gram matrices and pushes the update in the wrong direction. The geometry-aware adjoint \(G^{\adj}_{\mathrm{disc}} = \Mb^{-1}\Gb^{\T}\Wb_D\) (right) respects both inner products and produces a visibly different model-space direction. Lesson The transpose belongs to Euclidean coordinates. The adjoint belongs to the spaces. The moral of Act V The data space was easy, but not empty of choices. Its finite-dimensional nature gave us automatic completeness and friendly convergence, but its inner product still mattered. The noise covariance told us how to weight residuals. Whitening showed that data weighting can be moved into coordinates, provided we do so consistently. The forward map then forced us to confront the adjoint. The adjoint is defined by \(\inner{G m}{d}_{\D} = \inner{m}{G^{\adj} d}_{\M}\), which means it depends on the inner products of both spaces. Once basis functions enter, those inner products become Gram matrices. For a non-orthonormal model basis and a weighted data geometry, the discrete adjoint is \(G^{\adj}_{\mathrm{disc}} = \Mb^{-1}\Gb^{\T} \Wb_D\), not simply \(\Gb^{\T}\). Checkpoint We have now chosen the model space, the data space, the forward map, and the geometry needed to define the adjoint. The next act turns to the remaining ingredient: the prior measure. This is where the phrase "the prior is not just a matrix" finally gets its full teeth. References Michael Hinze, René Pinnau, Michael Ulbrich, and Stefan Ulbrich (2009). Optimization with PDE Constraints . Springer. Adjoint consistency and the discretize-vs-optimize question, in the PDE-constrained setting. doi:10.1007/978-1-4020-8839-1 Susanne C. Brenner and L. Ridgway Scott (2008). The Mathematical Theory of Finite Element Methods , 3rd edition. Springer. Gram and mass matrices: the finite element view. doi:10.1007/978-0-387-75934-0 ← Act IV: Functional Analysis Act VI: The Prior →

title: Act VI: The Prior Is Not Just a Matrix | Think First, Discretize Later | Adrian Mag
desc: Act VI of Think First, Discretize Later: Why the prior must be a probability measure on a function space, not just a matrix.
text:
Act VI: The Prior Is Not Just a Matrix A prior must be a probability measure on a function space, with a trace-class covariance operator. Part of Think First, Discretize Later . « Overview 1 Familiar Problem 2 Something Is Wrong 3 What Problem? 4 Functional Analysis 5 Data & Adjoint 6 The Prior 7 The Repair 8 The Verdict S Summary A Detour Through Measure Theory Why probabilities are measures We now reach the last major ingredient of the function-space Bayesian inverse problem: the prior. In the naive discretized problem, the prior was introduced as a covariance matrix, \(\mathbf{C}_N = \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_N\). For every fixed \(N\), this is a valid covariance matrix on \(\R^N\). But the failure of Act II showed us that this is not enough. A prior for a function space inverse problem must be a probability measure on a function space. This forces us to step briefly into measure theory. The reason is simple: probability is not fundamentally about densities. Probability is fundamentally about assigning mass to events. Events Let \(X\) be a space of possible outcomes. In our setting, \(X = \M\). An event is a subset of \(X\). For example, \(A = \{m\in\M : 
orm{m}_{\M}\leq 1\}\). If \(m\) is random, then we may ask for the probability \(\mathbb{P}(m\in A)\). In function space, events can be more subtle. We might ask whether a random function has small norm, whether it is positive on a subinterval, whether its derivative is bounded in some weak sense, or whether it lies near a reference model. The prior must assign probabilities to such events. Sigma-algebras Not every subset of an infinite-dimensional space can be assigned a probability in a consistent way. Instead, we choose a collection of admissible events called a sigma-algebra. A sigma-algebra \(\mathcal{A}\) on a set \(X\) is a collection of subsets of \(X\) such that: \(X\in\mathcal{A}\); if \(A\in\mathcal{A}\), then \(X\setminus A\in\mathcal{A}\); if \(A_1,A_2,A_3,\ldots\in\mathcal{A}\), then \( igcup_{n=1}^{\infty} A_n \in \mathcal{A}\). For a topological space, a common choice is the Borel sigma-algebra, generated by the open sets. If \(\M\) is a Hilbert space, we usually take its Borel sigma-algebra and define probability measures on it. Intuition A sigma-algebra is the list of questions the probability measure agrees to answer. Probability measures A probability measure on \((X,\mathcal{A})\) is a map \(\mu:\mathcal{A}	o[0,1]\) such that \(\mu(X)=1\) and, for any countable collection of disjoint events, \(\mu\left( igcup A_night) = \sum \mu(A_n)\). In Bayesian inverse problems, the prior is a probability measure \(\prior\) on the model space \(\M\). The posterior is another probability measure \(\post\) on the same space, obtained by updating the prior using the data. Thus, at the most fundamental level, we should write \(m\sim\prior\), not \(\mathbf{u}\sim\N(0,\sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_N)\), unless \(\mathbf{u}\) is truly the unknown object and the problem is genuinely finite-dimensional. Lesson A prior is a probability measure on possible models. A covariance matrix is only one finite-dimensional way of describing part of such a measure. Why densities are not fundamental In finite-dimensional probability, we often describe a distribution by a density. But a density is not a probability measure by itself. A density is always a density with respect to some reference measure. (On infinite-dimensional spaces there is no Lebesgue measure to be a density with respect to , which is why measures, not densities, must carry the theory. The rigorous home of this material is Bogachev [Bog98] ; its use in inversion is [Stu10] .) If \(\mu\) is absolutely continuous with respect to \(
u\), then there exists a density \(ho\) such that \(d\mu = ho\,d
u\). The density \(ho\) is the Radon-Nikodym derivative \(d\mu/d
u\). Warning A density is always relative to a background measure. Without the background measure, the density is only half a sentence. F6a, Density is not probability. A probability measure \(\mu\) is the fundamental object. A density \(ho\) is always a density with respect to a reference measure \(
u\): \(d\mu = ho\,d
u\). In finite dimensions, Lebesgue measure plays this role invisibly. In function space, there is no infinite-dimensional Lebesgue measure, so the prior must be specified as a measure directly. The role of Lebesgue measure in finite dimensions In \(\R^N\), the usual background measure is Lebesgue measure. When we write \(\mathbf{u}\sim\N( ar{\mathbf{u}},C)\), we mean that the probability measure has a density with respect to Lebesgue measure. The hidden reference measure is Lebesgue measure. It is so familiar that it becomes invisible. Why there is no infinite-dimensional Lebesgue measure In infinite-dimensional function spaces, there is no analogue of Lebesgue measure with the same useful properties. There is no translation-invariant, locally finite measure that plays the role of volume on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space. This changes everything. If there is no infinite-dimensional Lebesgue measure, then we cannot define a function-space prior by writing a density with respect to such a measure. Therefore, in function space, it is safer and more fundamental to define the prior directly as a measure: \(\prior\). The posterior is then often defined by specifying its density relative to the prior: \[  rac{d\post}{d\prior}(m) =  rac{1}{Z(\obs)} \exp(-\Phi(m;\obs)). \] Here the prior is the reference measure. The likelihood reweights it. F6h, The posterior reweights the prior, not Lebesgue volume. The prior \(\prior\) assigns mass to model-space sets. The posterior \(\post\) is the prior measure reweighted by the likelihood: \(d\post = L\,d\prior\). No Lebesgue density is involved, the prior is the reference measure. Lesson In finite dimensions, Lebesgue measure quietly carries the density formalism. In function space, that quiet support disappears. F6b, Finite-dimensional density versus function-space measure. In finite dimensions (left), a Gaussian is visualized by its density contours with respect to Lebesgue measure. In function space (right), the prior is better understood through the random functions it generates. There is no infinite-dimensional Lebesgue measure to carry the density. What changes on function spaces A prior must be a measure In a function-space inverse problem, the prior must be a probability measure on the model space: \(\prior \in \mathcal{P}(\M)\). The prior must be defined before discretization. A discretized prior should then be an approximation of this measure, not a new probability model invented at each resolution. This is exactly where the naive prior failed. The sequence \(\N(0,\sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_N)\) is a perfectly legal sequence of finite-dimensional Gaussian measures, but it does not define a sensible Gaussian probability measure on a Hilbert space whose covariance is \(\sigma^2 I\). Gaussian measures on infinite-dimensional spaces A Gaussian measure on a Hilbert space \(\M\) is a probability measure such that every continuous linear functional applied to the random model is a finite-dimensional Gaussian random variable. A Gaussian measure is characterized by its mean \(m_0\) and covariance operator \(C_0\): \(\mu = \N(m_0,C_0)\). The covariance is characterized by \(\Cov(\ell_1(m),\ell_2(m)) = \inner{C_0 h_1}{h_2}_{\M}\), where \(\ell_j(m)=\inner{m}{h_j}_{\M}\). In finite dimensions, almost any symmetric positive semidefinite matrix gives a Gaussian covariance. In infinite dimensions, the covariance operator must satisfy stronger conditions. It must be trace class if the Gaussian is to live on the Hilbert space itself. Typical samples versus pointwise intuition In function spaces, typical samples may be less regular than the covariance kernel or mean function suggests at first glance. A Brownian path is continuous but almost surely nowhere classically differentiable. When choosing a prior, we should ask: Do typical samples belong to the intended model space? Do they have physically plausible roughness? Do they satisfy the intended boundary conditions? Does the prior uncertainty remain controlled under discretization? Warning In function space, writing down a density without specifying the underlying measure is usually smoke without a fireplace. Gaussian Priors on Function Spaces Mean and covariance A Gaussian prior on the model space is written \(m \sim \N(m_0,C_0)\). The mean describes the central model before observing the data. The covariance describes the allowed uncertainty around that mean. A useful way to think about a Gaussian prior is through a random perturbation: \(m = m_0+\xi\), where \(\xi \sim \N(0,C_0)\). Intuition The prior mean says where the cloud is centred. The covariance operator says what shape the cloud has in function space. Covariance as an operator In a Hilbert space, covariance is an operator: \(C_0 : \M 	o \M\). It satisfies \(\E\left[ \inner{\xi}{f}_{\M} \inner{\xi}{g}_{\M} ight] = \inner{C_0 f}{g}_{\M}\) for all \(f,g\in\M\). The variance in direction \(f\) is \(\operatorname{Var}(\inner{\xi}{f}_{\M}) = \inner{C_0 f}{f}_{\M}\). If \(C_0\) has eigenpairs \(C_0 e_j = \lambda_j e_j\), then the prior can be represented by the Karhunen-Loeve expansion \(m = m_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \sqrt{\lambda_j}\,\xi_j e_j\), where \(\xi_j\sim\N(0,1)\) are independent standard normal random variables. The eigenvalue \(\lambda_j\) is the variance assigned to direction \(e_j\). Required properties Not every linear operator is a valid covariance operator. To define a Gaussian measure on a Hilbert space, the covariance must satisfy several important properties. Linearity: \(C_0(\alpha f+ eta g) = \alpha C_0 f+ eta C_0 g\). Symmetry: \(\inner{C_0 f}{g}_{\M} = \inner{f}{C_0 g}_{\M}\). This is the operator version of the symmetry of a covariance matrix. Positivity: \(\inner{C_0 f}{f}_{\M} \geq 0\). This is required because \(\inner{C_0 f}{f}_{\M} = \operatorname{Var}(\inner{\xi}{f}_{\M})\), and variances cannot be negative. Trace class In infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, positivity and symmetry are not enough. The covariance must also be trace class: \(\Tr(C_0) < \infty\). If \(C_0 e_j = \lambda_j e_j\) for an orthonormal basis, then \(\Tr(C_0) = \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\lambda_j\). Trace class means \(\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\lambda_j < \infty\). This condition says that the total variance assigned by the prior is finite. The eigenvalues must decay quickly enough that the Gaussian perturbation has finite expected squared norm in the model space. Warning A positive symmetric operator may still fail to define a Gaussian measure on the Hilbert space if its trace is infinite. Interactive: The Trace-Class Gate p (decay rate) 1.5 F6c, The trace-class gate. Eigenvalues \(\lambda_j = j^{-p}\) and their running sum \(\sum_{j=1}^{N} \lambda_j\). When \(p \leq 1\), the trace diverges, the operator is not trace class and cannot define a Gaussian measure on the Hilbert space. When \(p > 1\), the running sum converges. Trace class is a visible gatekeeper, not a cryptic condition. Why trace class matters Finite expected energy The expected squared norm is \(\E
orm{m-m_0}_{\M}^2 = \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\lambda_j = \Tr(C_0)\). This is the infinite-dimensional version of the finite-dimensional identity \(\E
orm{\mathbf{u}- ar{\mathbf{u}}}_2^2 = \Tr(C)\). The failure of the identity covariance Consider the tempting covariance \(C_0 = \sigma^2 I\). If \(\M\) is infinite-dimensional, every eigenvalue is \(\lambda_j=\sigma^2\), and \(\Tr(\sigma^2 I) = \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\sigma^2 = \infty\). This means that the formal Gaussian perturbation does not have finite expected squared norm in \(\M\): \(\E
orm{\xi}_{\M}^2 = \infty\). This is exactly the continuous analogue of the failure we saw in the naive discretization: \(\Tr(\sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_N)=\sigma^2 N	o\infty\). In finite dimensions, \(\sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_N\) is harmless for fixed \(N\). In infinite dimensions, \(\sigma^2 I\) is not a valid covariance operator for a Gaussian measure living on the Hilbert space. Lesson A covariance operator must produce actual random functions in the chosen model space. That requirement is far stronger than being a positive matrix after discretization. F6d, Identity covariance explosion. Prior samples \(m_N(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{N} \sigma\,\xi_j\,e_j(x)\) with identity covariance. As \(N\) grows, all modes receive equal variance and samples become increasingly violent. The trace \(\Tr(\sigma^2 I_N) = \sigma^2 N 	o \infty\) directly echoes the naive posterior pathology from Act II. What the covariance really chooses The covariance operator chooses more than variance. It chooses the regularity, correlation, length scale, and boundary behaviour of prior samples. If the eigenvalues decay rapidly, high-frequency modes are strongly suppressed, and samples are smoother. If the eigenvalues decay slowly, high-frequency modes retain more energy, and samples are rougher. The covariance operator encodes statements such as: how large model perturbations are expected to be; how correlated nearby points are; how smooth or rough samples should be; what boundary behaviour samples should satisfy; which directions are plausible and which are unlikely. Intuition A covariance matrix says how a finite vector wiggles. A covariance operator says how a random function breathes. Interactive: Covariance Operator as Spectral Filter s (smoothness) 2.0 Resample F6e, Covariance operator as a spectral filter. The Karhunen-Loève expansion \(m(x) = m_0 + \sum_j \sqrt{\lambda_j}\,\xi_j\,e_j(x)\) with \(\lambda_j = (\kappa^2 + ho_j)^{-s}\), where \(ho_j\) are the eigenvalues of \(-\Delta\). As \(s\) increases, high-frequency modes are damped more strongly and samples become smoother. The covariance operator is a knob panel controlling roughness. How to Build Covariances Covariances from differential operators The Laplacian The Laplacian is the differential operator \(\Delta\). On an interval, \(\Delta f = f''\). The negative Laplacian, \(-\Delta\), is often positive under appropriate boundary conditions. Its eigenfunctions provide natural spatial modes: \(-\Delta e_j = ho_j e_j\), where \(0\leq ho_1\leq ho_2\leq\cdots\), \(ho_j	o\infty\). (Building covariances as inverse powers of differential operators is standard practice in function-space inversion [Stu10] , and the precise link between such operators and familiar covariance families is the SPDE connection of Lindgren, Rue and Lindström [LRL11] .) Shifted elliptic operators A common construction uses the shifted elliptic operator \(A = \kappa^2 I - \Delta\), where \(\kappa>0\) sets a length scale. A covariance operator can then be defined as \(C_0 = \alpha (\kappa^2 I - \Delta)^{-s}\), where \(\alpha>0\) sets the overall variance scale and \(s>0\) controls smoothness. The covariance eigenvalues are \(\lambda_j = \alpha(\kappa^2+ho_j)^{-s}\). As \(j\) increases, \(ho_j\) grows, so \(\lambda_j\) decays. High-frequency modes receive less prior variance. Bessel-type priors Priors of the form \(C_0 = \alpha (\kappa^2 I - \Delta)^{-s}\) are often called Bessel-type priors or Matérn-type constructions. They connect the covariance operator, the smoothness of samples, and the differential geometry of the domain through the Laplacian. In one dimension, the eigenvalues of \(-\Delta\) typically grow like \(ho_j \sim j^2\), so \(\lambda_j \sim j^{-2s}\). The trace condition \(\sum \lambda_j < \infty\) requires \(2s > 1\), i.e., \(s >  rac{1}{2}\). The role of boundary conditions The operator \(-\Delta\) is not fully defined until its domain and boundary conditions are specified. These choices change the eigenfunctions and eigenvalues, and therefore change the covariance operator. This means that boundary conditions are part of the prior. Warning A Laplacian without boundary conditions is not yet a covariance recipe. It is only the beginning of one. Interactive: Laplacian Prior Sampler α (amplitude) 1.0 κ (length scale) 1.0 s (smoothness) 2.0 Boundary conditions: Dirichlet: m(0)=m(L)=0 Neumann: m′(0)=m′(L)=0 Mixed: m(0)=0, m′(L)=0 Resample F6f, Laplacian covariance as a smoothing prior. The covariance \(C_0 = \alpha(\kappa^2 I - \Delta)^{-s}\) has three knobs: \(\alpha\) controls amplitude, \(\kappa\) controls correlation length, and \(s\) controls smoothness. Boundary conditions (Dirichlet, Neumann, mixed) change the eigenfunctions and therefore the prior. The same formula with different boundary conditions is not the same prior. Covariances from kernels Another common way to build covariances is through covariance functions, also called kernels. A covariance function \(k:\Omega	imes\Omega	o\R\) is defined by \(k(x,x') = \Cov(m(x),m(x'))\). (The kernel view is the native language of Gaussian processes; the standard reference, free from its authors, is Rasmussen and Williams [RW06] .) A covariance kernel can define an integral operator: \((C_0 f)(x) = \int_\Omega k(x,x')\,f(x')\,dx'\). Under suitable assumptions on \(k\), it is symmetric and positive. A kernel \(k\) is positive definite if, for every finite set of points and every vector \(\mathbf{a}\), the matrix \(K_{ij}=k(x_i,x_j)\) satisfies \(\mathbf{a}^{	op} K\mathbf{a}\geq 0\). However, a positive-definite kernel still needs to be checked against the chosen function space. Warning A kernel that gives valid finite-dimensional covariance matrices still needs to be checked against the chosen function space. Operator view versus kernel view The kernel view is useful when prior information is naturally spatial: variance at each point, correlation decay, stationarity, smoothness of the covariance function. The operator view is useful when prior information is naturally geometric or spectral: which modes to damp, boundary conditions, differential operators, finite trace. Under suitable conditions, the kernel and operator views describe the same covariance. Spectrally, if \(C_0 e_j=\lambda_j e_j\), then the kernel may be written formally as \(k(x,x') = \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \lambda_j e_j(x)e_j(x')\). The correct object is a covariance operator that defines a valid prior measure on the chosen model space. Lesson The prior covariance is a modelling object first and a computational object second. F6g, Kernel view versus operator view. The kernel view (left) describes covariance through a spatial correlation function \(k(x,x')\). The operator view (right) treats covariance as an integral operator \(C_0\) that maps a test function \(f\) to its covariance response \(C_0 f\). The spectral decomposition \(k(x,x') = \sum_j \lambda_j e_j(x) e_j(x')\) bridges both perspectives. The moral of Act VI The naive prior failed because it treated covariance as a matrix attached to a mesh. In function space, this is the wrong starting point. A prior must be a probability measure on the model space: \(m\sim\prior\). If the prior is Gaussian, then it is described by a mean and a covariance operator: \(\prior=\N(m_0,C_0)\). That covariance must be linear, symmetric, positive, and trace class. The trace condition is the mathematical gatekeeper that prevents the prior from assigning infinite total variance to the model. The identity covariance failed because \(\Tr(\sigma^2 I)=\infty\) in infinite dimensions. The finite-dimensional symptom was \(\Tr(\sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_N)=\sigma^2 N	o\infty\). To build meaningful covariances, we may use differential operators, kernels, or spectral constructions. But in every case, the covariance must define a valid Gaussian measure on the chosen model space, and it must be discretized as an approximation of that continuous object. Checkpoint We now have all the pieces: model space, data space, forward map, adjoint, noise model, and prior measure. The next act puts them together and returns to the opening toy problem, where the pathologies of the naive posterior disappear once the formulation is done in the right order. References Vladimir I. Bogachev (1998). Gaussian Measures . American Mathematical Society. Gaussian measures on infinite-dimensional spaces, in full rigor. doi:10.1090/surv/062 Andrew M. Stuart (2010). “Inverse problems: A Bayesian perspective.” Acta Numerica 19, 451–559. Gaussian priors, covariance operators, and trace-class conditions for inversion. doi:10.1017/S0962492910000061 · free PDF (Cambridge Core) Finn Lindgren, Håvard Rue, and Johan Lindström (2011). “An Explicit Link between Gaussian Fields and Gaussian Markov Random Fields: The Stochastic Partial Differential Equation Approach.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B 73(4), 423–498. Covariances from differential operators: the SPDE link. doi:10.1111/j.1467-9868.2011.00777.x Carl E. Rasmussen and Christopher K. I. Williams (2006). Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning . MIT Press. The kernel view of covariances (free from the authors). book page · free PDF (authors’ edition) ← Act V: Data & Adjoint Act VII: The Repair →

title: Act VII: The Repair | Think First, Discretize Later | Adrian Mag
desc: Act VII of Think First, Discretize Later: Assembling the function-space Bayesian inverse problem and discretizing after formulation.
text: Act VII: The Repair The corrected computation on the same toy problem, and why the pathologies melt away. Part of Think First, Discretize Later . « Overview 1 Familiar Problem 2 Something Is Wrong 3 What Problem? 4 Functional Analysis 5 Data & Adjoint 6 The Prior 7 The Repair 8 The Verdict S Summary The Repair: Corrected Computation on the Same Toy Problem Act VI gave us the ingredients: a trace-class covariance operator, the Hilbert adjoint, and the function-space posterior. Now we put them to work on the same toy problem from Acts I and II. Same domain \(\Omega = [0,1]\), same Gaussian kernels, same \(N_d = 20\) data, same hat basis, same forward matrix \(\Gb\). The physical forward and data setup is unchanged. What changes is the Bayesian formulation: the prior is now a function-space-consistent covariance operator rather than a per-resolution diagonal matrix. We think first, discretize later. Lesson This is not a new physical problem. It is the same forward and data setup, placed in a function-space-consistent Bayesian formulation. The broken machine is rebuilt with the correct parts. F7a, The corrected prior In Act I, the prior was \(\mathbf{C}_N = \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_N\), a diagonal matrix invented at each resolution. Now the prior comes from a covariance operator: \[ C_0 = \alpha(\kappa^2 I - \Delta)^{-s}, \] discretized on the same hat basis: \(C_{0,N} \approx C_0\). We are not inventing a covariance matrix anymore. We are discretizing a covariance operator. The eigenvalue spectrum tells the difference immediately: the naive spectrum is flat (\(\sigma^2\) in every direction), while the Bessel spectrum decays, ensuring \(\Tr(C_0) < \infty\). F7a, The corrected prior on the same basis. Left: naive prior samples from \(\mathbf{C}_N = \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_N\) , uncorrelated, same variance in every direction. Right: samples from \(C_{0,N} \approx \alpha(\kappa^2 I - \Delta)^{-s}\) , smooth, correlated, with variance concentrated in low modes. Bottom: eigenvalue spectra. The naive spectrum is flat; the Bessel spectrum decays, ensuring \(\Tr(C_0) < \infty\). F7b, The corrected posterior samples In Act II (F2b), the posterior mean looked plausible but the samples fluctuated wildly. Now we draw samples from the corrected posterior \(m_N^{(s)} \sim \mu_N^{\obs}\) using the Bessel prior. Same data, same \(N = 30\) hats, same true model. But the posterior cloud has stopped screaming. The mean still tracks the truth; the samples no longer oscillate wildly; the \(\pm 1\sigma\) band is narrow and controlled. F7b, The corrected posterior: the cloud is controlled. True model (orange), posterior mean (green), posterior samples (light curves), and \(\pm 1\sigma\) band (green fill). Compare with F2b: the mean still tracks the truth, but the samples no longer oscillate wildly. The posterior uncertainty is concentrated where the data are uninformative, and bounded by the prior. Lesson The posterior mean may look similar to the naive case. The posterior measure does not. The samples tell the story that the mean hides. F7c, Corrected refinement: the uncertainty settles In Act II (F2e), the refinement slider showed the naive posterior's uncertainty band inflating as \(N\) increased. Now we run the same experiment with the corrected prior. As \(N\) increases, the uncertainty should stabilize rather than inflate. Refinement no longer opens new trapdoors of variance. It reveals finer pieces of the same probability measure. F7c, Corrected refinement slider. Drag the slider to change the number of basis functions \(N\). The posterior mean barely moves, and the uncertainty band stays controlled , the posterior converges. N = 21 (\(N_d=20\) data points, Bessel prior) true model \(\bar{m}(z)\) posterior mean \(m_N^{\obs}(z)\) \(\pm 1\sigma\) band Intuition Refinement no longer opens new trapdoors of variance. It reveals finer pieces of the same probability measure. F7d, Trace comparison: naive versus corrected The mathematical verdict in one plot. For the naive prior, \(\Tr(\mathbf{C}_N^{\obs}) \geq \sigma^2(N - N_d)\), the total posterior variance grows linearly with \(N\). For the corrected prior, \(0 \leq C^{\obs} \leq C_0\), so \(\Tr(C^{\obs}) \leq \Tr(C_0) < \infty\). The total posterior variance is bounded, no matter how fine the mesh. This is the heart of the cure: finite trace \(\Rightarrow\) controlled uncertainty. F7d, Posterior trace: naive diverges, corrected converges. The naive posterior trace (red) grows linearly with \(N\), tracking the lower bound \(\sigma^2(N-N_d)\) (orange, dashed). The corrected posterior trace (green) levels off, bounded by \(\Tr(C_0) < \infty\). Log scale reveals the four-order-of-magnitude gap between the two workflows. Proposition Let \(C_0\) be a positive symmetric trace-class covariance operator on \(\M\), and let \(G:\M\to\D\) be a bounded linear map into the finite-dimensional data space \(\D=\R^{N_d}\). Then the posterior covariance \(C^{\obs} = C_0 - C_0 G^{\adj} (G C_0 G^{\adj} + \Cd)^{-1} G C_0\) is positive and trace class, with \(\Tr(C^{\obs}) \leq \Tr(C_0) < \infty\). F7e, From operator to matrix: the translation table Every discrete object has a continuous parent. The discretization inherits meaning from the continuous formulation, not the reverse. The table below maps each function-space object to its discrete representation. Function-space object Discrete representation Naive shortcut (wrong) \(m \in \M\) \(\mathbf{u} \in \R^N\) represents \(m_N = \sum_j u_j \phi_j\) coefficients are the model \(G: \M \to \D\) \(G_{ij} = [G\phi_j]_i\) same matrix, but wrong adjoint \(G^{\adj}: \D \to \M\) \(G^{\adj}_{\mathrm{disc}} = M^{-1} G^{\T} W_D\) \(G^{\T}\) (ignores geometry) \(C_0: \M \to \M\) (covariance operator) \(C_{0,N}\) (operator matrix in basis) \(\sigma^2 I_N\) (invents covariance) \(\Tr(C_0) < \infty\) \(\Tr(C_{0,N}) \to \Tr(C_0)\) \(\Tr(\sigma^2 I_N) = \sigma^2 N \to \infty\) \(\post = \N(m^{\obs}, C^{\obs})\) \(\post_N \approx \post\) (converges) \(\post_N\) diverges with \(N\) F7e, Operator-to-discretization translation table. Each function-space object has a discrete representation, but the mapping is not a naive symbol substitution. The adjoint \(G^{\adj}\) becomes \(M^{-1}G^{\T} W_D\), not \(G^{\T}\). The covariance operator \(C_0\) becomes the operator matrix \(C_{0,N}\) in the chosen basis, not \(\sigma^2 I_N\). In a non-orthonormal basis, this operator matrix is not the same as the covariance matrix of the coefficient vector. The third column shows what goes wrong when the shortcut is taken. The corrected workflow The naive workflow was: (This corrected workflow is not ours alone: it is exactly the design of modern large-scale Bayesian inversion frameworks, which discretize the function-space posterior so that refinement converges by construction [Bui13] , [Stu10] .) mesh \(\Rightarrow\) basis \(\Rightarrow\) coefficient vector \(\Rightarrow\) matrix prior \(\Rightarrow\) posterior. The corrected workflow is: model space \(\Rightarrow\) data space \(\Rightarrow\) forward map \(\Rightarrow\) noise model \(\Rightarrow\) prior measure \(\Rightarrow\) posterior \(\Rightarrow\) discretization. More explicitly: Choose the model space \(\M\). Choose the data space \(\D\). Define the forward map \(G:\M\to\D\). Specify the noise model \(\noise\sim\N(0,\Cd)\). Choose the prior measure \(\prior=\N(m_0,C_0)\) on \(\M\). Define the posterior measure \(\post\) on \(\M\). Choose approximation spaces \(\M_N\subset\M\). Discretize \(G\), \(G^{\adj}\), \(C_0\), and the posterior consistently. This order protects the problem from accidental modelling choices. Lesson The cure is not a cleverer matrix. The cure is choosing the mathematical object first and discretizing it second. References Tan Bui-Thanh, Omar Ghattas, James Martin, and Georg Stadler (2013). “A Computational Framework for Infinite-Dimensional Bayesian Inverse Problems Part I: The Linearized Case.” SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing 35(6), A2494–A2523. The corrected workflow at scale: discretizations that converge to the function-space posterior. doi:10.1137/12089586X Andrew M. Stuart (2010). “Inverse problems: A Bayesian perspective.” Acta Numerica 19, 451–559. Why the corrected workflow is guaranteed to settle. doi:10.1017/S0962492910000061 · free PDF (Cambridge Core) ← Act VI: The Prior Act VIII: The Verdict →

title: Act VIII: The Verdict | Think First, Discretize Later | Adrian Mag
desc: Act VIII of Think First, Discretize Later: Re-solving the toy problem with the corrected workflow.
text: Act VIII: The Verdict Same setup, two formulations, the full story, side by side. Part of Think First, Discretize Later . « Overview 1 Familiar Problem 2 Something Is Wrong 3 What Problem? 4 Functional Analysis 5 Data & Adjoint 6 The Prior 7 The Repair 8 The Verdict S Summary The Verdict: Same Setup, Two Formulations Act VII said: the cure works. Act VIII says: now compare the whole story. We arrange the exhibits side by side. Same domain, same kernels, same data, same hat basis, same forward matrix. The physical setup is unchanged; the Bayesian formulation is different. The mathematics does the rest. Lesson This act introduces almost no new mathematics. It is a courtroom verdict: the evidence is already on the table. F8a, Same setup, two workflows The naive workflow starts with the mesh and invents the prior at each resolution. The corrected workflow starts with the function space and discretizes last. The diagram below shows the two pipelines in parallel. F8a, Same setup, two workflows. Left: the naive pipeline starts with the mesh, invents a diagonal prior, uses the transpose as adjoint, and produces a posterior whose coefficient-space trace diverges. Right: the corrected pipeline starts with function spaces, defines the forward map and prior operator, uses the geometry-aware adjoint, and produces a posterior with bounded trace. The same data and basis enter both pipelines; the Bayesian formulation is the difference. F8b, Naive versus corrected posterior samples Same \(N = 30\) hats, same \(N_d = 20\) data, same true model. The posterior means may look superficially similar. The posterior measures are radically different. On the left, the naive posterior samples oscillate wildly , the cloud is uncontrolled.
