title: Part 3d: Disintegration | Bayes, Measure-Theoretically | Adrian Mag
desc: Part 3d of Bayes, Measure-Theoretically: Disintegration, bundling eventwise conditional probabilities into conditional probability measures.
text: Part 3d: Disintegration From conditional expectation to conditional probability measures. Part of Bayes, Measure-Theoretically . « Overview 1 The Game 2 High-School Solution 3a Points → Events 3b Conditioning 3c Cond. Expectation 3d Disintegration 3e Bayesian Inversion 3f Back to Finite 4 Summary The loose end from conditional expectation In Part 3c , conditional expectation gave us, for each model event \(A\in\SigmaM\), a function \[\mathbb{P}(M\in A\mid D)=k_A(D),\] where \(k_A:\D\to[0,1]\) is measurable. Evaluating at observed data \(d\) gives the conditional probability \(\mathbb{P}(M\in A\mid D=d)=k_A(d)\). This is a powerful result, but it answers only one question at a time. Pick an event \(A\), get a function of \(d\). Pick another event \(A'\), get another function. Bayesian inference wants more than that: after observing \(d\), we want a full posterior distribution on \(\M\), a probability measure that can answer every model-event question simultaneously. One event is not enough: bundling into a measure Here is the key idea. For each fixed \(d\), we have a collection of numbers \(k_A(d)\), one for each \(A\in\SigmaM\). What if the assignment \(A\mapsto k_A(d)\) behaves like a probability measure on \(\M\)? Then for each data value \(d\), we would have a full probability measure, not just a collection of isolated conditional probabilities, but a coherent distribution that assigns probabilities to all model events at once. (The object we are about to assemble is a Markov kernel , and the theorem that guarantees the bundling works is the disintegration theorem . The program of this part, treating conditioning as disintegration rather than as a ratio of probabilities, follows Chang and Pollard’s classic account [CP97] ; the general theory is in Kallenberg [Kal21] .) Let us name this object: \[\mu_{\M\mid D=d}(A):=k_A(d).\] The notation is deliberate: \(\mu_{\M\mid D=d}\) is a measure (in \(A\)) that depends on the data value \(d\). For each \(d\), it is a probability measure on \((\M,\SigmaM)\). For each \(A\), the map \(d\mapsto\mu_{\M\mid D=d}(A)\) is measurable (it is just \(k_A(d)\), which we already know is measurable). The conceptual ladder Conditional expectation gives \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid D)=k_A(D)\) for one event \(A\). Doob–Dynkin lets us write \(d\mapsto k_A(d)\). Now flip the perspective: fix \(d\) and vary \(A\). If \(A\mapsto k_A(d)\) is a measure, we have \(\mu_{\M\mid D=d}(A)\). That is disintegration: conditional expectation, bundled over all events. When this bundling works, when \(A\mapsto k_A(d)\) is genuinely a probability measure for each \(d\), we call the resulting object a conditional distribution or posterior kernel . The theorem guaranteeing that it works, under good measurable-space assumptions (e.g. standard Borel spaces), is the disintegration theorem . A point of precision about what is and is not pinned down: a kernel is ordinarily presented as a function defined for every \(d\), one can always fill in arbitrary probability measures on an exceptional null set to achieve this. What is determined by the joint law is the kernel's equivalence class : two valid kernels must agree for \(\muD\)-almost every \(d\), but may differ freely on a \(\muD\)-null set. So the accurate slogan is not “defined almost everywhere” but “defined everywhere, unique almost everywhere.” The consistency identity Where does the joint law enter? Recall the defining property of conditional expectation from Part 3c : for any data event \(B\in\SigmaD\), \[\int_{D^{-1}(B)} \mathbb{P}(M\in A\mid D)\,d\mathbb{P} = \mathbb{P}(M\in A,\; D\in B).\] By Doob–Dynkin, \(\mathbb{P}(M\in A\mid D)=k_A(D)=\mu_{\M\mid D=D(\omega)}(A)\). The left side is an integral over outcomes \(\omega\), but since the integrand depends on \(\omega\) only through \(D(\omega)\), we can push it down to data space. The pushforward of \(\mathbb{P}\) under \(D\) is the predictive data measure \(\muD\), so: \[\mathbb{P}(M\in A,\; D\in B) = \int_B \mu_{\M\mid D=d}(A)\,\muD(dd).\] The left side is the joint probability of \((A,B)\). Writing \(\Pi\) for the joint measure on \(\M\times\D\), this becomes: \[\boxed{\;\Pi(A\times B)=\int_B \mu_{\M\mid D=d}(A)\,\muD(dd)\;}\] The aha The disintegration identity is not a new axiom lowered from the rafters. It is the defining property of conditional expectation, rewritten on data space via Doob–Dynkin. Disintegration is conditional expectation, bundled over all events and pushed onto the observed variable. The same trick in the other direction We just bundled the model-side conditional probabilities into a posterior kernel. The same logic works in the opposite direction, from model to data. For each data event \(B\in\SigmaD\), conditional expectation gives a function of the model: \[\mathbb{P}(D\in B\mid M)=\ell_B(M),\] where \(\ell_B:\M\to[0,1]\) is measurable. By the same bundling move, fix \(m\) and vary \(B\): if \(B\mapsto \ell_B(m)\) is a probability measure on \(\D\), we name it \[L(m,B):=\ell_B(m)=\mathbb{P}(D\in B\mid M=m).\] This is the observation kernel . For each fixed \(m\), \(L(m,\cdot)\) is a probability measure on \((\D,\SigmaD)\), it tells us how data is distributed when the model is \(m\). The same consistency argument gives the forward disintegration: \[\Pi(A\times B)=\int_A L(m,B)\,\muMzero(dm),\] where \(\muMzero\) is the prior, the marginal of \(\Pi\) on the model space, obtained by integrating out the data: \(\muMzero(A)=\Pi(A\times\D)\). This says: the joint probability of \((A,B)\) decomposes as the integral of the observation kernel \(L(m,B)\), weighted by the prior, over all model states in \(A\). The reverse ladder \(\mathbb{P}(B\mid M)=\ell_B(M)\) gives \(m\mapsto \ell_B(m)\) via Doob–Dynkin. Flip perspective: fix \(m\), vary \(B\). If \(B\mapsto \ell_B(m)\) is a measure, we have \(L(m,B)\). The same consistency identity then gives \(\Pi(A\times B)=\int_A L(m,B)\,\muMzero(dm)\). Two directions, one mechanism If a joint law \(\Pi\) is already given, then \(L(m,\cdot)\) is the disintegration of \(\Pi\) with respect to the model marginal, and \(\mu_{\M\mid D=d}\) is the disintegration with respect to the data marginal. In Bayesian inversion, we often specify the prior and the observation kernel first, and thereby build the joint law. Either way, the same mechanism produces both kernels. The finite switch problem as a discovery lab Let us see the bundling operation concretely. Recall the setup from Part 1 : \(\M=\{00,01,10,11\}\) with prior \(\muMzero\), and \(\D=\{0,1\}\). The joint table is: \(d=0\) \(d=1\) \(\muMzero(\{m\})\) 00 0.08 0.32 0.40 01 0.08 0.02 0.10 10 0.08 0.02 0.10 11 0.08 0.32 0.40 \(\muD(\{d\})\) 0.32 0.68 1 Each cell is \(\Pi(\{m\}\times\{d\})\). The last column gives row sums (the prior); the last row gives column sums (the predictive data measure). Columns → posterior kernel Fix a data value, say \(d=1\). The column \(\{0.32, 0.02, 0.02, 0.32\}\) sums to \(\muD(\{1\})=0.68\). Normalizing gives \[\mu_{\M\mid D=1}(\{m\})=\frac{\Pi(\{m\}\times\{1\})}{\muD(\{1\})}.\] This is the posterior distribution over models given \(d=1\): \(\{0.47, 0.03, 0.03, 0.47\}\). Repeating for \(d=0\) gives the posterior for the other observation. The column-normalization operation is the bundling: for each \(d\), it produces a full probability measure on \(\M\). Rows → observation kernel Now fix a model value, say \(m=00\). The row \(\{0.08, 0.32\}\) sums to \(\muMzero(\{00\})=0.40\). Normalizing gives \[L(00,\{d\})=\frac{\Pi(\{00\}\times\{d\})}{\muMzero(\{00\})}.\] This is the data distribution given \(m=00\): \(\{0.2, 0.8\}\). Repeating for each \(m\) gives the observation kernel. The row-normalization operation is the same bundling in the other direction. (We reserve the word likelihood for the density \(L(d\mid m)\) of Part 3e, or for the function \(m\mapsto L(d\mid m)\) once the data is fixed; the measure-valued object \(L(m,\cdot)\) is the observation kernel.) Two ways of reading the same table Columns (normalize by column sum) \(\Rightarrow\) posterior kernel \(\mu_{\M\mid D=d}(A)\). Rows (normalize by row sum) \(\Rightarrow\) observation kernel \(L(m,B)\). Both are disintegrations of the same joint table. F3d-1, Two ways of reading the same joint table. Normalizing columns (orange dashed) gives the posterior kernel \(\mu_{\M\mid D=d}\). Normalizing rows (green dashed) gives the observation kernel \(L(m,\cdot)\). Both are disintegrations of the same joint measure \(\Pi\). Two decompositions of the same joint law We now have two ways to decompose the same joint measure \(\Pi\) on \(\M\times\D\): \[\Pi(A\times B)=\int_B \mu_{\M\mid D=d}(A)\,\muD(dd) \qquad\text{(posterior: model given data)},\] \[\Pi(A\times B)=\int_A L(m,B)\,\muMzero(dm) \qquad\text{(observation kernel: data given model)}.\] The first disintegrates with respect to the predictive data measure \(\muD\) and produces the posterior kernel. The second disintegrates with respect to the prior \(\muMzero\) and produces the observation kernel. Both are decompositions of the same joint measure, they are two sides of the same coin. In the finite table, this is simply the observation that you can read the table by columns or by rows. In general spaces, the disintegration theorem guarantees that both decompositions exist and are unique (almost everywhere) under standard conditions. We do not yet set these two expressions equal. That will be the subject of Part 3e , where comparing them will give us Bayes' formula. For now, the point is that the joint measure admits two disintegrations, one in each direction, and both arise from the same conditional-expectation mechanism we developed in Part 3c . A warning about evaluation Conditional expectation does not magically assign a unique value at every zero-probability data point. It gives a version determined only up to \(\muD\)-null sets . To evaluate at a specific observed \(\dobs\), one often needs additional structure, such as a likelihood density, continuity, a chosen regular conditional distribution, or a geometric formula such as coarea in noiseless inverse problems. This is the anti-Borel–Kolmogorov charm: it keeps the exposition honest. The posterior kernel can be chosen everywhere but is unique only \(\muD\)-a.e., and pointwise evaluation at \(\dobs\) requires regularity that must be checked, not assumed. Summary Conditional expectation gives conditional probabilities one event at a time. Disintegration bundles them into full probability measures. The joint law \(\Pi\) admits two disintegrations: the posterior kernel \(\mu_{\M\mid D=d}\) (disintegration with respect to \(\muD\)) and the observation kernel \(L\) (disintegration with respect to \(\muMzero\)). Comparing them will give us Bayes' formula. References Joseph T. Chang and David Pollard (1997). “Conditioning as disintegration.” Statistica Neerlandica 51(3), 287–317. Conditioning as disintegration: the definitive treatment, with Bayes among its examples. doi:10.1111/1467-9574.00056 Olav Kallenberg (2021). Foundations of Modern Probability , 3rd edition. Springer. desc: Part 3e of Bayes, Measure-Theoretically: Bayesian inversion, prior, observation kernel, joint law, Bayes as equality of two disintegrations, density form, and additive noise.
text: Part 3e: Bayesian Inversion Bayes' formula as the equality of two disintegrations of the same joint law. Part of Bayes, Measure-Theoretically . « Overview 1 The Game 2 High-School Solution 3a Points → Events 3b Conditioning 3c Cond. Expectation 3d Disintegration 3e Bayesian Inversion 3f Back to Finite 4 Summary The inversion problem In Part 3d , we saw that the joint law \(\Pi\) on \(\M\times\D\) admits two disintegrations: \[\Pi(A\times B)=\int_B \mu_{\M\mid D=d}(A)\,\muD(dd) \qquad\text{(posterior: model given data)},\] \[\Pi(A\times B)=\int_A L(m,B)\,\muMzero(dm) \qquad\text{(observation kernel: data given model)}.\] (Bayes’ theorem as the equality of two disintegrations of one joint measure is the centrepiece of Chang and Pollard [CP97] , and it is the form of the theorem that survives the passage to function spaces [Stu10] .) In Bayesian inversion, we usually specify the problem in the opposite direction from what we want. We do not start by knowing the posterior. We start with: A prior on models, \(\muMzero(dm)\). A data-given-model kernel , \(L(m,B)=\mathbb{P}(D\in B\mid M=m)\). The kernel \(L\) says: if the model takes the value \(m\), then the data is distributed according to the measure \(L(m,\cdot)\) on \(\D\). This is also a conditional probability measure, but in the forward direction, from model to data. From these two ingredients, the joint law is determined: \[\Pi(dm,dd)=L(m,dd)\,\muMzero(dm).\] For model event \(A\) and data event \(B\): \[\Pi(A\times B)=\int_A L(m,B)\,\muMzero(dm).\] This is the forward disintegration, the generative direction. But the same joint law also admits the posterior disintegration: \[\Pi(A\times B)=\int_B \mu_{\M\mid D=d}(A)\,\muD(dd).\] Since both expressions equal \(\Pi(A\times B)\), we obtain the central measure-theoretic Bayes formula : \[\boxed{\;\int_B \mu_{\M\mid D=d}(A)\,\muD(dd)=\int_A L(m,B)\,\muMzero(dm)\;}\] Bayes as an identity This is not the density formula. Not yet “posterior \(\propto\) likelihood \(\times\) prior.” This is Bayes as an identity between two ways of decomposing the same joint probability. The left side disintegrates with respect to the data marginal; the right side disintegrates with respect to the model marginal. Both describe the same joint measure. F3e-1, Bayes as two disintegrations. The forward direction (top) builds the joint from the prior and observation kernel. The inverse direction (bottom) decomposes the same joint into the posterior kernel and predictive measure. Bayes' formula is the statement that both decompositions describe the same \(\Pi\). The density form as a special case The familiar formula “posterior \(\propto\) likelihood \(\times\) prior” appears only when the data-given-model kernel has a density with respect to a reference measure. Assume there exists a σ-finite reference measure \(\lambda\) on \((\D,\SigmaD)\) such that \(L(m,\cdot)\ll\lambda\) for \(\muMzero\)-a.e.\(m\). Then for each such \(m\) the Radon–Nikodým derivative \[L(d\mid m):=\frac{dL(m,\cdot)}{d\lambda}(d)\] exists \(\lambda\)-a.e. One further point deserves honesty: the derivatives are defined separately for each \(m\) , and choosing them so that \((m,d)\mapsto L(d\mid m)\) is jointly measurable is a genuine (if standard) extra step. It is guaranteed under the assumptions we work with throughout, \(\lambda\) σ-finite, the data σ-algebra countably generated (e.g. \(\D\) a standard Borel space), and \(L\) a measurable kernel, but it is not automatic on arbitrary measurable spaces. Granting joint measurability, the joint law admits the density representation: \[\Pi(dm,dd)=L(d\mid m)\,\lambda(dd)\,\muMzero(dm).\] Identification of the data marginal Integrating the joint density over \(\M\) yields: \[\muD(dd)=Z(d)\,\lambda(dd), \qquad Z(d):=\int_{\M} L(d\mid m)\,\muMzero(dm).\] The function \(Z(d)\) is the evidence (or marginal likelihood) , the same quantity that appeared as the denominator in our finite example. Comparing the two disintegrations Substituting the density form of \(\muD\) into the posterior disintegration: \[\Pi(A\times B)=\int_B \mu_{\M\mid D=d}(A)\,Z(d)\,\lambda(dd).\] On the other hand, combining the forward disintegration with the density representation of \(L(m,\cdot)\): \[\Pi(A\times B)=\int_B\left(\int_A L(d\mid m)\,\muMzero(dm)\right)\lambda(dd).\] Since these two expressions represent the same measure for all measurable \(B\), it follows that for \(\lambda\)-a.e.\(d\): \[\mu_{\M\mid D=d}(A)\,Z(d)=\int_A L(d\mid m)\,\muMzero(dm), \qquad A\in\SigmaM.\] (A technical footnote: for each fixed \(A\) this equality holds outside an \(A\)-dependent \(\lambda\)-null set. To get one exceptional null set that works for all \(A\) simultaneously, which is what the displayed statement asserts, one runs the argument over a countable generating class of model events and extends by a monotone-class argument. This is available when \(\SigmaM\) is countably generated, as it is for standard Borel model spaces. Alternatively, one can simply define the kernel by the ratio formula below wherever \(Z(d)>0\) and verify directly that it satisfies the disintegration identity.) Bayes' relation in density form If \(Z(d)\in(0,\infty)\) for \(\muD\)-a.e.\(d\), then the posterior measure is uniquely determined as: \[\boxed{\;\mu_{\M\mid D=d}(dm)=\frac{L(d\mid m)\,\muMzero(dm)}{Z(d)}\;}\] Equivalently, before normalization: \[\mu_{\M\mid D=d}(dm)\;\propto\;L(d\mid m)\,\muMzero(dm).\] Key point The familiar formula “posterior \(\propto\) likelihood \(\times\) prior” is not the foundation. It is the coordinate/density version of the deeper measure identity. It is valid only when suitable Radon–Nikodým derivatives exist. Remark on reference measures The likelihood \(L(d\mid m)\) depends on the choice of reference measure \(\lambda\) and is therefore not an invariant object. The posterior kernel \(\mu_{\M\mid D=d}\), by contrast, is determined up to \(\muD\)-null sets and does not depend on any reference measure. Even in the total absence of a dominating reference, the posterior kernel still exists as a regular conditional distribution provided the spaces are well-behaved , standard Borel spaces (Polish spaces with their Borel σ-algebras, which cover every finite, Euclidean, and separable Banach setting we care about) are the usual sufficient condition. On truly pathological measurable spaces, regular conditional distributions can fail to exist. Within the standard-Borel world: existence holds, uniqueness holds up to \(\muD\)-null sets, and only the simple density formula needs the dominating reference measure. The likelihood from forward models with additive noise In many inverse problems, the data-generating mechanism has a specific structure: a deterministic forward map perturbed by additive noise. We now show how the observation kernel arises naturally in this setting. Setup Assume: The data space is \(\D=\mathbb{R}^{N_d}\) with its Borel σ-algebra. (The additive structure below needs a vector space with measurable addition; for this section we simply take Euclidean data space, which is the practically relevant case.) \(M\sim\muMzero\) on \((\M,\SigmaM)\), the prior; \(\eta\sim\mu_\eta\) on \((\D,\SigmaD)\), the noise distribution; \(M\) and \(\eta\) are independent; The data is generated by \(D=G(M)+\eta\), where \(G:\M\to\D\) is a measurable forward map. The joint law of \((M,D)\) is the pushforward of the product measure \(\muMzero\otimes\mu_\eta\) under the map \(\Phi(m,\xi)=(m,\,G(m)+\xi)\): \[\Pi=\Phi_\#(\muMzero\otimes\mu_\eta).\] F3e-2, Additive noise forward model. The data \(D\) is generated by applying the forward map \(G\) to the model \(M\) and adding independent noise \(\eta\). The joint law is the pushforward of the product measure under \(\Phi(m,\xi)=(m, G(m)+\xi)\). The data-given-model kernel Fixing \(M=m\), the forward map value \(G(M)\) becomes the deterministic element \(G(m)\). The only remaining randomness in \(D\) comes from the noise \(\eta\). Hence: \[D\mid(M=m)\;\overset{d}{=}\;G(m)+\eta.\] Translating the event \(\{D\in B\}\) back to an event in terms of \(\eta\): \[\{D\in B\}=\{G(m)+\eta\in B\}=\{\eta\in B-G(m)\},\] where \(B-G(m):=\{\xi\in\D:\xi+G(m)\in B\}\). Taking probabilities under the noise law yields: \[L(m,B)=\mu_\eta\!\bigl(B-G(m)\bigr), \qquad B\in\SigmaD.\] In pushforward notation: \(L(m,\cdot)=(T_{G(m)})_\#\mu_\eta\), where \(T_y(\xi)=\xi+y\). The data-given-model kernel is simply the noise distribution shifted by the forward response. The likelihood as a shifted noise density Now take \(\lambda\) to be Lebesgue measure on \(\D=\mathbb{R}^{N_d}\), and assume the noise law \(\mu_\eta\) has a Lebesgue density \(\rho_\eta(\xi)=d\mu_\eta/d\lambda(\xi)\). The choice of Lebesgue measure is not cosmetic: the computation below slides the density along a translation, and Lebesgue measure is translation-invariant . For a general reference measure \(\lambda\), the density of the translated noise law with respect to \(\lambda\) is not simply \(\rho_\eta(d-G(m))\), one would pick up a Radon–Nikodým correction comparing \(\lambda\) to its own translate (and if \(\lambda\) and its translate are mutually singular, no such density exists at all). (This construction, the likelihood as a shifted noise density with respect to a translation-invariant reference measure, is exactly the mechanism that powers Bayesian inversion on function spaces, where Lebesgue measure no longer exists and the noise law itself takes over as the reference measure; see Stuart [Stu10] .) Testing \(L(m,\cdot)\) against a bounded measurable function \(f\) and performing the change of variable \(d=G(m)+\xi\) (using translation invariance of Lebesgue measure): \[\int_\D f(d)\,L(m,dd)=\int_\D f(d)\,\rho_\eta\!\bigl(d-G(m)\bigr)\,\lambda(dd).\] By the Radon–Nikodým theorem, the likelihood is: \[L(d\mid m)=\frac{dL(m,\cdot)}{d\lambda}(d)=\rho_\eta\!\bigl(d-G(m)\bigr).\] Intuition The likelihood is the noise density evaluated at the residual \(d-G(m)\), the mismatch between the observed data and the forward-model prediction. Whether a small residual is favoured depends entirely on the shape and centring of the noise density. For the familiar centred, unimodal noise models , Gaussian noise \(\rho_\eta(r)\propto\exp(-\tfrac12\lVert r\rVert^2_{\mathbf{C}^{-1}})\) being the canonical example, the density decreases with the size of the residual, so small residuals do mean high likelihood. But an arbitrary noise density can be asymmetric, multimodal, or even vanish at zero (noise concentrated near \(\pm 1\) makes a perfect data fit unlikely!). The exact statement is: the likelihood equals the noise density at the residual, nothing more, nothing less. The posterior for additive noise Substituting the likelihood into Bayes' relation, the posterior measure is: \[\mu_{\M\mid D=d}(dm)=\frac{\rho_\eta\!\bigl(d-G(m)\bigr)\,\muMzero(dm)}{Z(d)},\] where the evidence is: \[Z(d)=\int_{\M}\rho_\eta\!\bigl(d-G(m)\bigr)\,\muMzero(dm).\] This is the measure-theoretic Bayes' formula for inverse problems with additive noise. It requires no division by point probabilities. The denominator \(Z(d)\) is an integral over the model space, it is finite and positive under standard assumptions, even when the data space is continuous and \(\muD(\{d\})=0\). A finite-dimensional story, signpost for infinite dimensions Everything in this additive-noise section leaned on Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb{R}^{N_d}\). In infinite-dimensional data or model spaces there is no Lebesgue measure to lean on, no σ-finite, translation-invariant measure exists on an infinite-dimensional Banach space. Worse, translating a Gaussian measure can produce a mutually singular measure unless the shift lies in its Cameron–Martin space. The right infinite-dimensional formulation therefore expresses the posterior as a density with respect to the prior , \(\frac{d\mu^{d}}{d\mu^{0}}(m)\propto\exp[-\Phi(m;d)]\), rather than giving prior and posterior densities with respect to a (nonexistent) flat volume measure. This is the standard formulation of Bayesian inverse problems on function spaces; the finite-dimensional formulas of this section are its Lebesgue-dominated special case. F3e-3, Finite vs.continuous data spaces. In the finite case, each data point has positive predictive probability, so column normalization works. In continuous spaces, \(\muD(\{\dobs\})=0\), but the posterior kernel is still well-defined, it was constructed by disintegration, not by dividing by point probabilities. What we have achieved Let us take stock. We started in finite land with a simple ratio formula. We then climbed to the measure-theoretic level: Part 3c : Conditional expectation defines conditional probability via integrals, avoiding division by zero. Part 3d : Disintegration bundles eventwise conditional probabilities into conditional probability measures. Part 3e : Bayes' formula emerges as the equality of two disintegrations of the same joint law. The familiar density form is a special case. The measure-theoretic view keeps the underlying objects visible: \[\text{prior measure}, \qquad \text{observation kernel}, \qquad \text{joint measure}, \qquad \text{posterior kernel}.\] This is the language needed for regular conditional probabilities and for Bayesian inverse problems on general spaces. Warning In continuous spaces, \(\muD(\{\dobs\})=0\). The density formula \(\pi(m\mid d)\) is not the foundation, it is a representation of the posterior-kernel construction relative to chosen reference measures. The kernel form works in both finite and continuous settings. In Part 3f , we will take the integral Bayes formula we have just derived and apply it back to the finite switch problem, bringing everything home to where we started. References Joseph T. Chang and David Pollard (1997). “Conditioning as disintegration.” Statistica Neerlandica 51(3), 287–317. Bayes via two disintegrations of the joint measure. doi:10.1111/1467-9574.00056 Andrew M. Stuart (2010). “Inverse problems: A Bayesian perspective.” Acta Numerica 19, 451–559. The same structure on function spaces: Bayesian inversion in infinite dimensions. doi:10.1017/S0962492910000061 · free PDF (Cambridge Core) ← Part 3d: Disintegration Part 3f: Back to Finite Land →

title: Part 3f: Back to Finite Land | Bayes, Measure-Theoretically | Adrian Mag
desc: Part 3f of Bayes, Measure-Theoretically: Applying the integral Bayes formula to the finite switch problem, bringing everything back to finite land.
text: Part 3f: Back to Finite Land Applying the integral Bayes formula to the finite switch problem, bringing everything home. Part of Bayes, Measure-Theoretically . « Overview 1 The Game 2 High-School Solution 3a Points → Events 3b Conditioning 3c Cond. Expectation 3d Disintegration 3e Bayesian Inversion 3f Back to Finite 4 Summary The integral Bayes formula, applied to the switch problem In Part 3e , we derived the measure-theoretic Bayes formula: \[\int_B \mu_{\M\mid D=d}(A)\,\muD(dd)=\int_A L(m,B)\,\muMzero(dm).\] This is an identity between two disintegrations of the same joint law. It works in both finite and continuous spaces. Now we apply it to the finite switch problem, the same problem we started with in Part 1 and solved with ratios in Part 2 . The goal is to see that the measure-theoretic formula, when specialized to finite spaces, reproduces exactly the elementary Bayes' rule. The integrals become sums, the kernels become conditional probability tables, and the posterior kernel becomes the normalized column. Recall the setup The model space is \(\M=\{00,01,10,11\}\) with prior \(\muMzero\). The data space is \(\D=\{0,1\}\). The observation kernel is \(L(m,B)=\mathbb{P}(D\in B\mid M=m)\). The joint measure is: \[\Pi(A\times B)=\int_A L(m,B)\,\muMzero(dm).\] In the finite case, the integral is a sum: \[\Pi(A\times B)=\sum_{m\in A} L(m,B)\,\muMzero(\{m\}).\] The predictive data measure is: \[\muD(B)=\Pi(\M\times B)=\sum_{m\in\M} L(m,B)\,\muMzero(\{m\}).\] We computed these in Part 3d : \[\muD(\{0\})=0.32, \qquad \muD(\{1\})=0.68.\] Solving for the posterior kernel The posterior-side disintegration gives: \[\Pi(A\times B)=\int_B \mu_{\M\mid D=d}(A)\,\muD(dd).\] Because \(\D=\{0,1\}\), we can take \(B=\{d\}\) for each \(d\in\D\). The integral becomes a single term: \[\Pi(A\times\{d\})=\mu_{\M\mid D=d}(A)\,\muD(\{d\}).\] Since \(\muD(\{0\})=0.32>0\) and \(\muD(\{1\})=0.68>0\), we may divide: \[\mu_{\M\mid D=d}(A)=\frac{\Pi(A\times\{d\})}{\muD(\{d\})}=\frac{\int_A L(m,\{d\})\,\muMzero(dm)}{\int_{\M} L(m,\{d\})\,\muMzero(dm)}.\] The formula in finite land This is the integral Bayes formula applied to the finite case. The numerator is an integral over \(A\), in finite land, a weighted sum. The denominator is the evidence \(Z(d)\), also a sum. The ratio is exactly the normalized column of the joint table. Computing the posterior probabilities Case \(d=0\): the reporter says “0” For \(A=\{00\}\): \[\mu_{\M\mid D=0}(\{00\})=\frac{L(00,\{0\})\,\muMzero(\{00\})}{\muD(\{0\})}=\frac{0.2\cdot 0.4}{0.32}=\frac{0.08}{0.32}=\frac{1}{4}.\] Running the same computation for the other three states (\(0.8\cdot 0.1\), \(0.8\cdot 0.1\), and \(0.2\cdot 0.4\) in the numerator, respectively) gives \(0.08\) each time: \[\mu_{\M\mid D=0}(\{00\})=\mu_{\M\mid D=0}(\{01\})=\mu_{\M\mid D=0}(\{10\})=\mu_{\M\mid D=0}(\{11\})=\frac{1}{4}.\] When the reporter says “0”, the posterior is uniform. Note carefully what makes it uniform: it is not that \(d=0\) is equally likely under every model state, the likelihoods are \(L(m,\{0\})=(0.2,\,0.8,\,0.8,\,0.2)\) across \((00,01,10,11)\), far from equal. And the uniform posterior does not coincide with the prior \((0.4,\,0.1,\,0.1,\,0.4)\). What happens is that the likelihood exactly cancels the nonuniformity of the prior : the products \(L(m,\{0\})\,\muMzero(\{m\})\) all equal \(0.08\), so normalization flattens everything to \(1/4\). This is the same observation we made in Part 2 , equal products , not equal likelihoods. Case \(d=1\): the reporter says “1” For \(A=\{00\}\): \[\mu_{\M\mid D=1}(\{00\})=\frac{L(00,\{1\})\,\muMzero(\{00\})}{\muD(\{1\})}=\frac{0.8\cdot 0.4}{0.68}=\frac{0.32}{0.68}=\frac{8}{17}.\] For \(A=\{11\}\): \[\mu_{\M\mid D=1}(\{11\})=\frac{L(11,\{1\})\,\muMzero(\{11\})}{\muD(\{1\})}=\frac{0.8\cdot 0.4}{0.68}=\frac{8}{17}.\] For \(A=\{01\}\): \[\mu_{\M\mid D=1}(\{01\})=\frac{L(01,\{1\})\,\muMzero(\{01\})}{\muD(\{1\})}=\frac{0.2\cdot 0.1}{0.68}=\frac{0.02}{0.68}=\frac{1}{34}.\] The same computation gives \(\mu_{\M\mid D=1}(\{10\})=\frac{1}{34}\) as well (its likelihood and prior mass match those of \(01\)). So when the reporter says “1”, the posterior concentrates on the matching states \(\{00,11\}\): \[\mu_{\M\mid D=1}(\{00\})=\mu_{\M\mid D=1}(\{11\})=\frac{8}{17}\approx 0.471,\] \[\mu_{\M\mid D=1}(\{01\})=\mu_{\M\mid D=1}(\{10\})=\frac{1}{34}\approx 0.029.\] F3f-1, The posterior kernel for the switch problem. Left: when \(d=0\), the posterior is uniform , the likelihood exactly cancels the prior's nonuniformity. Right: when \(d=1\), the posterior concentrates on the matching states \(\{00,11\}\). These are exactly the same numbers we computed in Part 2 , now derived from the measure-theoretic Bayes formula. Plugging in the actual observation We have now constructed the full posterior kernel \(d\longmapsto \mu_{\M\mid D=d}\). Only at this point do we use the actual observed report. If the reporter announces \(\dobs\in\D\), then the posterior measure on the model space is: \[\mu^{\mathrm{post}}_{\M}(\cdot)=\mu_{\M\mid D=\dobs}(\cdot).\] Intuition The observation selects a measure from the posterior kernel. It does not create the update rule from scratch. The kernel was already constructed by disintegration; the observation merely picks the appropriate slice. The full circle Let us trace the journey: Part 1 : We posed the switch problem, a finite game with hidden states and a noisy reporter. Part 2 : We solved it with the elementary ratio formula \(\mathbb{P}(m\mid d)=\mathbb{P}(m,d)/\mathbb{P}(d)\), column normalization of the joint table. Parts 3a–3b : We saw that the elementary formula breaks when conditioning events have probability zero (Borel–Kolmogorov paradox). Part 3c : We defined conditional expectation via integrals, avoiding division by zero. Conditional probability falls out as conditional expectation of indicator functions. Part 3d : We bundled eventwise conditional probabilities into conditional probability measures via disintegration. Part 3e : We derived Bayes' formula as the equality of two disintegrations of the same joint law. The familiar density form appeared as a special case. Part 3f: We applied the integral formula back to the finite switch problem. The integrals became sums, the kernels became tables, and the answer is exactly the same as in Part 2. The payoff The measure-theoretic machinery, conditional expectation, disintegration, posterior kernels, reproduces the elementary answer in finite land, but it also works in continuous spaces where the elementary formula breaks down. We climbed to infinite land, built a more general framework, and descended back to find that the familiar answer was there all along. The story ends where it began, in finite land, but we now carry the tools to go beyond it. ← Part 3e: Bayesian Inversion Part 4: Summary →

title: Part 4: Summary & Notation Map | Bayes, Measure-Theoretically | Adrian Mag
desc: Part 4 of Bayes, Measure-Theoretically: Summary of the argument and a dictionary between elementary and measure-theoretic notation.
text: Part 4: Summary & Notation Map The two stories side by side, plus a dictionary. Part of Bayes, Measure-Theoretically . « Overview 1 The Game 2 High-School Solution 3a Points → Events 3b Conditioning 3c Cond. Expectation 3d Disintegration 3e Bayesian Inversion 3f Back to Finite 4 Summary Summary of the argument We have solved the same toy problem twice. The first solution used elementary finite probability. The second solution used measure-theoretic language. The answers were the same, but the second version exposed the structure that survives beyond finite tables. The finite arithmetic story In the finite arithmetic story, we began with two ingredients. First, we had a prior distribution on the hidden model space: \[\mathbb{P}(m).\] Second, we had the reporter rule: \[\mathbb{P}(d\mid m).\] Multiplying these gave the joint table: \[\mathbb{P}(m,d) = \mathbb{P}(m)\mathbb{P}(d\mid m).\] Adding down the data columns gave the predictive probabilities: \[\mathbb{P}(d) = \sum_{m\in\M}\mathbb{P}(m,d).\] Normalizing each column gave the posterior rule: \[\mathbb{P}(m\mid d) = \frac{\mathbb{P}(m,d)}{\mathbb{P}(d)}.\] Finally, once the actual report \(\dobs\) was heard, we selected the corresponding posterior: \[\mathbb{P}(m\mid d=\dobs).\] Thus the finite story is \[\text{prior} + \text{reporter rule} \Longrightarrow \text{joint table},\] \[\text{joint table} \Longrightarrow \text{predictive probabilities},\] \[\text{normalize each data column} \Longrightarrow \text{posterior rule},\] \[\text{observed report} \Longrightarrow \text{choose one posterior}.\] F4a, Side-by-side comparison. The elementary story (top) and the measure-theoretic story (bottom) follow the same chain. Each box in the top row has a direct counterpart in the bottom row. The arithmetic is the same; the language is different. The measure-theoretic story In the measure-theoretic story, the prior distribution became a probability measure \(\muMzero\) on the measurable model space \((\M,\SigmaM)\). The reporter rule became an observation kernel \[L(m,B), \qquad B\in\SigmaD,\] from the model space to the data space. Together, the prior measure and observation kernel defined the joint measure \[\Pi(A\times B) = \int_A L(m,B)\,\muMzero(dm).\] The predictive data measure was the data marginal of \(\Pi\): \[\muD(B) = \Pi(\M\times B) = \int_{\M} L(m,B)\,\muMzero(dm).\] The posterior update became a posterior kernel \[d\longmapsto \kappa(d,\cdot),\] characterized by the consistency identity \[\Pi(A\times B) = \int_B \kappa(d,A)\,\muD(dd).\] Finally, once the observed report \(\dobs\) was known, the posterior measure was obtained by evaluation: \[\mu^{\mathrm{post}}_{\M}(\cdot) = \kappa(\dobs,\cdot).\] Thus the measure-theoretic story is \[\muMzero + L \Longrightarrow \Pi,\] \[\Pi \Longrightarrow \muD,\] \[\Pi \text{ and } \muD \Longrightarrow \kappa,\] \[\dobs \Longrightarrow \kappa(\dobs,\cdot).\] Lesson The two stories are the same story. The elementary version uses tables of numbers; the measure-theoretic version uses measures and kernels. Both follow: prior + observation kernel → joint → predictive → posterior → plug in observation. Final slogan Key Idea In the finite case, Bayes is column normalization. In the general case, Bayes is the extraction of a posterior kernel from a joint measure. The finite table is the seed. The measure-theoretic construction is the tree. The tree is not decorative. The posterior-kernel form of Bayes is precisely what carries Bayesian inversion to function spaces, where densities with respect to Lebesgue measure no longer exist [Stu10] , and the two-disintegration view these notes built is set out definitively in Chang and Pollard [CP97] . Notation map Object Elementary notation Measure-theoretic notation Hidden states \(m\in\{00,01,10,11\}\) \((\M,\SigmaM)\) Reports \(d\in\{0,1\}\) \((\D,\SigmaD)\) Prior \(\mathbb{P}(m)\) \(\muMzero\) Reporter rule \(\mathbb{P}(d\mid m)\) \(L(m,\cdot)\) Joint law \(\mathbb{P}(m,d)\) \(\Pi\) Predictive law \(\mathbb{P}(d)\) \(\muD\) Posterior rule \(d\mapsto\mathbb{P}(m\mid d)\) \(d\mapsto\kappa(d,\cdot)\) Observed posterior \(\mathbb{P}(m\mid \dobs)\) \(\kappa(\dobs,\cdot)\) Dictionary between the elementary and measure-theoretic presentations. F4b, The full Bayesian chain at a glance. Prior and observation kernel combine into the joint measure, which splits into the predictive (by marginalization) and the posterior kernel (by disintegration). The observation selects one measure from the kernel. The consistency identity links all four objects. References Joseph T. Chang and David Pollard (1997). “Conditioning as disintegration.” Statistica Neerlandica 51(3), 287–317. The two-disintegration view of Bayes, set out definitively. doi:10.1111/1467-9574.00056 Andrew M. Stuart (2010). “Inverse problems: A Bayesian perspective.” Acta Numerica 19, 451–559. Why the kernel form matters: Bayesian inversion where densities fail. doi:10.1017/S0962492910000061 · free PDF (Cambridge Core) ← Part 3f: Back to Finite Land Overview →

title: Bayesian and Frequentist Inference | Adrian Mag
desc: A conceptual comparison of Bayesian and frequentist inference from the same starting point, an ontological–epistemological split.
text: Bayesian and Frequentist Inference From an ontological–epistemological split. 1 The Setup 2 The Observation Kernel 3 Bayesian Path 4 Frequentist Path 5 Beyond Additive What to expect Bayesian and frequentist inference do not merely give different answers to the same probabilistic question. They construct different epistemological objects around the same ontological situation. The divide is old, and its founding documents are all linked from these pages: Bayes’s essay [Bay63] and Jeffreys’s Theory of Probability [Jef39] on one side; Fisher’s foundations [Fis22] , the Neyman–Pearson theory of tests [NP33] , and Neyman’s confidence estimation [Ney37] on the other. Efron’s “Why Isn’t Everyone a Bayesian?” [Efr86] is the classic short meditation on why both survive. Each part closes with the references behind its claims. We begin with a simple observation equation: \[ \dobs=\dtrue+\nobs. \] Here \(\dobs\) is the observed datum, \(\dtrue\) is the unknown true datum, and \(\nobs\) is the realized noise. This equation is not yet Bayesian or frequentist, it is simply a statement about the relation between truth, observation, and error. The Bayesian introduces a probability measure on possible true data values to represent uncertainty about \(\dtrue\), then conditions on \(\dobs\) to obtain posterior probabilities over possible truths. The frequentist refuses to assign a probability law to \(\dtrue\), keeps it fixed but unknown, places probability on the data-generating procedure, and constructs calibrated procedures with controlled repeated-sampling behaviour. The goal is not to declare one perspective correct and the other incorrect. The goal is to make precise what each perspective is doing, what objects it constructs, what statements it licenses, and what statements it does not license. Sources & the divide The landmarks on both sides, all clickable: Thomas Bayes (1763). “An Essay towards solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances.” (Communicated by Richard Price.) Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society 53, 370–418. Probability on a representation of the truth: where it begins. doi:10.1098/rstl.1763.0053 Ronald A. Fisher (1922). “On the Mathematical Foundations of Theoretical Statistics.” Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A 222, 309–368. Likelihood and the foundations of estimation. doi:10.1098/rsta.1922.0009 Jerzy Neyman and Egon S. Pearson (1933). “On the Problem of the Most Efficient Tests of Statistical Hypotheses.” Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A 231, 289–337. The theory of tests: acceptance regions, errors of two kinds. doi:10.1098/rsta.1933.0009 Jerzy Neyman (1937). “Outline of a Theory of Statistical Estimation Based on the Classical Theory of Probability.” Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A 236(767), 333–380. Confidence sets and pre-observation coverage. doi:10.1098/rsta.1937.0005 Harold Jeffreys (1939). Theory of Probability . Oxford University Press (3rd edition 1961; Oxford Classic Texts reissue 1998). The classical Bayesian counterpoint. doi:10.1093/oso/9780198503682.001.0001 Bradley Efron (1986). “Why Isn’t Everyone a Bayesian?” The American Statistician 40(1), 1–5. Why the divide persists: a short, sharp essay. doi:10.1080/00031305.1986.10475342 Andrew Gelman, John B. Carlin, Hal S. Stern, David B. Dunson, Aki Vehtari, and Donald B. Rubin (2013). Bayesian Data Analysis , 3rd edition. CRC Press. Modern Bayesian practice (free from the authors). book page · free PDF (authors’ edition) The five parts Part 1, The Setup . The ontological observation equation: actual objects, what is known and what is hidden, and why the decomposition of \(\dobs\) into truth and noise is not identifiable from the observation alone. Part 2, The Observation Kernel . The noise model as an epistemological object. Candidate-dependent observation laws, the observation kernel as a map from candidate truths to probability measures on observations, and what it can and cannot say by itself. Part 3, The Bayesian Path . Introducing a prior, the epistemological true-datum random variable, the joint measure, the posterior kernel, and what collapses when the prior is removed. Part 4, The Frequentist Path . Truth fixed, observation random. Noise acceptance regions, confidence sets from shifted noise, the coverage statement, and what the frequentist does and does not claim. Part 5, Beyond Additive Noise . Heteroscedastic and non-additive observation laws, the general likelihood-based construction of confidence sets, test statistics, and decision rules with worst-case guarantees.

title: Part 1: The Setup | Bayesian and Frequentist Inference | Adrian Mag
desc: Part 1: The ontological observation equation, actual objects, what is known and hidden, and why the decomposition is not identifiable.
text:
Part 1: The Setup The ontological observation equation. Part of Bayesian and Frequentist Inference . « Overview 1 The Setup 2 The Observation Kernel 3 Bayesian Path 4 Frequentist Path 5 Beyond Additive The guiding question We begin with a simple observation equation: \[ \dobs=\dtrue+
obs. \] Here \(\dobs\) is the datum that has actually been observed, \(\dtrue\) is the unknown true datum, and \(
obs\) is the actual realized observational error. This equation is not yet Bayesian or frequentist. It is simply a statement about the relation between the true datum, the observed datum, and the error that occurred. The guiding question is: \[ 	ext{What can be said about } \dtrue 	ext{ after observing } \dobs\,? \] Since \(\dobs=\dtrue+
obs\), one might hope that knowing \(\dobs\) and having a probabilistic model for the noise would immediately yield a probabilistic statement about \(\dtrue\). But this is not automatic. If \(\dtrue\) were known, we could imagine repeating the observation many times: each time, the same true datum would be combined with a different noise realization, producing different observed data. The probability law of those observed data would be the noise law shifted by \(\dtrue\), and we could ask whether \(\dobs\) looks typical or atypical under that law. But in the inverse problem, \(\dtrue\) is precisely what is unknown. There is not one single observation law, there is a family of possible observation laws, one for each candidate true datum. Each candidate truth, combined with the noise model, generates its own prediction about what observations should look like. This family is called the observation kernel. It tells us how plausible the observed datum would be under each candidate truth, but by itself it does not assign probabilities to the candidate truths. The Bayesian and frequentist approaches part ways at this point: Bayesian question. Given \(\dobs\), how should probability be distributed over possible true data values? Frequentist question. Can we construct a procedure which reliably captures or tests the fixed truth under repeated observations? Both questions are meaningful, but they are not the same question. The actual objects The quantities involved in the real measurement are not random variables, they are realized quantities: True datum \(\dtrue \in \Dspace\): the datum that would be obtained if the observation process were perfect. Observed datum \(\dobs \in \Dspace\): the datum that was actually recorded. Realized noise \(
obs \in \Dspace\): the particular error that occurred in the observation process. These three quantities are not random merely because we do not know them. Once the observation has happened, reality has already selected the values \(\dtrue\), \(\dobs\), and \(
obs\). Some may be hidden from us, but their hiddenness is an epistemological issue, not an ontological one. Key distinction Random variables, mathematical objects introduced to represent uncertainty, variability, or repeated sampling , are epistemological constructions . They are not the same kind of object as the actual realized quantities \(
obs\), \(\dtrue\), and \(\dobs\). We will introduce such random variables in the next part, when we build the noise model and the observation kernel. What is known and what is hidden After the observation, the known quantity is \(\dobs\). The hidden quantities are \(\dtrue\) and \(
obs\). The true datum is hidden because the measurement is noisy. The realized noise is hidden because it can only be computed if \(\dtrue\) is already known. This creates a circular-looking difficulty: \[ 
obs=\dobs-\dtrue. \] To know the noise, we would need to know the truth. But to know the truth, we would need to know the noise. From the observed datum alone, the decomposition \(\dobs = \dtrue + 
obs\) is not identifiable . For any candidate true datum \(\mathbf d \in \Dspace\), one can define an implied realized noise \[ \mathbf n_{\mathrm{implied}} = \dobs - \mathbf d. \] The observation can always be explained by many different candidate truths, each paired with a different implied noise. The role of a noise model is to distinguish among these explanations by saying which implied noises are plausible and which are not. But that step already introduces an epistemological object, it is no longer just the realized observation equation. Why the distinction matters Many interpretational mistakes come from silently replacing ontological objects by epistemological random variables, or from using frequentist confidence statements as though they were Bayesian posterior probability statements. Here is a concrete example of the kind of confusion that arises. A frequentist confidence set is a rule that takes an observation and returns a set of candidate truths. Before the observation is made, the observation is random, so the confidence set is also random. The frequentist can calibrate the procedure so that, over many hypothetical repetitions of the experiment, the random confidence set contains the fixed true datum with a specified frequency, say \(95\%\). After the observation is made, the rule produces a concrete, fixed set. At this point, either the true datum lies inside that set or it does not, there is no more randomness in the frequentist model. It is tempting to say “the probability that the true datum lies in this set is \(95\%\),” but that statement requires a probability model for the true datum after observing, which is a Bayesian-type object, not something the frequentist construction provides. Common confusion The statement “the procedure catches the truth with frequency \(95\%\)” is not the same as “the probability that the truth lies in this particular realized set is \(95\%\).” The first is a pre-observation statement about a random procedure. The second is a post-observation statement that requires a probability law for the true datum. The organizing principle Once the ontological and epistemological layers are separated, the Bayesian and frequentist constructions become easier to compare: Bayesian inference places probability on an epistemological representation of the truth. Frequentist inference places probability on the observation procedure while keeping the truth fixed. Neither construction is a modern invention. The Bayesian move, probability on a representation of the truth, descends from Bayes’s essay [Bay63] and received its fullest classical defence from Jeffreys [Jef39] ; the frequentist move, probability on the procedure, truth held fixed, is Neyman’s program [Ney37] . Why intelligent people continue to disagree about which object to build is itself a classic question; Efron’s essay [Efr86] remains the sharpest short statement of the trade-offs. This separation will be the organizing principle for everything that follows. The next part introduces the first major epistemological construction built from the noise model: the observation kernel. ← Overview Part 2: The Observation Kernel → References Thomas Bayes (1763). “An Essay towards solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances.” (Communicated by Richard Price.) Oxford University Press (3rd edition 1961; Oxford Classic Texts reissue 1998). The classical, fully developed Bayesian position. doi:10.1093/oso/9780198503682.001.0001 Jerzy Neyman (1937). “Outline of a Theory of Statistical Estimation Based on the Classical Theory of Probability.” Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A 236(767), 333–380. Probability on the procedure: confidence estimation. doi:10.1098/rsta.1937.0005 Bradley Efron (1986). “Why Isn’t Everyone a Bayesian?” The American Statistician 40(1), 1–5. A short, honest account of why the divide persists. doi:10.1080/00031305.1986.10475342

title: Part 2: The Observation Kernel | Bayesian and Frequentist Inference | Adrian Mag
desc: Part 2: The noise model as an epistemological object, the observation kernel, and what it can and cannot say.
text:
Part 2: The Observation Kernel The noise model as an epistemological object. Part of Bayesian and Frequentist Inference . « Overview 1 The Setup 2 The Observation Kernel 3 Bayesian Path 4 Frequentist Path 5 Beyond Additive From realized noise to a noise model In the ontological observation equation \(\dobs = \dtrue + 
obs\), the quantity \(
obs\) denotes the actual noise that occurred. To reason about uncertainty, we introduce a mathematical model for possible noise realizations: a random variable \[ \Nrand : \Omega 	o \Dspace \] with probability law \(\Nrand \sim \muN\). The measure \(\muN\) describes which noise values are considered plausible, likely, unlikely, or extreme according to the assumed observation model. For example, if the noise is centred and Gaussian, noise values near zero receive high density, while large deviations receive low density. Two kinds of objects Ontological noise: \(
obs\) is the actual error that occurred. Epistemological noise model: \(\Nrand \sim \muN\) is the mathematical model for possible errors. The noise law \(\muN\) tells us how the observation procedure behaves probabilistically. It does not, by itself, identify the particular noise realization in the actual experiment. The shifted noise measure If \(\dtrue\) were known, we could combine it with the noise random variable and construct a random observed datum \(\Dobsrand = \dtrue + \Nrand\). Define the translation map \[ T_{\dtrue} : \Dspace 	o \Dspace, \qquad T_{\dtrue}(\mathbf n) = \dtrue + \mathbf n. \] The law of \(\Dobsrand\) is the pushforward of \(\muN\) through \(T_{\dtrue}\): \[ \mu_{\dtrue} = (T_{\dtrue})_{\#}\muN, \] meaning that for every measurable set \(A \subseteq \Dspace\), \[ \mu_{\dtrue}(A) = \muN(A - \dtrue). \] If \(\muN\) has a density \(p_N\), the shifted observation law has density \[ p_{\dtrue}(\mathbf d') = p_N(\mathbf d' - \dtrue). \] This expression already reveals the central difficulty. To evaluate how plausible the observation is under the true shifted noise law, one needs the residual \(\dobs - \dtrue\). But \(\dtrue\) is unknown. When a density exists, plausibility is measured by the density at \(\dobs\); when no density exists, one works directly with the noise measure of neighbourhoods around the implied residual. Candidate true data and the observation kernel Since \(\dtrue\) is unknown, we cannot construct the shifted noise law centred at \(\dtrue\). What we can do is consider possible candidate values. For each candidate \(\mathbf d \in \Dspace\), the observation model would be \(\Dobsrand_{\mathbf d} = \mathbf d + \Nrand\), with law \[ \mu_{\mathbf d} = (T_{\mathbf d})_{\#}\muN, \qquad \mu_{\mathbf d}(A) = \muN(A - \mathbf d). \] If a density exists, the density at the actual observed datum is \[ p(\dobs \mid \mathbf d) = p_N(\dobs - \mathbf d). \] This measures how plausible the observed datum would be if \(\mathbf d\) were the true datum. In continuous data spaces, the literal probability of observing exactly \(\dobs\) is zero; the density (or the probability of a small neighbourhood around \(\dobs\)) is the appropriate measure of plausibility. The assignment \[ \mathbf d \longmapsto \mu_{\mathbf d} \] is the observation kernel . More explicitly: \[ \L : \Dspace 	imes \Sigma_{\Dspace} 	o [0,1], \qquad \L(\mathbf d, A) = \mu_{\mathbf d}(A) = \muN(A - \mathbf d). \] For each fixed candidate truth \(\mathbf d\), the map \(A \mapsto \L(\mathbf d, A)\) is a probability measure on the observation space. For each fixed observation event \(A\), the map \(\mathbf d \mapsto \L(\mathbf d, A)\) describes how the probability of observing \(A\) depends on the candidate truth. Direction matters The observation kernel has the direction: \[ 	ext{candidate truth} \longmapsto 	ext{probability measure on possible observations}. \] It does not map observations to probability measures on truths. That reverse direction requires a prior. What the observation kernel can say The observation kernel can answer candidate-wise questions. For a proposed true datum \(\mathbf d\), it asks: if \(\mathbf d\) were true, would \(\dobs\) be a plausible outcome of the noise model? (Read as a function of the candidate \(\mathbf d\) with the observation held fixed, the kernel is precisely the object Fisher named the likelihood [Fis22] ; the measure-theoretic scaffolding that lets us treat all of these objects as honest probability measures is Kolmogorov’s [Kol33] .) In the additive setting, this reduces to examining the implied noise \(\dobs - \mathbf d\). If this lies in a high-probability region of \(\muN\), the candidate is compatible; if it lies in a low-probability region, the candidate is less compatible. For example, if \(E_\alpha \subseteq \Dspace\) is a noise region with \(\muN(E_\alpha) = 1 - \alpha\), then a candidate \(\mathbf d\) is compatible at level \(1-\alpha\) if \(\dobs - \mathbf d \in E_\alpha\), or equivalently \(\mathbf d \in \dobs - E_\alpha\). This is the basic frequentist compatibility idea that will later become a confidence set. What the observation kernel cannot say alone The observation kernel does not, by itself, assign probabilities to candidate true data values. It tells us how plausible the observation would be if \(\mathbf d\) were true , via density or neighbourhood probability, not literal point probability in continuous settings, but not how probable \(\mathbf d\) is given the observation. A posterior distribution would have the opposite direction: \(\dobs \longmapsto\) probability measure on possible true data values. To construct such a posterior, one needs a prior measure on possible true data values. Without that prior, the likelihood values \(\ell_{\dobs}(\mathbf d) = p_N(\dobs - \mathbf d)\) are compatibility scores , not probabilities over \(\mathbf d\). Not licensed by likelihood alone The statement \(\Prob(\dtrue \in A \mid \dobs) = 0.95\) requires a probability model for \(\dtrue\). The observation kernel provides only the family of observation laws \(\{\mu_{\mathbf d} : \mathbf d \in \Dspace\}\). It does not provide a probability law on \(\mathbf d\). The observation kernel is therefore a crucial object shared by both Bayesian and frequentist reasoning, but it is not yet a full inference about the truth. What one does with that family of laws is where the Bayesian and frequentist constructions begin to diverge. ← Part 1: The Setup Part 3: Bayesian Path → References Ronald A. Fisher (1922). “On the Mathematical Foundations of Theoretical Statistics.” Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A 222, 309–368.
