title: The Box Everyone Knows - Adrian Mag
desc: Why a bare chat box can fail through model errors or missing context, and what a harness adds.
text: The Box Everyone Knows Movement I · What you are actually talking to 1 Box 2 Kernel 3 Chat box 4 CPU 5 Anatomy 6 AGENTS.md 7 Skills 8 Hooks 9 Tools 10 Context 11 Orchestration S Summary Act 1 Current as of July 2026 You have used one. A box, a cursor, an answer. Perhaps it was useful. Perhaps it told you something false with complete confidence and you have not been back since. That failure is probably not evidence of what you think it is. The interface is the same everywhere. One box. You type into it, an answer appears, and that is the whole of the machine as far as anyone can see. In one respect it is an honest interface: it hides nothing on purpose. For exactly that reason it is also misleading. There is no visible difference between the box with almost nothing behind it and the box with a great deal. Most people’s judgement of this technology was formed at that box. That is a reasonable place to form it. It is also a bit like judging an engine by driving the car around a car park. Two bad experiences that look identical Think about the last time one of these systems disappointed you. It was probably one of two failures, and they have almost nothing in common. The first is the famous one. You asked for a fact and got a confident fabrication: a citation that does not exist, a function that was never in the library, a date off by three years. Everyone can name this one. It is a hallucination. It may never disappear entirely, though it has receded a long way in the past two years. screenshot · ChatGPT web interface Exhibit 1 The answer is 483. The setup is correct : subtracting a negative does give 241 + 241 + 1. Then 241 + 241 becomes 483, which is 482 with the final 1 already folded in, and the 1 is added a second time. Nothing in the tone marks either error. Ages quickly Undated screenshot. The model version was not recorded, so treat it as an illustration of a failure mode, not as a claim about any current model. This particular sum may well be answered correctly today. The mechanism behind it has not changed. Fluent text does not mark its own failures. A response can state a plausible route, invent a source, or make a quiet mistake in the middle of a calculation while its tone stays completely steady. The system has no built-in signal that distinguishes a well-formed sentence from a checked answer. Later acts add workspace examples with inspectable source, recorded checks, and explicit limits alongside this small, honest exhibit. The distinction matters because hallucination is not limited to the failure the word usually conjures. Sometimes the problem is invented material; sometimes it is an unverified step that sounds ordinary. Act 2 is about why fluent prediction and correctness are different jobs. The second is quieter, and I think far more common now. You asked something reasonable and got an answer that was not wrong, exactly, but was useless. Generic. Correct for someone, somewhere, in some situation, just not for you in yours. You wanted advice about your codebase and got advice about codebases. You wanted to know what a term means in your field and got the meaning it has in someone else’s. The first failure is a defect in the model. The second is not a defect at all. It is the correct behaviour of a system that was never told which situation it was in, and had no way to find out. The question this series is actually about If you conclude from that second experience that the technology is oversold, you have drawn a conclusion about capability from an observation about context . The model answered the question it was given. The question it was given was missing almost everything that would have made a good answer possible: what you are working on, what you already tried, what your constraints are, what is in the file you are staring at, what your field means by that word. None of that arrived, because nothing was there to bring it. The box does not know about your files. It cannot look anything up unless someone built it a way to look things up. It has no memory of yesterday unless someone gave it one. It has none of what a capable assistant would need, and the interface gives you no hint that this is what is missing. The useful question is not how smart is the model? That question has a moving answer and everyone is already shouting about it. Ask instead: what would you have to build around it before its answers were about your situation rather than a generic one? The software that supplies those missing pieces is called a harness. Almost everything that changed in the past few years happened there rather than in the model. People who get startling results are not, for the most part, using a different model from you. They are using a different machine around it. To see why that machine is necessary, and why it takes the peculiar shape it does, you need to know exactly what sits at the centre of it. Act 2 examines that centre, and it is shorter than you might fear. ← Series overview Inside the Kernel →

title: What It Knows - Adrian Mag
desc: How harnesses assemble context through instructions, retrieval, files, tool results, and checked handoffs.
text: What It Knows Movement III · What you can change 1 Box 2 Kernel 3 Chat box 4 CPU 5 Anatomy 6 AGENTS.md 7 Skills 8 Hooks 9 Tools 10 Context 11 Orchestration S Summary Act 10 Current as of July 2026 Context is the budget that every instruction, source, and tool result shares. Retrieval assembles that context, files provide durable memory, and compaction keeps long sessions within the limit. A model only knows the material that arrives with the request. In this workspace, that material can include the task, selected instructions, source files, tool results, and a small amount of state. None of it is the model’s memory. It is a packet assembled by the harness, then discarded when that request ends. Context is a budget, not a library. An instruction that helps on every task earns a place near the start. A detailed procedure belongs in a skill until it applies. A source file is read when the task makes it useful. The order matters as well as the size: long-context research finds that relevant material can be used less reliably in the middle of an input. 1 One workspace task, assembled in stages Mechanism diagram 1. Start 2. Inspect 3. Preserve Task request AGENTS.md bootstrap Skill catalogue metadata The detailed files remain on disk. The first packet supplies routing information, not every fact in the repository. Retrieval is context assembly Retrieval is the act of choosing what to add next. It can be a search over embeddings and chunks, but it can also be a direct file lookup. This workspace uses the second form constantly: the task points to a plan, the plan points to a source dossier, and the agent reads only the relevant section. The result is still retrieval because it changes the next context packet. The historical RAG paper paired generated text with retrieved material; the modern phrase is often used more loosely for chunk, search, and prompt assembly. In practice, retrieval does not make the model remember a repository. It gives a particular request a carefully selected view of one. 2 Memory has a place to live For this workspace, durable continuity lives in files. The tracked plan and source dossier record public decisions and evidence. The local control pack records the current handoff and checks whether it still applies to the Git state. The split is deliberate: a public plan should be reviewable; live control state should not silently become a public exhibit. Long sessions eventually need compression. A summary can retain a next safe action and discard a long trail of intermediate work, but it is not a replacement for source. The website-control workflow therefore checks Git before trusting its handoff. When the state and the files disagree, the files win. Context engineering, checked 24 July 2026 Context windows, retrieval mechanisms, compaction, and prompt caching are harness behaviour, not a new faculty of the language model. The practical design question is always the same: what should this next request see, and what evidence lets us correct it when it is wrong? References Liu, N. F. et al. (2023). “Lost in the Middle.” TACL . arXiv:2307.03172 . Used for the position-sensitivity finding. Lewis, P. et al. (2020). “Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks.” arXiv:2005.11401 . Used for the original RAG framing. ← New Senses: How a Capability Becomes Available Orchestration →

title: Orchestration - Adrian Mag
desc: When orchestration earns its cost, and why most workspace tasks need one well-equipped agent rather than many.
text: Orchestration Movement III · What you can change 1 Box 2 Kernel 3 Chat box 4 CPU 5 Anatomy 6 AGENTS.md 7 Skills 8 Hooks 9 Tools 10 Context 11 Orchestration S Summary Act 11 Current as of July 2026 When one loop is not enough, a harness can route work through graphs or delegate it to subagents. Most tasks do not need that extra machinery. Orchestration begins when one loop is no longer enough. Instead of one agent choosing the next action, a harness can route work through several steps, branches, or agents. A graph is a useful picture: nodes do work or hold state; edges say what can happen next. The graph can quickly become theatrical. It is not proof that a system needs many agents, and a second model call does not repair a vague task. In the small website workflow used throughout these acts, the useful graph is mostly ordinary engineering: instructions route to a plan, the plan routes to source and page files, checks feed evidence back into a handoff, and the next task starts from verified state. A single-agent control graph Workspace structure One agent can follow a graph without spawning another agent: request ↓ AGENTS.md and selected skill ↓ plan + source dossier + page files ↓ change → focused checks → handoff ↘ ↙ next verified task Every box is represented by a real component in this workspace. The map below makes the relationships inspectable. Open the interactive workspace map When a graph earns its cost Split work only when the split gives something concrete: independent evidence, a different permission boundary, a separate tool contract, or a review point with a named owner. The public hook and tool demonstrations in this workspace are good examples of boundary nodes. They do not make a multi-agent system; they make particular operations inspectable and repeatable. Multiple agents add queues, duplicated context, conflicting summaries, and a new question: who checks the checker? For most changes, a single well-informed loop with retrieval, tests, and a handoff is cheaper and easier to audit. Anthropic’s current workflow guidance makes the same caution: improve a single call and its context before adding orchestration. 1 Control is not deployment The map is a description of this workspace’s agent-facing structure, not a deployed service architecture. The browser serves static files. The agent-docs library holds plans, references, citation evidence, and the soft Agent Ledger. The local control overlay helps an agent resume work through a legacy continuity bridge. The figure-generation scripts create assets on demand. None of those facts imply background workers, autonomous changes, or a hidden team of agents. The final discipline is to identify the loop and its boundary, then point to the evidence. If a box cannot be pointed to in source or observed in a check, it belongs in a proposal, not in a capability claim. Reference Anthropic. “Building effective agents.” Checked 24 July 2026. anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents . Used for the workflow/agent distinction and the caution against premature orchestration. ← What It Knows The Instrument →

title: Inside the Kernel - Adrian Mag
desc: Tokens, next-token prediction, and the distinction between transformer layers and harness layers.
text: Inside the Kernel Movement I · What you are actually talking to 1 Box 2 Kernel 3 Chat box 4 CPU 5 Anatomy 6 AGENTS.md 7 Skills 8 Hooks 9 Tools 10 Context 11 Orchestration S Summary Act 2 Current as of July 2026 Strip away the interface, the memory, the tools, the safety systems, and the personality, and what remains is smaller and stranger than the word “intelligence” suggests. It is a function. Text goes in; a probability distribution over the next chunk of text comes out. That is the whole of it. We are going to spend one act on the model itself and then leave it alone. The inside of these systems is technically rich, but almost nothing in the rest of this series depends on it. You need a working picture, not a full one, and the working picture is simple. It does not read words Before anything else happens, your text is chopped into tokens : fragments, roughly sub-word sized, drawn from a fixed vocabulary decided before training. Common words usually survive intact. Unusual ones shatter. A leading space is generally part of the token rather than a separator, so ·the and the are different tokens entirely. Tokenisation may sound like trivia, but it is the unit in which everything is counted, billed, and limited. Every context window, every price, every truncation you will meet later in this series is measured in these things. Type something into the panel, ideally something from your own field, and watch where it breaks. This panel needs JavaScript. It does not produce an answer Given a sequence of tokens, the model returns a probability distribution over what the next one might be. Not a decision. A distribution. Every token in its vocabulary receives some share, most of them vanishingly small. Something outside the model then picks one. That choice is a policy, not a fact: take the most likely token every time and you get flat, repetitive text; sample from further down the tail and you get variety and more mistakes. The dial governing that trade is temperature, and it lives in the software around the model, not in the model. The chosen token is then appended to the input, and the whole thing runs again. The loop (predict, pick, append, repeat) is how a paragraph gets written, one fragment at a time, with no plan for the sentence it is halfway through. This panel needs JavaScript. Notice what the second and third prompts do that the first does not. “The capital of France is” has one overwhelming continuation; the distribution barely has a tail. “My favourite colour is” spreads across several perfectly good answers, because there is no fact of the matter. So the same question, asked twice, can honestly give you two different replies. Much of what people experience as unreliability is this, seen from the outside. Two different things called “layers” The word “layers” names two different things here. Confusing them makes the rest of the series needlessly difficult. Inside the model there are layers: dozens of stacked arithmetic operations that the input passes through, each refining a numerical representation of the text. They were shaped during training, they are frozen afterwards, and you cannot change them. When someone mentions a “96-layer model”, this is what they mean. Outside the model there are also layers: the system prompt, the conversation being replayed, retrieved documents, tool definitions, memory files, permission checks. These were written by engineers, and they change weekly. These outer layers are the ones you can change. The two have nothing to do with each other beyond the shared word. This series is exclusively about the second kind. Understanding transformer layers is not a prerequisite for understanding harness layers. What the model does not have The limits are concrete, and every later act responds to one of them. It has no memory . Two calls are unrelated events; the second does not know the first happened. It has no access to your files , or to the internet, or to anything else. It emits text and nothing more. It has no clock : it cannot tell whether a second or a year passed between calls, or what today’s date is. And it cannot act . It cannot run a command, send a message, or edit a file. It can produce text that describes doing so, and something else may choose to act on that text, but that something else is not the model. Every one of those absences is filled, later, by machinery. That machinery is the subject of this series. One thing that did happen inside A raw predictor trained on text is not helpful. Continue “How do I sort a list in Python?” by pure prediction and a plausible continuation is three more forum questions, because that is what such text looks like in the wild. Turning a predictor into something that answers rather than continues took additional training: demonstrations of desired behaviour, then tuning against human comparisons of competing outputs. 1 That work happens inside the model, and it is why the box responds to a question instead of writing more questions. It is also, more or less, where the inside stops mattering for us. In short, the model has no memory, senses, hands, or clock. It is a function that returns a distribution over text fragments. Everything you have seen it do beyond that was something else, wrapped around it: remembering your name, reading your file, searching the web, running your code. The next act starts with the smallest such wrapper, the one you have already used. References Ouyang, L., Wu, J., Jiang, X., et al. (2022). “Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback.” arXiv:2203.02155. arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155 , the InstructGPT paper. Its headline result is worth the detour: a 1.3B-parameter tuned model was preferred by human raters to the 175B-parameter model it was derived from, “despite having 100x fewer parameters”. Vaswani, A., Shazeer, N., Parmar, N., et al. (2017). “Attention Is All You Need.” arXiv:1706.03762. arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762 , where the transformer architecture was introduced. Cited here for that origin only: the paper describes an encoder–decoder model for machine translation, and is not a description of how a modern chat model is built. The two are frequently conflated. ← The Box Everyone Knows Even the Chat Box Is a Harness →

title: Even the Chat Box Is a Harness - Adrian Mag
desc: How stateless model calls become coherent conversations through transcript replay and surrounding software.
text: Even the Chat Box Is a Harness Movement I · What you are actually talking to 1 Box 2 Kernel 3 Chat box 4 CPU 5 Anatomy 6 AGENTS.md 7 Skills 8 Hooks 9 Tools 10 Context 11 Orchestration S Summary Act 3 Current as of July 2026 Tell a chatbot your name. Ten messages later it still knows. That feels like memory, so it is reasonable to assume that it is. It is not. On every turn, software you never see re-reads a transcript it is keeping on your behalf. The previous act left the model with an uncomfortable property: it is a function. Context goes in, a distribution over next tokens comes out. A function does not remember what you asked it last time. So how does a conversation work? The answer follows from the constraint. If the model cannot remember, and a conversation nonetheless coheres, then something else is doing the remembering . And there is only one place that something can put what it remembers: back into the input, on the next call. The conversation has to be re-sent. Every turn. In full. This fact drives nearly everything else in the series. It is worth watching it happen rather than taking my word for it. Loading the demonstration… Both runs put the same three questions to the same model. The only difference is one line in the client: whether the earlier turns are included in the request. With them, the model knows what “resolution” means in your field, and what you told it first. Without them it is meeting you for the first time, three times in a row. Watch the token counter as you step through. In the first run it climbs, because the whole conversation is being re-sent (and re-billed) every turn. In the second it stays flat. The number is also an invoice: you are demonstrably paying to send your own conversation back to a model that did not keep it. What else the chat box is doing Re-sending the transcript is the minimum. A production chat product does more on every turn: prepending a system prompt you never see, deciding which older turns to drop as the conversation outgrows the context window, sometimes retrieving things you said in previous sessions, sometimes deciding a question warrants a web search or a code interpreter, and passing the exchange through safety classification. The internals of a closed consumer product are not public, so this is the general case rather than a claim about any particular company. Each item follows from the same constraint as before: a stateless model, plus a conversation that is coherent, personalised and tool-using, requires that something assemble all of it before the model sees a single token. That assembling machine is the harness. You have been using one all along. The distinction matters for everything that follows. The harness around a consumer chat box is small, because it is built for one job: keep a conversation going, safely, for a stranger. Swap it for a bigger one and the same model does dramatically more because it gains hands, eyes, and a memory that outlives the conversation. Act 4 examines that larger harness. ← Inside the Kernel The CPU and the Computer →

title: The CPU and the Computer - Adrian Mag
desc: Why an agent's model requests tools while the harness executes them and returns evidence.
text: The CPU and the Computer Movement II · The harness 1 Box 2 Kernel 3 Chat box 4 CPU 5 Anatomy 6 AGENTS.md 7 Skills 8 Hooks 9 Tools 10 Context 11 Orchestration S Summary Act 4 Current as of July 2026 A processor is a remarkable object that can do nothing on its own. It cannot store anything for later, reach a disk, notice the passage of time, or produce a single visible effect in the world. It computes, and it waits to be asked. Everything else you think of as “the computer” is the machinery built around that fact. The comparison comes from Andrej Karpathy, who popularised the framing of a language model as “not a chatbot, but the kernel process of a new Operating System”. 1 I want to narrow it, because the narrower version is more useful: the model is the processor , and the harness is the rest of the computer. Locating it that way makes the interesting question obvious. It is not “how fast is the chip?” but “what has been wired to it?” He drew it, which saves a great deal of description. diagram · Andrej Karpathy, X, 11 November 2023 Figure 1 The model sits where the processor sits, and the context window is drawn inside it, labelled RAM. Everything else in the picture is wired to that one box: storage, tools, a network, and other models. That is the whole argument of this act in one diagram, borrowed rather than restated. Diagram by Andrej Karpathy, reproduced here for commentary under fair dealing. It is not covered by this site’s CC BY licence, and rights remain with the author. 2 Read the specs, not just the boxes The post that carried this diagram listed GPT-4 Turbo at 20 tokens per second, 128K tokens of RAM, and Ada002 as the filesystem. Those product specifications have aged. The boxes and arrows have not. This series date-stamps product detail and argues from structure wherever it can. A local computer around one model Workspace structure model request ↕ context assembled from instructions and files ↕ tools and focused checks ↕ public source and generated assets ↕ local continuity record, checked against Git Every layer in this sketch is represented by a component in this workspace. The full interactive map appears in Act 11. Open the workspace map Architecture, not product specifications This is a local relationship diagram, not a measurement of any model’s speed, context window, or product features. The durable point is structural: a language model becomes useful only when surrounding software supplies context, I/O, and checks. My one quarrel with the picture is the CPU box itself, and it is the reason for the narrowing. Drawing the LLM as the CPU invites you to read the diagram as a portrait of the model. It is not. It is a portrait of everything the model is missing. Line up what Act 2 established against what a processor lacks and the correspondence is almost embarrassing. The machine needs Supplied by Somewhere to hold what it is working on The context window: small, fast, wiped between runs Storage that outlives the run Files, databases, memory directories Input and output Tools, the only way anything reaches the world A clock The harness, which knows what time it is Something to decide what runs, and whether it may The agent loop and its permission system None of that is in the model. All of it is in the machinery around it, and every item is something a person wrote and can change. The mechanism: it asks, it never acts The mechanism is easy to miss when one of these systems appears to edit a file. The model cannot run anything. When it “runs a command”, what actually happens is that it emits text in a structured form: a request naming a tool and its arguments. That request goes to the harness. The harness decides whether to honour it, executes it, captures the output, and appends that output to the conversation. Then the whole enlarged conversation goes back to the model, which reads the result and decides what to ask for next. Predict, request, execute, append, repeat. That loop is the whole of what the word agent denotes. Anthropic’s working definition is worth borrowing because it is unusually plain: agents are “systems where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage, maintaining control over how they accomplish tasks”, as against workflows, where those steps are “orchestrated through predefined code paths”. 3 The distinction is about who chooses the next step, not about how clever the system is. The interleaving of reasoning and acting (think a little, do a little, look at what came back, think again) was studied under the name ReAct well before any of this reached products. 4 Nearly every coding agent you can use today is a descendant of that shape. Below is a recorded loop from this website’s own session logs. Step through it. Watch which side of the exchange ever does anything. Loading the recorded trace… The three-step trace is the entire mechanism with nothing else in the way. The model wanted to know the working directory. It could not look. It asked, something else looked, and the answer arrived as text it then read back. The longer trace is the same mechanism doing something that feels much more capable, and it shows the cost. To look at a web page (something you do in a fraction of a second, continuously, without noticing) the model must ask for a scroll, then ask for a screenshot, then ask to read the resulting image file. Three round trips, repeated for each screenful. It is not seeing the page. It is requesting narrow slices of evidence about the page and assembling a belief from them. The pattern generalises. Everything these systems appear to do decomposes into asking for evidence and asking for effects. The apparent capability is a property of what they are permitted to ask for, which is to say a property of the harness. Why this makes the harness the interesting object Once the loop is visible, apparent mysteries become ordinary engineering questions. Why can one assistant edit your files while another cannot? Because someone gave the first a file-editing tool. Why does one stop and ask before deleting something? Because the harness classified that request as needing confirmation. Why does one seem to know your project’s conventions? Because something put them in the context before the model ever saw the question. Why does one degrade badly on a long task? Because the loop keeps appending, the context window is finite, and something has to decide what to drop. None of those are questions about intelligence. They are questions about wiring. Every one of them has an answer you can inspect, and usually change. The next question is concrete: what is actually inside one of these harnesses? References Karpathy, A. (2023). Post on X, 28 September 2023. x.com/karpathy/status/1707437820045062561 , the LLM-as-operating-system framing. Cited as the popularisation rather than the source of record; a social-media post is a weak citation, and the idea has been articulated more systematically elsewhere. Karpathy, A. (2023). “LLM OS” diagram, post on X, 11 November 2023. x.com/karpathy/status/1723140519554105733 , source of Figure 1, reproduced for commentary. Rights in the diagram remain with the author; it is not covered by this site’s CC BY licence. Anthropic (2024). “Building Effective Agents”, 19 December 2024. anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents , source of the agent/workflow definitions quoted above. A vendor engineering post, not peer-reviewed; used here for its definitions, which are clear and widely adopted. Yao, S., Zhao, J., Yu, D., Du, N., Shafran, I., Narasimhan, K., & Cao, Y. (2022). “ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models.” arXiv:2210.03629; published at ICLR 2023. arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629 ← Even the Chat Box Is a Harness Anatomy of a Coding Agent →

title: Anatomy of a Coding Agent - Adrian Mag
desc: The tools, permissions, context management, persistence, and subagents that make up a coding-agent harness.
text: Anatomy of a Coding Agent Movement II · The harness 1 Box 2 Kernel 3 Chat box 4 CPU 5 Anatomy 6 AGENTS.md 7 Skills 8 Hooks 9 Tools 10 Context 11 Orchestration S Summary Act 5 Current as of July 2026 The same model sits behind the chat box and behind the tool that refactors a codebase overnight. If the processor is identical, the difference has to be somewhere else. It lies in a visible list of components, each of which someone decided to build. This act is an inventory, the least conceptual part of the series and possibly the most useful. Once you can name the components you can ask which ones you have. Tools: the entire surface between the model and the world Everything a model can affect, it affects through a tool. There is no other channel. A coding harness typically exposes something like: read a file, write a file, edit part of a file, list files matching a pattern, search file contents, run a shell command, fetch a URL, search the web. The list is deliberately mundane. There is no “understand the codebase” tool. What looks like understanding is a great many small requests (search for this, read that, look at the file the first search pointed to) assembled in the loop from Act 4. The capability is emergent from a boring inventory plus a lot of round trips. Granularity matters. A harness that offers only “run a shell command” can technically do everything, since editing a file is a shell command. But then every action arrives as an opaque string, and the harness cannot tell a harmless search from a destructive delete. Promoting an action to its own tool, with named arguments, is what makes it possible to gate it, display it properly, log it, or run several in parallel. That trade-off is Act 9. Permissions: which requests are honoured The harness sits between the request and the execution, so it can refuse. Typically: some tools run freely, some require confirmation, some are forbidden outright, and the rules can vary by directory or by argument. This is the first component that is a safety mechanism rather than a capability. It does not depend on the model’s cooperation. A model that has been talked into something by a malicious web page still only emits a request , and that request still hits the same gate. Act 8 is about what follows from that, and about how much less it guarantees than it first appears. Context management: deciding what the model is allowed to know The loop appends. Every request and every result joins the transcript, and the transcript is re-sent every turn. On a long task it will outgrow the context window. Not might. Will. So something must decide what to drop: summarise the middle, discard old tool output, keep the current file and forget the one from an hour ago. Those decisions are invisible, unglamorous, and they largely determine whether a long session stays coherent. Act 10 is entirely about this. Subagents: buying a second context window A harness can start a second loop with its own fresh context, hand it a narrow task, and receive only the answer. The expensive intermediate reading never enters the main transcript. This is a resource-management move rather than a clever trick: the scarce resource is context, and a subagent is how you spend someone else’s. Persistence: what survives the session Files on disk, notes the model was told to keep, a project instruction file read at startup. The model has no memory; a harness can give it a filing cabinet. Acts 6 and 10 cover the two ends of this. The comparison Same processor. Different machine. Component Consumer chat box Coding harness Tools Few, generic: often web search and a sandboxed interpreter A dozen or more, aimed at a filesystem and a shell Reaches your machine No Yes. That is the entire point Permissions Fixed by the vendor Configurable by you, per tool and per project Context management Automatic, opaque Configurable, inspectable, often noisy about it Subagents No Commonly Persistence Vendor-managed memory, if any Files, instruction files, notes you can read and edit You can change Your wording Nearly all of the above The last row is the one that matters, and it is the hinge of this series. In a chat box, the only variable under your control is how you phrase things, which is why prompt-wording advice became a genre. In a harness, the wording is one small input among many, and it is usually not the one that is limiting you. An honest caveat Bigger is not better by default. Every component above is a place to misconfigure something: a tool nobody needed, a permission rule that fires on the wrong thing (Act 8 has a real example of exactly that), a context strategy that discards the thing you were about to need, a subagent dispatched for work that would have taken one search. A large harness is not a more powerful assistant. It is a more powerful instrument , which is a different claim, and it includes the possibility of using it badly. The remaining acts take the components one at a time, cheapest first. Act 6 begins with a text file that the harness reads before doing anything else. ← The CPU and the Computer Steering by Text →

title: Steering by Text - Adrian Mag
desc: How AGENTS.md places repository-specific guidance in context, and why guidance is not enforcement.
text: Steering by Text Movement III · What you can change 1 Box 2 Kernel 3 Chat box 4 CPU 5 Anatomy 6 AGENTS.md 7 Skills 8 Hooks 9 Tools 10 Context 11 Orchestration S Summary Act 6 Current as of July 2026 The cheapest lever is a file that the harness reads and injects into context. It provides guidance, not enforcement, which is both its weakness and its strength. When I wanted an agent to stop treating every repository as the same repository, I added a text file. The file is called AGENTS.md . It is not a model, a plug-in, or a program. It is ordinary Markdown containing the facts and working agreements that would otherwise have to be repeated at the start of every conversation: where the real source lives, how to run the tests, what must never leave the machine, and what “finished” means here. A supporting harness finds the file and places its contents in the context it assembles for the model. That is the whole mechanism. Nothing is trained, and no weight inside the model changes. The machine from Acts 4 and 5 simply adds one more piece of text before asking the model what to do. What enters the context? Mechanism diagram AGENTS.md included Harness You are a coding agent working in this repository. AGENTS.md After editing a notes page, rebuild media/search-index.json. User Draft the next act of the series. The project rule is present as input to the model. The harness has not turned it into executable code. Use the button. With the file absent, the model receives the same task but loses the repository-specific fact. It might discover the search-index command by exploring. It might not. With the file present, the work begins with that fact already available. The file for this website The example below is not an idealised template. It is a verbatim snapshot of this website’s own AGENTS.md , screened for credentials, addresses, hostnames, and private material on 24 July 2026. Open it and read it as a working document. It is deliberately mundane. Adrian-Mag.github.io/AGENTS.md The website Page maps, cache busting, search indexing, and the site’s no-build setup. Open file A useful file answers some combination of five questions: Question What the file supplies Where am I? The purpose of the repository and the files that actually matter How is work done? Commands, environments, paths, and established workflows What is forbidden? Privacy boundaries, dangerous operations, and integrity rules Where should I look first? Living references, source inventories, and routing instructions How do I know I am finished? Builds, tests, regenerated assets, and other verification steps This is why a useful file looks more like an operations note than a personality prompt. “Be careful” does not identify a risk. “After editing any notes page, run python3 tools/build_search_index.py ” identifies an action, its trigger, and the artifact that should change. One can be checked. The other can only be admired. Which file applies? The filename is a convention interpreted by the harness, so the precise discovery rules are product features rather than properties of language models. They have to be dated. Codex behaviour, checked 24 July 2026 Codex reads an instruction chain once at the start of a run. It first checks the user’s Codex home, then walks from the project root down to the working directory. A file closer to the work appears later in the combined instructions and overrides broader guidance where they conflict. Empty files are skipped; the default combined project-instruction limit is 32 KiB. Other harnesses may discover or order instruction files differently. 1 Nesting lets a repository say “run the test suite before stopping” at its root, while a directory containing slow numerical experiments can give the exact command and resource limits that apply only there. The reader gets a route from general to specific instead of one enormous manual for every possible task. Guidance is not enforcement The file in the panel is text. The harness may give it a privileged place in context, but no separate process watches the model and forces the search index to be rebuilt. The instruction can be ambiguous. It can conflict with something more specific. It can be truncated from an overgrown instruction chain. The model can simply make a mistake. The weakness of AGENTS.md is that it changes the evidence and instructions available to a probabilistic system rather than the laws of the computer around it. Writing “never stage the private control overlay” is useful, but it does not alter the Git index. Writing “run the tests” does not make a failing test prevent a commit. The same property is also a strength. The file costs almost nothing to create, can be reviewed in the same pull request as the code, travels with the repository, and changes on the next run. You do not need to build a tool or retrain a model to teach the harness that this website has no build step. Use text to state intent, context, and working practice. Use settings, permissions, hooks, tests, and sandboxes for properties that must hold even when the model is confused. Official Codex guidance makes the same separation, recommending that project guidance be paired with enforcing infrastructure such as hooks, linters, and type checkers. 1 Act 8 will make that boundary concrete. Write the scar tissue The best rule usually begins with a mistake that actually happened. An agent edited a notes page and left the search index stale. The next sentence in AGENTS.md says exactly when and how to rebuild it. A command was run from the wrong directory, so the file records the correct working directory. A reviewer had to ask twice for source-grounded claims. The instruction becomes durable on the second occurrence. Start with those scars. Keep the file short enough to be read, concrete enough to be followed, and close enough to the relevant work to stay true. If a rule needs a page of explanation, point to that page. If it needs expertise, examples, scripts, and references that should load only for one kind of task, a flat instruction file has reached its limit. Act 7 examines that larger package: a skill. References OpenAI. “Custom instructions with AGENTS.md.” Codex documentation, checked 24 July 2026. learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/agents-md (official OpenAI documentation). Used for Codex’s current discovery, precedence, size-limit, and verification behaviour. These details are product-specific and date-stamped above. ← Anatomy of a Coding Agent Packaging Expertise →

title: Packaging Expertise - Adrian Mag
desc: How agent skills use progressive disclosure to load task-specific instructions, references, and scripts.
text: Packaging Expertise Movement III · What you can change 1 Box 2 Kernel 3 Chat box 4 CPU 5 Anatomy 6 AGENTS.md 7 Skills 8 Hooks 9 Tools 10 Context 11 Orchestration S Summary Act 7 Current as of July 2026 Progressive disclosure keeps a short description in the initial catalogue and loads the body on demand. Context is finite, and everything loaded competes with everything else. A small instruction file has a natural limit. One repository fact belongs in AGENTS.md . A detailed continuity procedure, a state validator, and the instructions for interpreting its result do not. Loading all of that before every task would make the model read a maintenance manual while it was trying to change one sentence. A skill is a way to put that material on a shelf and give the harness a good index card. The index card is designed to be cheap enough to show. The book comes down only when the task needs it. A directory, not a new intelligence In the open Agent Skills format, a skill is a directory with one required file: SKILL.md . Its frontmatter gives the skill a name and describes what it does and when it applies. The Markdown body contains the working instructions. Optional directories can hold scripts, references, templates, images, or other resources. 1 Nothing in that definition changes the model. A skill is not training, memory, or a new model capability. It is a package the harness knows how to discover and reveal. The useful idea is not the filename. It is progressive disclosure . How much of one skill enters context? Measured files · mechanism diagram 1. Session starts 2. Website task 3. Validate state Tier 1 Catalogue entry In context website-control docs/agent-docs/control/skills/website-control/SKILL.md Mandatory continuity and handoff workflow for every development, analysis, review, planning, resume, or handoff task in this worktree. 70 whitespace-delimited words in the full description Tier 2 SKILL.md instructions On disk # Website Control ... ## Start or resume 4. Run controlctl.py --repo . begin 5. If that check fails, stop and rebuild the notes ... ## Close or hand off 120 lines in the local skill body Tier 3 Bundled validator On disk scripts/validate_control.py Validate the local control pack without dependencies. Checks manifest, handoff applicability, private-path rules, and bootstrap wiring. 487 lines; invoked only when the workflow reaches validation The harness can see enough metadata to consider the skill. Its instructions and validator remain on disk. This panel is built from a real local skill used to maintain this website. The snippets and file counts were checked on 24 July 2026. The buttons show the documented loading mechanism; they are not a recorded conversation. Lines are an inspectable measure of the files, not a claim about their token count. At the first stage, the description has one job: help the harness decide whether this skill belongs in the task. A website task is a plausible match; an unrelated calculation is not. At the second stage, the body supplies the workflow. Only when the workflow reaches validation does the third component become useful. This is retrieval rather than compression. The missing text has not been squeezed into the description. It is absent from context until the harness or agent goes to fetch it. Open the working parts The control pack itself is intentionally local-only. These are screened teaching excerpts and a real run, published by request. Live handoff, state, and configuration records are not included. docs/agent-docs/control/skills/website-control/SKILL.md Selection metadata and workflow The exact catalogue frontmatter and the workflow that enters through controlctl.py --repo . begin . Open excerpt docs/agent-docs/control/skills/website-control/scripts/validate_control.py A script beside the instructions Selected source from the 487-line standard-library validator and its main check sequence. Open excerpt python3 …/controlctl.py --repo . begin Instructions become an action The actual entry command and its one-line structural result, captured 24 July 2026. Open record The description is a routing rule The description is not a miniature manual. It needs to say what the skill does and when to use it. In current Codex, the initial catalogue contains the name, description, and file path. The full body is loaded after explicit selection or when the task matches the description. 2 Implementations checked 24 July 2026 The three-tier shape comes from the open Agent Skills specification. Exact search paths, catalogue budgets, invocation controls, and context lifecycle are harness behaviour. The shared file format does not make any one client’s loading behaviour a law of language models. A vague description such as “helps with documents” saves words but destroys the signal used for routing. A useful description names the task, the relevant inputs, and the boundaries. It is closer to the label on a laboratory drawer than to the contents of the drawer. Automatic selection is still a model decision. A good skill can fail to trigger, or trigger for the wrong request. Most supporting harnesses also offer an explicit invocation for cases where the user wants certainty. Triggering and quality are separate tests: first ask whether the right tasks load the skill, then ask whether the loaded workflow improves the result. The body can carry a runnable procedure The website-control body does not put every check in its frontmatter. Its 120 lines say which state files matter, when to record a handoff, and when to invoke the local entry command that performs validation. The body is the bridge between a natural-language trigger and an actual command. Optional scripts let a skill package a repeatable calculation, validator, or converter beside the instructions. Here, the instructions say when to run the validator and how much to trust its result. The script checks structural facts deterministically. The agent must still run it through a tool, and the harness’s permissions still decide whether that request is honoured. A skill can explain a procedure and carry its implements; it does not bypass the machine around the model. The validator does not certify prose, citations, or visual quality. It checks only the control structure it was written to check. This division of labour is useful: prose tells the agent what the result means, while code makes a narrow, repeatable test harder to forget or improvise. The complete control pack remains local. The public page shows only safe excerpts needed to teach the pattern, not its live handoff, current-state, or configuration records. A skill can therefore bundle useful local machinery without turning every working file into public documentation. Choose the smallest durable lever If the need is... Put it in... A fact or rule that should accompany nearly every task in one repository AGENTS.md A reusable workflow with task-specific instructions, references, or scripts A skill A property that must hold even when the model ignores its instructions A hook, permission, test, or sandbox A new way to sense or change the world A tool A skill sits between the two. It is richer than one always-loaded instruction file and cheaper than putting an encyclopedia into every prompt. It packages the part of expertise that can be written down: the order of work, the questions to ask, the references to consult, the checks that catch familiar errors. A skill still asks the model to follow text. When that is not good enough, Act 8 moves from advice to interception. References Agent Skills. “Specification.” Checked 24 July 2026. agentskills.io/specification . Used for the shared directory format and the three progressive-disclosure tiers. OpenAI. “Build skills.” Codex documentation, checked 24 July 2026. learn.chatgpt.com/docs/build-skills . Used for current Codex catalogue, activation, and discovery behaviour. ← Steering by Text Mechanism, Not Trust →

title: Mechanism, Not Trust - Adrian Mag
desc: How hooks, sandboxes, and approvals move selected decisions outside a language model, with a recorded blocklist example.
text: Mechanism, Not Trust Movement III · What you can change 1 Box 2 Kernel 3 Chat box 4 CPU 5 Anatomy 6 AGENTS.md 7 Skills 8 Hooks 9 Tools 10 Context 11 Orchestration S Summary Act 8 Current as of July 2026 When text is not enough, a hook can intercept an action whether or not the model cooperates. The example here is a blocklist: it over-blocks and has gaps. A mechanism without a stated threat model is marketing. Suppose an instruction says, “Do not edit the generated search index directly.” That is useful guidance. It can also be forgotten, displaced by a long conversation, or ignored by a model that has found what it thinks is a quicker route. A hook changes the location of the decision. Instead of asking the model to remember a rule, the harness pauses at a lifecycle event and runs ordinary code. For a tool call, that code can inspect the proposed input before the tool runs and return a verdict. The model proposes; the mechanism decides. A real hook, built for this page The exhibit below comes entirely from this public website repository. It protects media/search-index.json , a generated file that should normally be replaced by running python3 tools/build_search_index.py . The policy is deliberately small: permit that exact rebuild command, deny every other Bash command containing the protected path, and allow everything else. PreToolUse interceptor Recorded protocol probes Approved rebuild Direct delete Safe read Constructed path 1 · model Proposes Bash → 2 · harness Runs PreToolUse → 3 · verdict Allow python3 tools/build_search_index.py ALLOW The one explicitly approved way to replace the generated file. These outcomes were recorded on 21 July 2026. A recorder sent four documented PreToolUse payloads to the exact hook process on standard input and captured its output. It classified the candidate commands but never executed them. One additional ephemeral Codex session produced a live denial: the harmless rg command in the third button was stopped before it ran. Codex-specific, checked 24 July 2026. The event name, JSON fields, discovery rules, and denial response shown here belong to the current Codex hook interface. They are harness behaviour, not a property of a language model or a universal agent protocol. 1 Open the mechanism The cards contain the complete public artifacts. The first is the policy code. The second is the wiring that asks Codex to run it before Bash. The third is a screened extract of the live denial. They are text, not screenshots, so the exact rule and event can be inspected. figure_generation/harness/hook_demo/public_asset_guard.py The complete policy A small executable blocklist with one protected path and one approved rebuild. Open file figure_generation/harness/hook_demo/hooks.json The complete wiring A Bash matcher connected to the policy at the PreToolUse event. Open file media/research/harness/hook-live-denial.txt The intercepted event The requested command, Codex router event, model-facing report, and screening note. Open recording The threat model is the product This hook is designed to reduce one narrow failure: an agent accidentally touching a generated file through a plainly written Bash command. It is not designed to stop a hostile program. The two right-hand buttons make the boundary visible. The safe read is a false positive. It contains the protected path, so the hook blocks it even though rg would not write anything. The constructed-path example is a false negative. The full filename never appears as one string, so the hook allows a command whose apparent intent is deletion. That command was only classified by the recorder; it was not executed. More careful parsing could shrink both errors, but it would not turn this particular hook into a complete security boundary. In current Codex, some specialised paths may bypass the normal hook path, hosted tools such as web search are not covered, project hooks depend on trust, and malformed responses using unsupported fields can fail to block. 1 Matching command hooks for the same event can also run concurrently, so one hook is not a global ordering mechanism for all other hooks. The defensible claim is narrower: for an event the harness exposes, valid code can make a deterministic decision outside the model. Permissions are not just another hook A hook is user-supplied lifecycle code. A sandbox is an enforced boundary around what spawned commands may read, write, or reach over the network. An approval policy decides when the agent must stop and ask before crossing that boundary. Current Codex documentation treats these as two controls that work together. 2 Hook Custom policy at a named event. Flexible, inspectable, and only as complete as its matcher, code, response, trust, and event coverage. Sandbox and approval Harness controls around execution. The sandbox constrains the command; the approval flow mediates requests to cross the chosen boundary. The three levers are distinct. AGENTS.md puts durable advice into context. A skill reveals a detailed procedure when it is relevant. A hook or permission boundary moves a decision out of prose. None of them changes the model. Each changes the machine around it. title: New Senses: How a Capability Becomes Available - Adrian Mag
desc: How tool descriptions, schemas, handlers, and MCP connections make a capability available to a model.
text: New Senses: How a Capability Becomes Available Movement III · What you can change 1 Box 2 Kernel 3 Chat box 4 CPU 5 Anatomy 6 AGENTS.md 7 Skills 8 Hooks 9 Tools 10 Context 11 Orchestration S Summary Act 9 Current as of July 2026 A tool definition is an interface contract, and its description helps the model decide when to use it. Four pressures justify promoting a command to a dedicated tool: gating, rendering, auditing, and parallelisation. A short MCP section closes the act with one recorded invocation. A model can ask for a capability only if the harness tells it that the capability exists. Usually that introduction is a compact definition: a name, a description, and a schema for the arguments. The implementation remains outside the model. What enters context is the interface. A tool definition is more than API paperwork. It is a contract between three parties. The model sees what it may request. The harness learns how to validate and route the request. The implementation promises what it will return. If the contract is vague, all three can disagree while every component is behaving exactly as specified. A real tool for this website The tool below was built inside this public repository for this act. inspect_site_page accepts one repository-relative HTML path and returns a page title, meta description, heading outline, and local CSS and JavaScript dependencies. It cannot edit a file, return the page's body prose, inspect another file type, or follow a path outside the repository. One contract, three visible layers Explanatory view of real contract Identity Selection Structure name + title inspect_site_page A distinct, action-shaped identity gives the model and router an unambiguous handle. model request → schema validation → handler → structured result The middle button contains the exact 50-word description in the public definition. It states the job, the circumstances in which it is useful, and four things it must not be used for. That text is load-bearing because it is part of what the model receives when deciding whether the capability fits a request. Current OpenAI function-calling guidance likewise defines a description as explaining when and how to use a function, and recommends stating purpose, output shape, and when not to use it. 1 The schema constrains the input. It says that page is required, that extra properties are not accepted, and that the input must look like a relative .html path. The handler then performs the security-relevant check that a regular expression cannot: it resolves the path and verifies that the result still lies under the repository root. The handler, actually called Recorded 21 July 2026 Inspect Act 8 Try ../outside.html {"page":"pages/research/overview/harness/act-8.html"} EXIT 0 Mechanism, Not Trust - Adrian Mag 6 headings · 4 stylesheets · 3 scripts A recorder launched the complete public handler as a subprocess for both inputs. The first call parsed the real Act 8 file. The second was rejected with outside_repository before any outside path was read. Open the artifacts to inspect the complete contract, the gating code, and the full capture. figure_generation/harness/tool_demo/tool.json The complete contract Description, input and output schemas, and behavioural hints in one public definition. Open file figure_generation/harness/tool_demo/inspect_site_page.py The path gate The complete validation function that rejects absolute, non-HTML, outside, and missing paths. Open function media/research/harness/tool-demo.json The complete recording Both inputs, exit codes, structured responses, and the files that produced them. Open recording When a command deserves a dedicated tool A general shell is an excellent starting point. It already knows how to combine small programs, so there is little value in wrapping every command. Promotion becomes useful when repetition reveals a boundary that deserves a name. Four pressures are especially practical: Gate Constrain paths, fields, actions, or permissions before implementation code runs. Render Turn a messy source into the small structured result the next step actually needs. Audit Give repeated work a stable request and response shape that can be logged and tested. Parallelize Split independent units into separate calls that a harness can schedule concurrently. This exhibit meets the first three grounds for promotion. The path check gates access. The parser renders HTML as a compact outline. The schema and recorder make calls auditable. A harness could issue independent page inspections concurrently, but this single handler does not itself run work in parallel. A dedicated tool is not automatically safer. Its description can be misleading, its schema can admit dangerous inputs, and its implementation can ignore both. Even the read-only and idempotent annotations in this contract are hints. The stable MCP specification tells clients not to trust tool annotations unless the server itself is trusted. 2 Enforcement still belongs in code and in the harness boundary around it. MCP: a standard connection, not another model Tool definitions solve the local interface problem. The Model Context Protocol standardizes how an application connects to external providers of tools and context. In the stable 2025-11-25 architecture, a host is the LLM application coordinating the experience and security boundaries. A client inside that host maintains an isolated connection to one server. The server exposes a focused set of capabilities. 3 Host LLM application coordinates clients, context, consent contains → Client one connection speaks the protocol to one server connects → Server capability provider publishes tools, resources, prompts There is one real MCP-mediated invocation already in this series. On 18 July 2026, while this website was being inspected, a Claude Code session requested the Playwright screenshot tool and the harness returned the saved viewport. The exact request and result below are reused from the screened Act 4 trace. MODEL REQUEST mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__browser_take_screenshot argument: ai-page-5.png Open the recorded request and result Protocol and product boundary, checked 24 July 2026. Host, client, server, tool schema, and connection behaviour above refer to the stable MCP 2025-11-25 specification. The long mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__... name is product-side namespacing visible in this particular trace, not a naming format required by MCP. A release candidate targeting 28 July 2026 was already available when this page was rechecked, but /specification/latest still resolved to 2025-11-25, so the candidate was not yet the stable specification. 4 None of this changes the model. The definition makes a capability legible, the handler implements it, and the harness validates the request and returns the result. MCP gives hosts and capability providers a shared way to connect those pieces. The new sense belongs to the machine around the model. title: The Instrument - Adrian Mag
desc: The files, skills, hooks, tools, checks, and handoffs that turn a language model into an inspectable instrument.
text: The Instrument Closing 1 Box 2 Kernel 3 Chat box 4 CPU 5 Anatomy 6 AGENTS.md 7 Skills 8 Hooks 9 Tools 10 Context 11 Orchestration S Summary Summary Current as of July 2026 The machinery exists to support verification and audit while making its limits visible. The model is not the whole machine. It predicts the next token from the context it receives. The harness decides what that context contains, which tools may be called, what checks run, where results are stored, and whether a later session can recover the work. A bare chat box can feel brittle while a carefully built workspace feels capable because the latter supplies ordinary machinery: instructions, files, retrieval, permissions, tools, validation, and a loop that puts the result of one action into the next request. The levers, in order Need Workspace lever What it cannot promise Persistent guidance AGENTS.md That the model follows every word A reusable procedure A skill with instructions and optional scripts Permission to bypass the harness A rule that must run Hook, sandbox, test, or approval Complete security without a threat model A new capability A tool contract and handler Correct selection or correct results by itself Continuity Files, plans, evidence, and a checked handoff Perfect memory or an unchanging summary Build an instrument, not a story The public examples in this series come from this website workspace: instructions, a skill and validator, a hook policy, a tool handler, recorded checks, and the relationships between them. They are useful precisely because they can be inspected, tested, or corrected. The interactive map gathers that structure on one page. Explore the workspace’s agentic structure Use the smallest lever that makes the behaviour legible. Add a file before a framework. Add a test before a second agent. Add a tool only when a named operation needs a contract. Add orchestration only when the graph buys a boundary, evidence, or parallelism that a single loop cannot. The honest limit None of this turns a language model into an authority. It can still misunderstand a request, select the wrong file, invent a claim, or follow a plausible route through the wrong graph. The safeguard is a design that leaves evidence behind: inspectable source, narrow checks, explicit uncertainty, and a human who can stop or reverse the change. That is the machine around the model. Not a promise that the model will be right, but an instrument for finding out when it is not. ← Orchestration Series overview →

title: The Machine Around the Model - Adrian Mag
desc: How agentic AI systems actually work: what the model is, what the harness around it does, and which parts of that harness you can build or change.
text: The Machine Around the Model The language model is the CPU. Almost everything that makes it useful is the computer built around it. 1 Box 2 Kernel 3 Chat box 4 CPU 5 Anatomy 6 AGENTS.md 7 Skills 8 Hooks 9 Tools 10 Context 11 Orchestration S Summary Notes on AI in Practice What this series is If you have used a chatbot, been unimpressed, and concluded the technology is oversold, this series is written for you. That experience was real. Its usual cause has changed. The models did get better. Routine, obvious arithmetic failures are less representative than they were. Bad experiences did not disappear, but they now often come from elsewhere. A stronger model can still fail if it is asked the wrong question, if the surrounding situation is missing, or if the harness gives it no way to check its own work. The same question can have many correct answers depending on context, and by default a model has almost none of it. Expecting a bare model to handle a hard problem consistently is a mistake on our side of the screen. The capability has to be harnessed, and the machinery that harnesses it is what this series is about. The series has eleven acts in three movements, running from the chat box everyone knows to machinery a user can build and change. I wrote it while learning the subject, using examples from a real setup. The exhibits are of two kinds. Some are real artifacts: screenshots, recorded runs, and files from this workspace, shown as they are. Most of the interactive panels are illustrative: built to show a mechanism faithfully, with invented particulars. Each one is labelled on the page, so you always know which kind you are looking at. Movement I · What you are actually talking to Act 1: The Box Everyone Knows . Start where the reader is: text in, text out, magic between. Name the common experience honestly: confident nonsense, and the conclusion that the technology is oversold. Promise: that experience was real, and it measured the scaffolding, not the intelligence. Act 2: Inside the Kernel . What an LLM is: a function from a token sequence to a distribution over next tokens. Name the two meanings of “layer” (transformer layers inside, harness layers outside), then leave the inside alone. The model has no memory, no filesystem, no clock, no ability to act. Act 3: Even the Chat Box Is a Harness . The hinge of the series. A chat product is already several systems around the model. The reveal: the API is stateless, so the whole conversation is re-sent every turn. “Memory” is an illusion assembled by software. Argued from necessity, not from undocumented internals. Movement II · The harness Act 4: The CPU and the Computer . The metaphor formalised, then the mechanism: the model never executes anything. It emits a request; the harness executes and appends the result; the loop repeats. That loop is what “agent” means. Act 5: Anatomy of a Coding Agent . Concrete inventory of a large harness: tool suite, permission system, context management, subagents, session persistence. Same kernel, different machine. The capability gap is an engineering gap. Movement III · What you can change Act 6: Steering by Text . The cheapest lever is a file that the harness reads and injects into context. It provides guidance, not enforcement, which is both its weakness and its strength. Act 7: Packaging Expertise . Progressive disclosure: a short description sits in context permanently; the body loads on demand. Context is a scarce, paid resource, and everything loaded competes with everything else. Act 8: Mechanism, Not Trust . Where text stops being enough. Deterministic interception that runs whether or not the model cooperates. Includes the honest limitation: this is a blocklist, it over-blocks, and it has gaps. A mechanism without a stated threat model is marketing. Act 9: New Senses: How a Capability Becomes Available . Tool definitions as interface contracts, including why descriptions are load-bearing. The act gives four reasons to promote a command to a dedicated tool: gating, rendering, auditing, and parallelisation. It closes with a short MCP section and one recorded invocation. Act 10: What It Knows . Context as the budget everything competes for. Retrieval as context assembly, not magic. Memory as files. Compaction, and why long sessions degrade. Act 11: Orchestration . When one loop is not enough: graphs, subagent delegation, who supplies the harness versus who supplies the deployment. With the counterweight: most tasks do not need this. Closing Summary: The Instrument . What the machinery is for, where its limits lie, and which problems it still handles badly.
