title: What are Linear Inversions and Inferences?
desc: An accessible introduction to linear inversions and inferences in seismology, with math rendered using MathJax.
text: What are Linear Inversions and Inferences? Image credit: earthhow.com Without Maths With Maths We can't dig a hole to the center of the Earth. In fact, we've only ever drilled a few kilometers down—just a tiny scratch on the surface. So how do we know anything about what's happening thousands of kilometers below our feet? This is one of the big questions in geophysics, the science that studies the physical properties of the Earth. And one of the cleverest ways we explore the deep Earth is through a method called seismic tomography . It's kind of like taking an X-ray or a CT scan of the planet, using waves from earthquakes instead of light or radiation. But there's a problem: we can only measure what happens at the surface. We record how fast earthquake waves arrive, how they travel, and how they change. But we can't see directly what's inside. So scientists work backwards from the measurements to figure out what the inside of the Earth must be like. To do that, we use two powerful ideas: linear inversion and linear inference . They sound similar, but they are actually quite different. Linear inversion is like trying to solve a mystery by building a complete picture of what happened. Scientists use the data from the surface to guess what kind of internal structure would cause waves to behave the way they do. The goal is to find one possible model of the Earth's interior that fits all the measurements and assumptions we have. Of course, there may be more than one model that works—so inversions often need us to make subjective choices to get to a final, unique, picture. Linear inference , on the other hand, doesn't try to build the whole picture. Instead, it focuses on answering a specific question. For example: "What's the average temperature under this region?" or "How deep is this particular boundary?" Even if we can't tell exactly what's inside, we might still be able to say something useful about one key property. This is what inference does—it looks for reliable answers to specific questions, even when the full story remains uncertain. To put it simply: inversion tries to reconstruct the full puzzle; inference tries to answer a question without needing every piece . Both of these methods are essential for exploring our planet. They help us learn about how Earth works—from the movement of continents, to where earthquakes happen, to how heat flows through the deep interior. Even though we can't go there ourselves, we can still learn a lot by listening carefully to what the Earth tells us. We cannot directly sample the deep Earth beyond a few kilometres, yet seismic waves generated by earthquakes or controlled sources traverse the whole planet and are recorded at the surface. Recovering a description of the interior from these surface records is therefore an inverse problem. Below we outline the logical steps and the key mathematical facts you need to understand the difference between inversion and inference , and the practical remedies used to stabilize solutions. This discussion places the emphasis on the continuous (function-space) viewpoint while remaining accessible to practitioners. Model and data (function-space viewpoint) A natural and physically faithful perspective is to treat the Earth as a continuum: the model \(m\) is a function (e.g. a velocity field, density, or elastic-parameter field) belonging to a model space \(\mathcal{M}\). In practice \(\mathcal{M}\) is chosen as a separable Banach space or separable Hilbert space (for example, an \(L^2\) or Sobolev space) that encodes the regularity and boundary behaviour expected of the physical parameter: $$m \in \mathcal{M} \quad\text{(function-space model)}.$$ The measurements collected at the surface are finite in number: $$\mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_d} \quad\text{(observed travel times, amplitudes, waveforms, \dots)}.$$ Between models and data there exists a mapping \(G\) that we call the forward operator . In this document we will assume that \(G\) is linear and bounded. Mathematically, we write: $$\mathbf{d} = G(m) + \boldsymbol{\eta}, \qquad G : \mathcal{M} \to \mathbb{R}^{N_d},$$ where \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\) denotes measurement and modelling error. Inversion vs inference (practical meaning) Both inversion and inference can be formulated either deterministically or probabilistically. The essential difference lies in the object of interest . In both cases we adopt a reference model \(\bar{m}\in\mathcal{M}\): the model taken to generate the data under our chosen physical idealisation. This is a working assumption—not a claim that reality has a unique, exact representative inside \(\mathcal{M}\). Inversion. The goal of an inversion is to estimate this model \(\bar{m}\). Because a finite dataset rarely pins \(\bar{m}\) down uniquely, in practice an inversion returns a regularized representative (deterministic view) or a posterior distribution over models (probabilistic view), rather than \(\bar{m}\) exactly. Inference. The goal of an inference is to constrain one or more properties of this reference model \(\bar{m}\). More specifically, we define a property mapping \(\mathcal{T}:\mathcal{M} \to \mathcal{P}\) that acts on models to extract some property: $$p = \mathcal{T}(m).$$ These properties live in a property space \(\mathcal{P}\). The goal of an inference is to estimate the property of the reference model: $$\bar{p} = \mathcal{T}(\bar{m}).$$ Note that the two tasks are closely related: inversion can be used as a route to inference, but direct inference about \(\mathcal{T}(m)\) can be more robust and cheaper—especially when only a small set of properties is of interest. In both deterministic and probabilistic approaches the choice of regularizer or prior crucially affects stability and the interpretation of uncertainties. Why the continuous inverse problem is hard (ill-posedness) In the continuous setting three related difficulties typically arise: Non-uniqueness: the forward map \(G\) may have a nontrivial kernel, so many distinct functions \(m\in\mathcal{M}\) produce the same data \(\mathbf{d}\). Instability (unbounded inverse): even when a solution exists, the inverse mapping \(G^{-1}\) (from data space to model space) is often unbounded: arbitrarily small perturbations of the data can create large perturbations in the recovered model. This instability is a fundamental operator-theoretic effect in infinite dimensions. Modeling error and nonlinearity: the true physics is nonlinear and modelling simplifications (background approximations, incomplete physics) add bias that must be controlled in any interpretation.

title: About — Adrian Mag
desc: Learn about Adrian Mag's background, education, and research interests in seismology.
text: Background I am a PhD candidate in the Department of Earth Sciences at the University of Oxford, specializing in deep Earth seismic imaging. My research focuses on improving and developing tomography methods, primarily linear inversions and inferences. Most of my research focuses on linear inference methods rooted in the foundational work of Backus and Gilbert. The core philosophy of these approaches is to constrain properties of the true Earth model—rather than attempting to recover the model itself, which is often ill-posed due to non-uniqueness. The methods I use and develop emphasize a rigorous mathematical formulation of the inverse problem prior to its numerical solution. This includes a clear understanding of the functional spaces involved, the linear operators connecting them, and the nature of the constraints and assumptions underpinning the formulation. A central aspect of my work is examining the role of discretization in shaping the outcome of inversions, ensuring that it does not introduce spurious features or distort the interpretation. I place strong emphasis on making assumptions explicit, ensuring well-posedness, and carefully analyzing the mathematical structure of the problem. This approach is essential not only for producing interpretable and reliable inferences, but also for avoiding the risk of mistaking artefacts for geophysically meaningful structures. Research Interests Inverse and inference theory Sensitivity kernels and adjoint methods Computational seismology and numerical methods Deep Earth processes and core-mantle interactions Education PhD in Seismology (ongoing) University of Oxford (current) Supervisors Dr. Paula Koelemeijer — Website Dr. Christophe Zaroli — University page Dr. Andrew Walker — Website MSci Geophysics University College London Focus on theoretical studies Course load more inclined towards mathematics and physics (especially small-scale physics such as statistical physics, quantum mechanics, and particle physics) MSci Thesis: Explored the use of wavelet-based sparsity for regularizing geophysical inverse problems. Demonstrated that promoting sparsity in a wavelet basis (using L1 norm and proximal algorithms) can recover multi-scale Earth structures from seismic data, preserving small-scale features better than traditional smoothing regularizations. Applied the method to S-wave velocity inversion in the upper mantle, with synthetic and real data tests compared to standard techniques. Beyond Research Hiking is probably my oldest hobby. Growing up in Oradea, Romania, the mountains were never far away, so half-day hikes became a regular part of my life. I spent most of my time in the Piatra Craiului and Bihor Mountains—partly because they were close, but mostly because their karst landscapes are incredible. Thousands of caves, dozens of ravines, and narrow canyons give these modestly tall mountains a surprisingly dramatic character. It’s no wonder that hiking eventually led me to caving. I don’t have as much time for it these days, but whenever I go back home, I still try to explore a cave or two. Exploring caves in the Bihor Mountains About six years ago my sister received a telescope as a gift, and I quickly became interested in photographing the Moon through it. After many nights of struggling to line up my phone with the eyepiece, I finally decided to buy my first DSLR. That was my gateway into astrophotography. All the banner images on this website were captured with my camera and a simple astrophotography setup. Moon through my 200mm lens Soon after getting into astrophotography, I started taking my DSLR on hikes, and that naturally led me into landscape photography.
